title: Saying what something is, politely
meaning: です: ends a noun or adjective sentence politely; after a noun it links the topic to what it is ("X is Y").
when: Use it at the end of a sentence whose main word is a noun or an adjective, when you are speaking politely: これは本です, 静かです, 高いです. It changes form for the negative (じゃありません), the past (でした) and questions (ですか). With a noun or a な-adjective it says what the topic is or what it is like; with an い-adjective it only makes the sentence polite.
why: です does two jobs at once. After a noun or a な-adjective it is what links the topic to its description, and its plain counterpart is だ: 学生です, 学生だ. It also marks the sentence as polite. An い-adjective is already a complete predicate on its own (高い already means "is expensive"), so です after it adds only politeness. That is why the tense and the negative go on the い-adjective itself: 高かったです, 高くないです, not 高いでした. です describes and identifies; it does not usually say that something exists or is present somewhere. "There is a cat" uses あります／います, not です.

formation.note: Past: でした. Question: add か, as in 学生ですか.

formation.form: Noun / な-adjective + じゃありません
formation.note: Also ではありません, which sounds more formal, and じゃないです, which is very common in speech. Past negative: じゃありませんでした / じゃなかったです.
Tense and negation go on the adjective: 高かったです, 高くないです (or 高くありません).

examples.reading: これはわたしのかばんです。

examples.english: This is my bag.

examples.romaji: tanaka-san wa gakusei ja arimasen.

examples.reading: きのうはあめでした。
examples.romaji: kinō wa ame deshita.

examples.reading: このへやはしずかです。

mistake.wrong: 昨日は楽しいでした。
mistake.problem: 楽しい is an い-adjective, so it carries its own past tense. でした is the past of です after a noun or a な-adjective, not after an い-adjective.
mistake.right: 昨日は楽しかったです。

distinguish_from.note: です says what something is or is like (これはペンです). ～があります says that a thing exists or is somewhere (ペンがあります).
To say that a person or animal is present somewhere, use ～がいます (庭に猫がいます). です is not a verb of existence, though it can identify where a known person is (先生は職員室です).
でしょう is a guess built on the same ending: 雨です states it, 雨でしょう says it is probably so.

review.note: Left out on purpose: sentences where です stands in for a verb in context (僕はコーヒーです when ordering, 田中さんは会議室です for 'is in the meeting room'). They are natural but would blur the 'describes, does not say where' line; the entry says 'does not usually' to leave room. Please confirm the relative formality given for ではありません / じゃありません / じゃないです is stated as a tendency, not a rule.

reviews.note: The OJG-0010 distinction is too absolute: です can identify someone's location, as in 先生は職員室です. Replace the note with: "To say that a person or animal is present somewhere, use ～がいます (庭に猫がいます). です is not an existential verb, though it can identify a known person's location (先生は職員室です)."
The explanation, formation, examples, and contrasts are accurate.

title: Also, too, and not … either
meaning: も adds a word as one more case of what was said: "also", "too"; with a negative verb, "not … either".
when: Use it on a word to say the same thing is true of it as well: 私も学生です, "I am a student too". With a negative it gives "not … either". AもBも says "both A and B" (or "neither A nor B" with a negative). Forms such as 何も and だれも combine with a negative predicate to mean "nothing" and "nobody": 何も食べません, "I don't eat anything". Another particle can come before も to mark the word’s role: どこにも行きません means “I don’t go anywhere”, with に marking the destination; どこも行きません is also used, especially in conversation.
why: も says "this one as well": it adds the word it follows to something already said or understood. So it goes directly on the word that is "also" true, and moving it changes the meaning: 私もコーヒーを飲みます is "I too drink coffee", and 私はコーヒーも飲みます is "I drink coffee too (as well as other things)". In the ordinary additive use taught here, も replaces は, が and を (not はも, がも). をも also occurs for emphasis, especially in written Japanese. After other particles, も is added on: 東京にも, 友だちとも. With 何 and だれ and a negative predicate, も gives "not a single one": 何も, だれも. Another particle can come before も to mark the word’s role: どこにも行きません means “I don’t go anywhere”, with に marking the destination; どこも行きません is also used, especially in conversation. いつも is a fixed expression meaning "always" or "usually", with either a positive or a negative predicate.

formation.note: In the ordinary additive use, replaces は, が or を: 私も, 本も. をも also occurs for emphasis, mostly in writing.
に, で, と, から and others stay: 日曜日にも, 友だちとも.

formation.form: Noun A + も + Noun B + も
formation.note: "Both A and B"; with a negative verb, "neither A nor B".
何も～ません "nothing", だれも～ません "nobody"; another particle can come first to mark the word’s role: どこにも行きません (どこも行きません is also used, especially in conversation). いつも "always" is a fixed expression.

mistake.wrong: 私はも学生です。
mistake.problem: も replaces は; the two are not used together. Put も directly on the word that is "also" true.
mistake.right: 私も学生です。

distinguish_from.note: Both can go on the topic. は sets it up, often in contrast with others; も says it is one more case of what was already said.
AとB lists items together; AもBも stresses that the same is true of each, "both A and B".

review.note: Not covered: も after a number or amount for emphasis (三時間も, 'as much as three hours'), and をも in formal writing. Question: is the statement that も 'replaces を' fine at this level, given that をも exists in written style?

reviews.note: Two claims need qualification. (1) The prohibition on stacking も with を is overstated: をも occurs in contemporary Japanese, particularly for emphatic 'even'. Write: "In the ordinary additive use taught here, も replaces は, が and を. をも also occurs for emphasis, especially in written Japanese." (2) 'Question word + も + negative verb' is not a general rule meaning 'not any': いつも retains its 'always/usually' meaning with negative predicates too. Replace this rule in when, why and formation with: "Forms such as 何も and だれも combine with a negative predicate to mean 'nothing' and 'nobody'. Some require another particle, as in どこにも行きません, 'I don't go anywhere'. いつも is a fixed expression meaning 'always/usually', with either a positive or a negative predicate."

The statements that some question words “need another particle first,” illustrated by どこにも行きません, overstate the requirement. どこも行きません is also natural, especially in conversation. In when, why, and the final formation note, replace this claim with: “Another particle can come before も to mark the word’s role: どこにも行きません means ‘I don’t go anywhere.’ Here に marks the destination; どこも行きません is also used, especially in conversation.”
The explanations, formation, examples, readings, romaji, mistake correction, and distinctions are accurate. The meaning and N5 placement are appropriate.

title: Where an action happens, and what it is done with
meaning: で marks the setting or the means of an action: where it happens, or with what, by what, or in what language.
when: Use it for the place where an action happens (図書館で勉強します), the tool or means (はしで食べます, バスで行きます), the language (日本語で話します), and a total or a way of doing something counted in people (全部で千円, 一人で行きます).
why: で marks the setting an action happens in, or what the action is carried out with: the frame around the action, not its goal. That is why a place takes で when something is done there, and に when something simply is there: 部屋で勉強します, but 部屋に猫がいます. Verbs of existing and staying, such as ある, いる and 住む, normally take に. An event, though, is something that happens, so where it takes place takes で even with ある: パーティーは友だちの家であります. The means and tool uses follow from the same idea: バスで is "by way of the bus", and 日本語で is "by way of Japanese".

formation.note: Where the action happens.
はしで, 電車で, 日本語で.
全部で "altogether", 一人で "on my own", 二人で "the two of us".

examples.romaji: nihongo de hanashite kudasai.
examples.english: Please speak in Japanese.

examples.reading: ぜんぶでせんえんです。
examples.romaji: zenbu de sen'en desu.
examples.english: That's 1,000 yen altogether.

mistake.wrong: 図書館に勉強します。
mistake.problem: Studying is an action, and the library is where it happens, so the place takes で. に would mark where something is, or where someone goes.
mistake.right: 図書館で勉強します。

distinguish_from.note: Place + に says where something is (公園に子どもがいます); place + で says where an action happens (公園で遊びます).
In バスで学校に行きます, で marks how you go and に／へ marks where you arrive.
友だちと marks who you do it with; 一人で says you do it alone.

review.note: Not covered: で for a cause with a noun (風邪で休みました), material (木で作る), and the て-form of だ (学生で、…), which looks the same but is not the particle. Should cause be added here at N5, or left to a later entry?

title: Where you are going
meaning: に／へ after a place with a verb of movement: where someone goes, comes, returns or arrives.
when: Use it on the destination of a verb of movement such as 行く, 来る, 帰る, 着く or 入る: 学校に行きます, 日本へ来ました. This entry covers only destinations; に's other uses (time, where something is, the person an action is aimed at) are OJG-0005. へ is written with the kana へ but pronounced え.
why: に marks the point something ends up at, and へ marks the direction something heads in. With 行く, 来る and 帰る the two describe the same trip, so in everyday use they are largely interchangeable: 京都に行きます and 京都へ行きます mean the same. The difference shows at the edges. With verbs of arriving or entering, such as 着く and 入る, に is the usual choice, because the point is reaching the place. Only へ can be followed by の to make a phrase that modifies a noun: 母への手紙, "a letter to my mother". Some learners mark the destination with を, as in English "visit Japan"; を with a verb of movement marks the ground you move along or leave, not where you arrive (OJG-0006).

formation.note: Focus on arriving at the place. Usual with 着く and 入る.
Focus on the direction. Pronounced え. へ + の modifies a noun: 日本への旅行.

examples.japanese: 明日、京都へ行きます。
examples.reading: あした、きょうとへいきます。
examples.romaji: ashita, kyōto e ikimasu.
examples.english: I'm going to Kyoto tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 友だちが私の部屋に来ました。
examples.reading: ともだちがわたしのへやにきました。
examples.romaji: tomodachi ga watashi no heya ni kimashita.
examples.english: A friend came to my room.

examples.japanese: 八時に駅に着きました。
examples.reading: はちじにえきにつきました。
examples.romaji: hachiji ni eki ni tsukimashita.
examples.english: I arrived at the station at eight.
examples.note: The first に marks the time (OJG-0005); the second marks the destination.

mistake.wrong: 日本を行きたいです。
mistake.problem: The place you go to is the destination, marked with に or へ. With a verb of movement, を marks the route you pass along or the place you leave.
mistake.right: 日本に行きたいです。

distinguish_from.note: に also marks times, the place where something exists, and recipients or other targets of an action. へ does not replace the time or existence uses, but with suitable verbs it can mark a recipient or addressee, as in 母へ手紙を送る. It cannot replace every に on a person: 友だちに会う, not 友だちへ会う.
With a verb of movement, を marks the ground covered or the place left (道を歩く, 家を出る), not the destination.
で marks how you travel (バスで); に／へ marks where you arrive.
In 買い物に行く, に marks the purpose of going, not a place.

review.note: The claim that に is 'the usual choice' with 着く and 入る is stated as a tendency; 部屋へ入る occurs. Please check it is not overstated. Also left out: へ in written headings and messages (～へ as 'to' on a gift or letter), and に／へ with 送る (sending to a place). Revised after review: the OJG-0005 note no longer says へ has only the direction use; it now allows へ for a recipient with suitable verbs (母へ手紙を送る).

title: A point in time, where something is, and who an action is aimed at
meaning: に pins something to a point: a time (三時に), the place where something is (机の上に), or the person an action is aimed at.
when: Use it for a clock time, date, month or year (七時に起きます); for the place where something or someone is, with ある, いる and 住む (机の上に本があります); and for the person or thing an action is directed at: who you give to, write to, phone, ask or meet (母に花をあげます, 友だちに会います). It also appears in rates such as 一日に三回, "three times a day". Destinations of movement (学校に行きます) are OJG-0004.
why: Across these uses, に fixes something to a point: a point in time, a spot where something sits, a person an action reaches. For time, に goes on times that are points on the calendar or the clock: 三時に, 五月に, 二〇二五年に. Relative-time expressions such as 今日, 明日, 昨日 and 来週 normally appear without に, because they already locate the time relative to now. Recurring-time expressions such as 毎日 and 毎朝 also normally appear without に. Days of the week can go either way: 日曜日に and 日曜日 are both common. For place, に marks location with verbs such as ある, いる and 住む, while で normally marks the setting where an activity takes place, as in 図書館で勉強する (OJG-0003). The choice also depends on the verb and on the role of the place: 椅子に座る uses に for the position someone takes. For people, に marks the one on the receiving end: the one who gets the flowers, the letter or the call.

formation.note: Clock times, dates, months, years. Usually no に with relative times (今日, 明日, 昨日, 今週, 来年) or recurring ones (毎日, 毎朝).
一日に三回 "three times a day": に marks the unit over which the amount or frequency is counted.

formation.form: Place + に + ある / いる / 住む
formation.note: Where something exists or someone lives.

formation.form: Person + に + あげる / 書く / 電話する / 聞く / 会う …
formation.note: The person the action is directed at.

mistake.wrong: 昨日に映画を見ました。
mistake.problem: 昨日 normally works as a time expression on its own, without に. に goes on clock times and dates.
mistake.right: 昨日映画を見ました。

distinguish_from.note: に after a place with a verb of movement marks the destination; that use is its own entry, together with へ.
に marks location with verbs of existence and residence; で normally marks the setting of an activity. This is not a rule that every action verb takes で: 椅子に座る.
In ～に～があります, に marks the place and が marks the thing that is there.
Some verbs that take a direct object in English take に in Japanese: 友だちに会う, 電車に乗る.

review.note: Time words vary: 朝, 夜, 週末 and seasons are sometimes heard with に and sometimes without. I left them out rather than guess a rule; please say whether a tendency is worth stating at N5. The rate use (一日に三回) is included briefly; is it N5 enough? Recurring-time expressions such as 毎日 and 毎朝 also normally appear without に.” Update the mistake diagnosis accordingly: “昨日 normally functions as a time expression without に; say 昨日映画を見ました.” (2) The entry describes rates but omits their formation. The choice also depends on the verb and the place’s role: 椅子に座る uses に for the position someone assumes.' Revise the distinction to: 'に marks location with existence/residence verbs; で normally marks the setting of an activity. This is not a rule that every action verb takes で.'

title: What an action is done to, and the ground a movement covers
meaning: を marks what an action acts on (パンを食べる), and with verbs of movement the route taken or the place left.
when: Use it on the direct object of a verb: what is eaten, read, bought, made (コーヒーを飲みます). With verbs of movement it marks the ground you move along or through (公園を散歩します, 道を歩きます) or the place you leave (家を出ます, 電車を降ります). を is pronounced お.
why: を marks what the action passes over or works on. For most verbs that is the thing affected: the bread that gets eaten, the letter that gets written. With verbs of movement, the ground covered is treated the same way, as the thing the movement goes over: 道を歩く, "walk along the road"; and a place you leave is what you move away from: 家を出る. Whether a verb takes を is a fact about the Japanese verb, not about its English translation. 会う ("meet") normally marks the person with に or と, and 乗る ("ride") normally marks the vehicle with に. In the basic patterns taught here, わかる ("understand") marks what is understood with が, and 好き and ほしい, which are adjectives, mark what is liked or wanted with が.

formation.note: The thing acted on.
The route (歩く, 散歩する, 渡る, 走る) or the place left (出る, 降りる).

title: Inviting someone: won't you...?
meaning: V-ませんか: a polite invitation, "won't you V (with me)?", that leaves the choice to the listener.
when: Use it to invite someone to do something, often together with you (一緒に映画を見ませんか), or to offer them something to do (お茶を飲みませんか). In another context the same form is a plain negative question: 肉を食べませんか can also ask "Don't you eat meat?" The situation and intonation tell them apart.
why: ませんか is a negative question: "won't you V?" Asking in the negative does not assume the answer is yes, so it is easy for the listener to decline, and that is why it feels considerate as an invitation. A positive question, 映画を見ますか, tends to be heard as asking about the listener's plans or habits rather than inviting them, although context can make it an invitation too. To accept, people often say いいですね or reply with ましょう (ええ、行きましょう); to decline, they usually soften it (ちょっと…) rather than saying いいえ outright.

formation.note: 行きます → 行きませんか; 食べます → 食べませんか.
Makes the "with me" explicit.
Casual: 行かない？ with rising intonation.

examples.japanese: 一緒に昼ご飯を食べませんか。
examples.reading: いっしょにひるごはんをたべませんか。

mistake.wrong: 一緒に映画を見るませんか。
mistake.problem: ませんか attaches to the ます-stem, not to the dictionary form. 見る has the stem 見 (見ます), so it is 見ませんか.
mistake.right: 一緒に映画を見ませんか。

distinguish_from.note: ましょう proposes and expects agreement ("let's"); ませんか asks, leaving the listener free to say no.
ましょうか also asks, but about doing something together or about the speaker doing it for the listener ("shall we / shall I"). ませんか asks whether the listener wants to.

review.note: Revised after review: the mistake is now a formation error (見るませんか), as the reviewer proposed, because 一緒に映画を見ますか can itself work as an invitation in context. The why still says the positive question "tends to" be heard as asking about plans, with the context caveat; the reviewer did not object to that sentence.

reviews.note: The mistake incorrectly treats 一緒に映画を見ますか as a faulty invitation and says it usually asks about an independently planned activity. With 一緒に and suitable context, it can naturally offer the listener the choice of watching together, as the explanation itself acknowledges. Replace the mistake with a genuine formation error: wrong “一緒に映画を見るませんか。”; problem “ませんか attaches to the ます-stem, not the dictionary form. 見る has the stem 見.”; right “一緒に映画を見ませんか。”

title: Setting up what you are talking about
meaning: は marks the topic: what the sentence is about. What follows says something about it. It can also set up a contrast.
when: Use it to name what you are going to say something about, then say it: 私は学生です, "As for me, I'm a student". Use it also to contrast one thing with another: 肉は食べますが、魚は食べません. は is written with the kana は but pronounced わ.
why: は does not mark the subject; it marks the topic, the frame for the rest of the sentence. The topic is often the subject, which is why the two are easy to confuse, but it need not be. In この本はもう読みました, the topic is the book, the thing that was read. In 田中さんは背が高いです, the topic is Mr Tanaka, while the subject of 高い is 背, his height. Because the topic is what you comment on, は tends to go on something already known or already in the conversation, and the new information comes after it. が, by contrast, tends to put the focus on the noun itself, as the new or the answering piece. So a question word asking who or what did something, which is the unknown, is not made the topic: だれが来ましたか, not だれは. Inside a clause that describes a noun, the subject is normally marked with が, not は: 私が作ったケーキ. は normally replaces が or を. It can follow other particles, as in 東京には and 学校では. Whether the other particle stays depends on its job; a time に can be dropped before は, as in 日曜日は.

formation.note: Normally replaces が or を when that noun is the topic.
It can follow other particles: 東京には, 学校では. Whether the particle stays depends on its job; a time に can be dropped: 日曜日は休みです.

mistake.wrong: だれは来ましたか。
mistake.problem: だれ is the unknown the question asks about, so it cannot be the topic. The unknown takes が, and so does the answer: 田中さんが来ました.
mistake.right: だれが来ましたか。

distinguish_from.note: も also goes on the topic position, but says "this one as well" instead of setting it apart.
机の上に猫がいます presents the presence of a cat on the desk, often introducing it into the conversation. 猫は机の上にいます takes the cat as the topic and states where it is.
The same pattern with things: 本がありますか asks whether there is one; 本はどこにありますか asks where the known book is.

review.note: は and が is a large subject; the entry stays with topic vs subject, known vs new, question words, contrast, and が inside noun-modifying clauses, each stated as a tendency where it is one. Questions: is the question-word point narrow enough as stated (limited to a question word in the doer position)? Is the noun-modifying-clause point too advanced for N5, or worth keeping because learners meet it early? Revised after review: particle stacking before は is now stated as depending on the particle's job (a time に can drop); the OJG-0010 note no longer says が means the cat was unknown.

reviews.note: Two statements are too absolute. (1) Other particles do not invariably remain before は: temporal に can be omitted, as in 日曜日は休みです. Replace “は replaces が and を, and follows other particles” and the formation note saying に stays with: “は normally replaces が or を. It can follow other particles, as in 東京には and 学校では. Whether another particle remains depends on its function; temporal に can be omitted before は, as in 日曜日は.” (2) 机の上に猫がいます does not necessarily introduce a cat nobody knew about; が does not entail that the referent is unknown. Replace the OJG-0010 note with: “机の上に猫がいます presents the presence of a cat on the desk, often introducing it into the conversation. 猫は机の上にいます takes the cat as the topic and states its location.”

title: Saying a thing is there, or that you have it
meaning: N があります: there is N (a thing, plant or event, not a person or animal), or someone has N. が marks what is there.
when: Use it to say that a thing is somewhere (机の上にかばんがあります), that an event will take place (明日テストがあります), and to say you have something or do not (時間がありません). The negative is ありません in polite speech and ない in plain speech.
why: ある normally describes things, plants, events and abstract things such as time or plans; いる normally describes people and animals. The choice follows the thing that exists, not the place, and it can also depend on how the speaker presents that thing (see OJG-0010). が marks that thing. It often presents something the listener has not heard about yet, which is why the usual order is place first, as the setting, and the new thing last: 机の上にかばんがあります. When the thing is already the topic and the question is where it is, it takes は and the place becomes the new information: かばんは机の上にあります. "I have N" works the same way: literally "for me, N exists", so N still takes が, not を. For an event, the place where it is held usually takes で, because an event is something that happens there: 公園でお祭りがあります.

formation.form: place に + N が あります
formation.note: Introduces something new: "there is N at the place". Past: ありました. Negative: ありません.

formation.form: N は + place に あります
formation.note: Says where a known thing is.

formation.form: (person は) + N が あります
formation.note: Having something: 時間があります, "I have time".

formation.form: (time) + (event location で) + event が あります
formation.note: For an event taking place somewhere, use で: 公園でお祭りがあります. Relative time words such as 明日 or 今日 normally appear without に; clock times and dates take に: 三時に会議があります.
Plain forms. The plain negative of ある is ない, not あらない.

mistake.wrong: 私は車をあります。

mistake.right: 私は車があります。

distinguish_from.note: います is for people and animals; あります is for things, plants and events. The choice depends on what exists, not on where it is.
です says what something is or is like (これは本です). あります says that something exists or is somewhere (本があります).

The reviewer's note said time words "normally appear without に"; that holds for relative words (明日, 今日) but not for clock times or dates (三時に), so the note distinguishes the two.

The choice can also depend on how the speaker presents the subject (see OJG-0010).' This accommodates the vehicles and personified objects discussed in the linked entry.

title: Saying a person or animal is there, or that you have family or pets
meaning: N がいます: there is N (a person or animal), or someone has N, such as a brother or a pet. が marks who is there.
when: Use it to say that a person or animal is somewhere (公園に子どもがいます), to ask whether someone is in (田中さんはいますか), and to talk about family, friends and pets you have (姉が一人います). The negative is いません in polite speech and いない in plain speech.
why: いる is the verb of existence for beings that move of their own will: people, animals, birds, fish, insects. Things, plants and events take ある (OJG-0009). What decides is how the speaker sees the subject, so the same word can go either way: a fish swimming in a tank いる, a fish on a plate ある. A few cases are usually described like this rather than fixed by rule. Plants are alive but normally take ある. A robot or a toy is usually a thing and takes ある, though people may use いる for a robot that moves around like a pet or a character. A taxi or bus waiting with its driver is often spoken of with いる, while a car simply parked usually takes ある. As with ある, が marks who is there and often introduces them as new, after the place: 公園に子どもがいます. When the person is already the topic, は marks them and the place is the new part: 田中さんは教室にいます. The place takes に, because being somewhere is not an action.

formation.form: place に + N が います
formation.note: Introduces someone new: "there is N at the place". Past: いました. Negative: いません.

formation.form: N は + place に います
formation.note: Says where a known person or animal is.

formation.form: (person は) + N が + number + います
formation.note: Family and pets: 兄が二人います. The number with its counter goes before います.
Plain forms.

title: And (joining nouns), and together with
meaning: と joins nouns into a complete list, "A and B"; after a person it can also mean "with" (友だちと).
when: Use it between nouns to list them all: パンと牛乳, "bread and milk". It joins nouns only; adjectives, verbs and whole sentences are joined in other ways, such as the て-form. After a person, と marks who you do something with (友だちと映画を見ました) or the other party of a verb like 話す, 会う or 結婚する.
why: と presents the nouns it joins as the whole list: these, and nothing else being mentioned. That is the difference from や, which lists examples. It stays between the items and normally does not follow the last one. Since と is a particle that works with nouns, it cannot link adjectives or verbs the way English "and" can: "big and clean" is 広くてきれい, not 広いときれい. The "with" use comes from the same idea of putting two together: 友だちと is "together with a friend". 一緒に is often added to make the "together" explicit.

formation.form: Noun A + と + Noun B (+ と + Noun C …)
formation.note: In the basic pattern, と goes between the nouns. A final と is also possible (パンと牛乳とを買いました), but is normally omitted in simple lists.
Who you do it with, or the other party: 友だちと話す, 友だちと一緒に行く.

title: Let's do it
meaning: V-ましょう: "let's V", a polite proposal to do something together, or agreeing to one.
when: Use it to propose doing something together when you expect the listener to agree (そろそろ帰りましょう), and to accept an invitation (ええ、行きましょう). Teachers, signs and announcements also use it for a gentle instruction to a group: 手を洗いましょう, "let's wash our hands", meaning "please wash your hands".
why: ましょう is the polite form of the volitional, the form that expresses the will to do something. Said to a listener, it presents that will as shared: "let's". Because it states a decision rather than asking a question, it fits best when agreement is already likely: replying to an invitation, or when the plan is settled. To suggest something the listener may not want, speakers often choose the softer ませんか or ましょうか, which ask instead of deciding.

formation.note: 行きます → 行きましょう; 食べます → 食べましょう; します → しましょう.
Casual: 行こう, 食べよう, しよう, 来よう.

title: Shall I...? / Shall we...?
meaning: V-ましょうか: "shall I V?" offering to do something, or "shall we V?" suggesting it and asking the listener's view.
when: Use it to offer help (荷物を持ちましょうか, "Shall I carry your bags?"), to suggest doing something together while checking the listener agrees (ちょっと休みましょうか), and with a question word to ask what to do (何時に会いましょうか, "What time shall we meet?").
why: ましょう expresses the will to do something; か turns it into a question. Instead of deciding, the speaker puts the intention to the listener. Who would do the action is not said and comes from the situation. When the action would help the listener and only the speaker would do it, it is heard as an offer. When both would do it, it is a suggestion, softer than a plain ましょう because it asks. With a question word, it asks the listener to help choose. An offer is typically answered with お願いします or declined with 大丈夫です; a suggestion with そうしましょう.

formation.note: 持ちます → 持ちましょうか.
何を食べましょうか, "What shall we eat?"
Casual: 持とうか, often just 持とうか？ with rising intonation.

title: Please do...
meaning: V-てください: "please V", a polite request, instruction or invitation for the listener to do something.
when: Use it to ask someone to do something (ちょっと待ってください), to give directions or instructions (ここに名前を書いてください), and to urge a guest to do something for their own sake (どうぞ食べてください). For a thing rather than an action, use N をください: 水をください.
why: ください is an honorific request form of くださる, a verb meaning "give (to me)". After the て-form it asks the listener to give you the doing of V: to do it for you, or as you ask. So this construction is polite in form, though it can sound directive: it still tells the listener what to do, which is why it is common for instructions and directions. When asking a favour of someone above you or a stranger, speakers often soften it further, for example with ～てくださいませんか. With an ordinary action verb, ～てください asks the listener to perform that action; it does not by itself mean "May I…?" A causative form such as 行かせてください ("please let me go") can ask the listener to let the speaker act.

formation.note: 待つ → 待ってください; 書く → 書いてください; 見る → 見てください.
Asking for a thing: 水をください.
Casual: 待って, 見て.

distinguish_from.note: ないでください is the negative request: "please don't V".
てもいいですか asks whether an action is permitted, often the speaker's own; てください requests an action from the listener.

review.note: Revised after review: why now calls ください an honorific request form of くださる, says the construction is polite in form but can sound directive, and replaces "cannot ask permission" with the ordinary-verb statement plus the causative 行かせてください. The causative is N4 or later; it is mentioned only as the exception, not taught. distinguish_from note reworded as proposed. Unchanged question: the mistake is framed as a learner asking a teacher; the "wrong" sentence itself is grammatical, only wrong for the intended meaning. Is that acceptable for the mistake field?

reviews.note: The claim that てください cannot ask permission for something the speaker wants to do is too absolute: トイレに行かせてください means 'Please let me go to the toilet.' Replace the last sentence of why with: 'With an ordinary action verb, ～てください asks the listener to perform that action; it does not by itself mean “May I…?” A causative form such as 行かせてください can ask the listener to let the speaker act.' Also replace 'Because it is a request form, it is polite' with 'ください is an honorific request form of くださる, so this construction is polite in form, though it can sound directive.' In distinguish_from, write: 'てもいいですか asks whether an action is permitted, often the speaker’s own; てください requests an action from the listener.'
The request construction, its directive potential, and its distinction from asking permission are accurately explained.

title: It's all right to...; may I...?
meaning: V-てもいいです: "it's all right to V", giving permission; as V-てもいいですか, asking for it.
when: Use it to ask permission (写真を撮ってもいいですか), to give it (ここで食べてもいいです), and to say that something is acceptable (鉛筆で書いてもいいです, "Writing in pencil is fine"). To grant permission, people often just say いいですよ or どうぞ; to refuse, they usually soften it (すみません、ちょっと…).
why: The て-form with も means "even if you do V", and いい means "good". Put together: "even if you do V, it is fine", so nothing bad follows and the action is allowed. てはいけません (OJG-0016) is built on the same frame the other way round: "if you do V, it is no good". The same pattern works with adjectives and nouns: 高くてもいいです, "it's fine even if it's expensive"; 明日でもいいです, "tomorrow is fine too".

formation.form: V (て-form) + も + いいです
formation.note: Question: V-てもいいですか.
Casual, often without も: 座っていい？

formation.form: い-adj: replace the final い with く, then add てもいいです
formation.note: 高い → 高くてもいいです. いい becomes よくてもいいです.

formation.form: な-adj stem + でもいいです
formation.note: 静かでもいいです, "it is fine even if it is quiet".
明日でもいいです, "tomorrow is fine too".

examples.japanese: 写真を撮ってもいいですか。
examples.reading: しゃしんをとってもいいですか。
examples.romaji: shashin o totte mo ii desu ka.
examples.english: May I take a photo?

examples.japanese: この部屋で食べてもいいです。
examples.reading: このへやでたべてもいいです。
examples.romaji: kono heya de tabete mo ii desu.
examples.english: You may eat in this room.

examples.japanese: 鉛筆で書いてもいいです。
examples.reading: えんぴつでかいてもいいです。
examples.romaji: enpitsu de kaite mo ii desu.
examples.english: It's fine to write in pencil.

mistake.wrong: ここに座るもいいですか。
mistake.problem: も attaches to the て-form, which gives "even if (I) sit". The dictionary form cannot take も here.
mistake.right: ここに座ってもいいですか。

distinguish_from.note: The same frame reversed: てもいい allows ("even if you do it, fine"), てはいけない forbids ("if you do it, no good").
てください asks the listener to act; てもいいですか asks whether an action is permitted, often the speaker's own.

review.note: Revised after review: formation now lists い-adjectives (with いい → よくても), な-adjectives (静かでもいい) and nouns as separate lines, and the distinguish_from note no longer limits permission questions to the speaker's own actions. Unchanged question: is the dictionary-form error (座るもいい) a common enough real mistake, or would another be better?

reviews.note: The explanation extends the construction to adjectives, but formation omits な-adjectives. Add 'な-adjective stem + でもいいです: 静かでもいいです (“It is fine even if it is quiet”).' Clarify the い-adjective rule as 'Replace final い with く, then add てもいいです; いい becomes よくてもいいです.' The distinguish_from note also unnecessarily restricts permission questions to the speaker’s own actions: 子供も来てもいいですか asks whether the child may come. Replace it with: 'てください asks the listener to act; てもいいですか asks whether an action is permitted, often the speaker’s own.'

title: You must not...
meaning: V-てはいけません: "you must not V", a prohibition; literally "if you V, it is no good".
when: Use it to state rules and prohibitions (ここでたばこを吸ってはいけません), as teachers, parents, signs and rules do. As a question, V-てはいけませんか asks "Is it not allowed?" Said directly to an equal or someone above you, it can sound strict, so in conversation people often use ないでください or a softened refusal instead.
why: The て-form with は sets up a condition: "doing V, as a case". いけません means "it won't do". So the sentence says "if you do V, it is no good", and that is a prohibition. It is the same frame as てもいいです (OJG-0015) turned the other way: "even if you do V, it is fine". Because it states a rule rather than making a request, it tends to come from someone with authority or to describe a general rule.

formation.form: V (て-form) + は + いけません
formation.note: Plain: V-てはいけない. The は is pronounced わ.

formation.form: V-ちゃいけない / V-じゃいけない
formation.note: Casual speech: ては becomes ちゃ, and では becomes じゃ (飲んではいけない → 飲んじゃいけない).

examples.japanese: ここでたばこを吸ってはいけません。
examples.reading: ここでたばこをすってはいけません。
examples.romaji: koko de tabako o sutte wa ikemasen.
examples.english: You must not smoke here.

examples.japanese: テストのとき、辞書を見てはいけません。
examples.reading: テストのとき、じしょをみてはいけません。
examples.romaji: tesuto no toki, jisho o mite wa ikemasen.
examples.english: You must not look at a dictionary during the test.

examples.japanese: この川で泳いではいけません。
examples.reading: このかわでおよいではいけません。
examples.romaji: kono kawa de oyoide wa ikemasen.
examples.english: You must not swim in this river.
examples.note: 泳ぐ has the て-form 泳いで, so it is ではいけません.

mistake.wrong: 明日は来てはいけません。
mistake.problem: Meant as "You don't have to come tomorrow", but てはいけません forbids: "You must not come tomorrow." English "don't have to" means "not required", which Japanese says with ～なくてもいいです, "it's fine even if you don't".
mistake.right: 明日は来なくてもいいです。

distinguish_from.note: The same frame reversed: てもいい allows, てはいけない forbids.
ないでください asks the listener not to do something; てはいけません states that it is not allowed, and sounds stricter.
なくちゃいけない is the same "no good" logic applied to not doing V, so it means "must V".

review.note: The "right" sentence uses ～なくてもいい, which is not one of the N5 ids (usually listed at N4). Is it acceptable in the mistake field, or should the mistake be a formation error instead?

title: Giving a reason: because
meaning: Clause + から: "because". The reason usually comes first, then the result, request or decision.
when: This entry is から after a clause, giving a reason: 雨だから、行きません, "It's raining, so I won't go". The reason normally comes before the main clause, but it can follow as an added explanation: 行きません。雨ですから。 It can also end a sentence, especially in answer to どうして: 頭が痛かったからです. The particle から after a noun, meaning "from" (九時から, 東京から), is a different use of the same word.
why: から marks a starting point: 東京から is "from Tokyo". After a clause, the same idea marks the situation the rest of the sentence starts from, which is its reason. So in the usual order the reason clause comes first and the main point last, the reverse of English "X because Y"; the reason can also be added afterwards as a separate sentence ending in から. For a nonpast affirmative noun or な-adjective predicate, use だ or です before this から: 雨だから, 静かですから. Without it, 雨から reads as "from the rain". Past or negative predicates use the matching form: 雨だったから, 静かではないから. から is common with requests, invitations and decisions: 寒いから窓を閉めてください. Compared with ので, から tends to sound more like the speaker's own reasoning, and ので more like a plain statement of circumstances, so ので is often preferred for polite excuses and requests. This is a tendency, and both are used in all of these situations.

formation.form: Verb / い-adjective (plain or polite) + から
formation.note: 行くから, 行きますから, 高いから, 高いですから. The polite form before から is more polite.

formation.form: Noun / な-adjective + だから (or ですから)
formation.note: For nonpast affirmative predicates; 雨から would mean "from the rain". Past or negative: 雨だったから, 静かではないから.
Gives a reason, often answering どうして or なぜ: 行くからです, 高いからです, 雨だからです, 静かだったからです. Use the plain form inside this construction; the final です supplies the politeness.

examples.japanese: 今日は雨だから、どこにも行きません。
examples.reading: きょうはあめだから、どこにもいきません。
examples.romaji: kyō wa ame da kara, doko ni mo ikimasen.
examples.english: It's raining today, so I'm not going anywhere.

examples.japanese: 暑いですから、窓を開けてください。
examples.reading: あついですから、まどをあけてください。
examples.romaji: atsui desu kara, mado o akete kudasai.
examples.english: It's hot, so please open the window.

examples.japanese: 明日はテストがありますから、今晩勉強します。
examples.reading: あしたはテストがありますから、こんばんべんきょうします。
examples.romaji: ashita wa tesuto ga arimasu kara, konban benkyō shimasu.
examples.english: I have a test tomorrow, so I'll study tonight.

examples.japanese: 「どうして来なかったんですか。」「頭が痛かったからです。」
examples.reading: 「どうしてこなかったんですか。」「あたまがいたかったからです。」
examples.romaji: "dōshite konakatta n desu ka." "atama ga itakatta kara desu."
examples.english: "Why didn't you come?" "Because I had a headache."

mistake.wrong: 雨から、行きません。
mistake.problem: In a nonpast affirmative sentence, a noun before the "because" から needs だ or です. Without it, 雨から reads as the particle "from": "from the rain".
mistake.right: 雨だから、行きません。

distinguish_from.note: ので also gives a reason. It tends to sound softer and more like a statement of circumstances; から tends to sound more like the speaker's own reasoning.
～てから means "after doing": 食べてから is "after eating", not "because I eat".

review.note: The から / ので contrast is kept deliberately soft; please check it does not overstate. Sentence-final から without です in casual speech (だって、痛かったから) is not covered. Revised after review: the だ／です rule is limited to nonpast affirmative predicates, with past and negative forms shown; reason-first order is now 'usually', with the afterthought order (行きません。雨ですから。) mentioned.

reviews.note: The noun/な-adjective rule is stated too categorically: だ／です applies to nonpast affirmative clauses, not forms such as 雨だったから or 静かではないから. Replace the rule in why and formation with: 'For nonpast affirmative noun and な-adjective predicates, use だ／です before から: 雨だから、静かですから. For past or negative predicates, use the appropriately conjugated copula: 雨だったから、静かではないから.' Apply the same nonpast-affirmative qualification to the mistake diagnosis. Also qualify the reason-first wording in meaning, when and why: 'The reason normally precedes the main clause, but it can follow as an added explanation: 行きません。雨ですから。' Japanese does not invariably require the reverse of English 'X because Y' order.

The formation for sentence-final からです needs a restriction. The earlier permission to use plain or polite clauses before から does not carry over unchanged to this explanatory construction; combining the rules would produce forms such as 行きますからです. Replace the third formation with: “Plain-form clause + からです. Used to give a reason, often answering どうして or なぜ: 行くからです, 高いからです, 雨だからです, 静かだったからです. Use the plain form inside this construction; the final です supplies politeness.”
The explanation and formation correctly cover causal から, including sentence-final explanations. The examples, correction, and comparison with ので are sound.

title: Doing something now, or being in the state a change left
meaning: V-ている: an action under way, something done regularly, or the state that follows a change.
when: Use it for an action going on now (本を読んでいる), for something done repeatedly or an ongoing situation (毎朝走っている, 大阪に住んでいる), and for the state a subject is in after a change (結婚している, 窓が開いている).
why: いる says that a living thing is there. After the て-form of a verb it says the subject is there in the middle of the action, or in the state that follows it. Which reading you get depends on the verb and on the context. With a verb for an activity that lasts (読む, 食べる), ている often describes an action in progress. With a verb for a change (結婚する, 開く, 知る), it often describes the state after the change: 結婚している normally means "is married", and 知っている means "know". Words of frequency and other context can instead give a habitual reading (毎朝走っている), and 大阪に住んでいる describes an ongoing situation. The いる here is a helper and stays いる even when the subject is a thing: 窓が開いている.

formation.note: Polite: V (て-form) + います.
Casual speech often drops the い: 読んでる, 食べてる.

examples.japanese: 子どもが本を読んでいます。
examples.reading: こどもがほんをよんでいます。
examples.romaji: kodomo ga hon o yonde imasu.
examples.english: The child is reading a book.

examples.japanese: 姉は大阪に住んでいます。
examples.reading: あねはおおさかにすんでいます。
examples.romaji: ane wa ōsaka ni sunde imasu.
examples.english: My older sister lives in Osaka.

examples.japanese: 窓が開いています。
examples.reading: まどがあいています。
examples.romaji: mado ga aite imasu.
examples.english: The window is open.
examples.note: 開く is a change, so this is the state after it, not an action under way.

mistake.wrong: 私はその人を知ります。
mistake.problem: 知る is the change of coming to know. Knowing someone now is the state after that change, so it takes ている.
mistake.right: 私はその人を知っています。

distinguish_from.note: With a verb of change, both describe a state: 窓が開いている, 窓が開けてある. ている only says the window is open; てある says someone opened it on purpose and left it so.

review.note: First complete entry, adapted from the Mieru Nihongo note on 〜ています and rewritten to stand on its own.

reviews.note: The explanation, formation, examples, mistake correction, and comparison are accurate; N5 is plausible.

title: Going (or coming) somewhere to do something
meaning: V (ます-stem) + に行く／来る／帰る: go, come or go home in order to do V.
when: Use it when you move somewhere for a purpose: to see a film, to buy bread, to eat lunch at home. The purpose goes before に, and a verb of movement follows, most often 行く, 来る or 帰る. A noun that names an activity, such as 買い物 or 散歩, can also take this に directly: 買い物に行く, “go shopping”. The destination, if you say it, is usually marked with へ or に earlier in the sentence.
why: The ます-stem of a verb (食べ from 食べます, 見 from 見ます) works a little like a noun that names the activity. に marks where the movement is aimed, and here it is aimed at an activity rather than a place: 見に行く is “go towards seeing”. That is why the verb before に is in the stem form, not the dictionary form, and why the verb after it is one of moving somewhere. Because a sentence can name both a place and a purpose, it can contain two に; many speakers prefer へ for the place in that case (図書館へ本を借りに行く), though に for the place is also heard.

formation.form: V (ます-stem) + に + 行く／来る／帰る
formation.note: Polite: 行きます, 来ます, 帰ります. Tense and politeness go on the verb of movement: 見に行きました.

formation.form: activity noun + に + 行く／来る
formation.note: With nouns that name an activity, often ones that also take する: 買い物に行く, 散歩に行く. 買い物をしに行く is also possible.

formation.form: place へ／に … purpose に + 行く
formation.note: The place and the purpose can both appear: デパートへ買い物に行く.

examples.japanese: 友だちと映画を見に行きます。
examples.reading: ともだちとえいがをみにいきます。
examples.romaji: tomodachi to eiga o mi ni ikimasu.
examples.english: I’m going to see a film with a friend.

examples.japanese: 昼ご飯を食べに家へ帰ります。
examples.reading: ひるごはんをたべにいえへかえります。
examples.romaji: hirugohan o tabe ni ie e kaerimasu.
examples.english: I go home to eat lunch.

examples.japanese: 日曜日にデパートへ買い物に行きました。
examples.reading: にちようびにデパートへかいものにいきました。
examples.romaji: nichiyōbi ni depāto e kaimono ni ikimashita.
examples.english: On Sunday I went shopping at the department store.
examples.note: 買い物 is an activity noun, so it takes に directly.

examples.japanese: 田中さんが本を返しに来ました。
examples.reading: たなかさんがほんをかえしにきました。
examples.romaji: tanaka-san ga hon o kaeshi ni kimashita.
examples.english: Mr Tanaka came to return the book.

mistake.wrong: 昼ご飯を食べるに行きます。
mistake.problem: The purpose before に is the ます-stem of the verb, not the dictionary form. English “go to eat” makes the dictionary form feel right, but 食べるに does not work here.
mistake.right: 昼ご飯を食べに行きます。

distinguish_from.note: に／へ after a place marks where you go (駅に行く). The に of this pattern follows a verb stem or activity noun and marks what you go to do (本を買いに行く). Both can appear in one sentence.

review.note: Two points to confirm: (1) the claim that many speakers prefer へ for the place when a purpose に follows is a tendency I believe is right but have stated softly; (2) the list of movement verbs is limited to 行く／来る／帰る as the scope asked, though 出かける and 戻る also occur. Not covered: ～ために as a general purpose form, which is not N5.

title: Please don't...
meaning: V-ないでください: "please don't V", a polite request not to do something.
when: Use it to ask someone not to do something (ここで写真を撮らないでください), on signs and notices, and for reassurance or reminders: 心配しないでください, "please don't worry"; 忘れないでください, "please don't forget".
why: The ない-form is the plain negative of a verb. ないで joins it to what follows in the sense of "not doing V", and ください asks the listener to give you that. So the sentence asks for the listener's not doing V. Because it is a request rather than a statement of a rule, it is usually softer than てはいけません. To build it, make the ない-form and add でください. For godan (う-) verbs, change the final kana to its あ-row counterpart and add ない; a final う becomes わない (書く → 書かない, 買う → 買わない). For ichidan (る-) verbs, replace る with ない (食べる → 食べない). する becomes しない, 来る becomes 来ない (こない), and ある has the exceptional negative ない.

formation.note: 撮る → 撮らない → 撮らないでください; する → しないでください; 来る → 来ないでください.
Casual: 見ないで, 行かないで.

examples.japanese: ここで写真を撮らないでください。
examples.reading: ここでしゃしんをとらないでください。
examples.romaji: koko de shashin o toranaide kudasai.
examples.english: Please don't take photos here.

examples.japanese: 心配しないでください。
examples.reading: しんぱいしないでください。
examples.romaji: shinpai shinaide kudasai.
examples.english: Please don't worry.

examples.japanese: 宿題を忘れないでください。
examples.reading: しゅくだいをわすれないでください。
examples.romaji: shukudai o wasurenaide kudasai.
examples.english: Please don't forget your homework.

mistake.wrong: 心配しなくてください。
mistake.problem: ない has two connecting forms, なくて and ないで, and a request takes ないで. なくて cannot be followed by ください.
mistake.right: 心配しないでください。

distinguish_from.note: てください asks the listener to do V; ないでください asks them not to.
てはいけません states a prohibition, like a rule; ないでください is a request, and usually softer.

review.note: Revised after review: the conjugation sentence now follows the reviewer's wording, including final う → わない and the exception ある → ない. ある rarely if ever appears in ないでください itself; the exception is kept because the sentence teaches the ない-form in general. Pattern normalised to ～ないでください (source lists ないでください without the tilde). The why describes the ないで/なくて split only as "a request takes ないで"; the fuller contrast (なくて as reason) is left out for N5. Confirm that is not misleading.

reviews.note: The explanation of how to form the negative omits the exception ある → ない and should explicitly explain verbs ending in う. Replace the conjugation instructions with: “For godan (う-) verbs, change the final kana to its あ-row counterpart and add ない; final う becomes わない (書く → 書かない, 買う → 買わない). For ichidan (る-) verbs, replace る with ない (食べる → 食べない). する becomes しない, 来る becomes 来ない (こない), and ある has the exceptional negative ない.”

title: Saying you like doing something
meaning: V (dictionary form) + のが好きです: someone likes doing V. の turns the verb phrase into a noun that 好き can take.
when: Use it to say that you, or someone else, like an activity: reading, cooking, going for walks. The opposite is 嫌い (dislike), and 大好き makes it stronger. With a plain noun you do not need の: 犬が好きです.
why: 好き is a な-adjective, and the thing that is liked is marked with が: 犬が好きです. Only a noun can stand in front of that が, so an activity has to be turned into a noun first. Adding の after the dictionary form of a verb does that: 本を読む becomes 本を読むの, "reading books". The verb phrase keeps its own particles inside it (本を読む), and the が that belongs to 好き comes after の. The person who does the liking usually takes は: 私は…のが好きです. こと can also make a verb into a noun here (読むことが好きです), and both are common in this pattern. The two are not interchangeable in every pattern, so learn this pairing as it is rather than treating の and こと as the same word.

formation.form: V (dictionary form) + のが好きです
formation.note: Plain: のが好きだ. Negative: のが好きではありません, or in speech のが好きじゃないです.

formation.form: V (dictionary form) + のが嫌いです
formation.note: The opposite: dislike doing V. In conversation 好きじゃない often sounds softer than 嫌い.

formation.form: person は … V + のが好きです
formation.note: The person who likes it takes は; the activity takes が.

examples.japanese: 私は本を読むのが好きです。
examples.reading: わたしはほんをよむのがすきです。
examples.romaji: watashi wa hon o yomu no ga suki desu.
examples.english: I like reading books.

examples.japanese: 弟は料理を作るのが好きです。
examples.reading: おとうとはりょうりをつくるのがすきです。
examples.romaji: otōto wa ryōri o tsukuru no ga suki desu.
examples.english: My younger brother likes cooking.
examples.note: 料理を stays inside the verb phrase; が comes after の.

examples.japanese: 朝早く起きるのが嫌いです。
examples.reading: あさはやくおきるのがきらいです。
examples.romaji: asa hayaku okiru no ga kirai desu.
examples.english: I hate getting up early.

examples.japanese: 休みの日に散歩するのが大好きです。
examples.reading: やすみのひにさんぽするのがだいすきです。
examples.romaji: yasumi no hi ni sanpo suru no ga daisuki desu.
examples.english: I love going for walks on my days off.

mistake.wrong: 私は泳ぐが好きです。
mistake.problem: The activity marked by が before 好き must be a noun. 泳ぐ on its own is a verb, so add の to make it one: 泳ぐのが好きです.
mistake.right: 私は泳ぐのが好きです。

distinguish_from.note: The same frame, V + のが + adjective. 好き is about liking an activity; 上手 is about being good at it.
～たい is a wish to do something, often now or on a particular occasion. のが好き is a general liking: 泳ぐのが好き is true even when you do not want to swim today.

review.note: Revised after review: the mistake explanation now says が comes before 好き (the first draft wrongly said 'after'). Still open: the entry says only that の and こと are both common here and not interchangeable everywhere, with no claim about which sounds more formal.

reviews.note: The mistake diagnosis says “が after 好き,” but が precedes 好き. Replace that sentence with: “The activity marked by が before 好き must be expressed nominally; 泳ぐ alone is a verb, so add の: 泳ぐのが好きです.”

title: Saying someone is good at doing something
meaning: V (dictionary form) + のが上手です: someone is good at V. Mostly said of others; for yourself, 得意 is the usual word.
when: Use it to say that someone does an activity well: singing, drawing, speaking a language. It is often a compliment, said to or about another person. With a noun for the skill, no の is needed: 料理が上手です.
why: 上手 is a な-adjective about skill, and the skill is marked with が, the same frame as 好き. A verb needs の to become a noun before it can take that が: 歌う becomes 歌うの, "singing". The person whose skill it is usually takes は. 上手 is a judgement of someone's skill, which is why it works as praise. For the same reason, using it about your own skill tends to sound like boasting, so speakers usually describe their own strengths with 得意 ("my strong point") instead. It is not forbidden about yourself: saying you are not good, 上手じゃありません, is a normal modest thing to say. When someone says 上手ですね to you, a modest reply is the usual response.

formation.form: V (dictionary form) + のが上手です
formation.note: Plain: のが上手だ. Negative: のが上手ではありません, or in speech 上手じゃないです.
With a noun for the skill, no の: 日本語が上手です.

formation.form: V (dictionary form) + のが得意です
formation.note: The usual way to name your own strong point.

examples.japanese: 田中さんは歌うのが上手です。
examples.reading: たなかさんはうたうのがじょうずです。
examples.romaji: tanaka-san wa utau no ga jōzu desu.
examples.english: Tanaka-san is good at singing.

examples.japanese: 友だちは絵をかくのがとても上手です。
examples.reading: ともだちはえをかくのがとてもじょうずです。
examples.romaji: tomodachi wa e o kaku no ga totemo jōzu desu.
examples.english: My friend is very good at drawing.

examples.japanese: 日本語が上手ですね。
examples.reading: にほんごがじょうずですね。
examples.romaji: nihongo ga jōzu desu ne.
examples.english: Your Japanese is good.
examples.note: A compliment to the listener. With a noun, no の is needed.

examples.japanese: 私は泳ぐのが得意です。
examples.reading: わたしはおよぐのがとくいです。
examples.romaji: watashi wa oyogu no ga tokui desu.
examples.english: Swimming is my strong point.
examples.note: About yourself, 得意 is the usual word rather than 上手.

mistake.wrong: 私はテニスをするのが上手です。
mistake.problem: The grammar is fine, but calling your own skill 上手 tends to sound like bragging. English "I'm good at" is more neutral. For your own strengths, 得意 is the usual choice.
mistake.right: 私はテニスをするのが得意です。

distinguish_from.note: 下手 is the opposite and uses the same frame. The tendencies also reverse: 下手 is a normal, modest thing to say about yourself, and can sound blunt about someone else.
Same frame, V + のが + adjective. 好き is about liking an activity; 上手 is about doing it well.

review.note: 得意 is not usually N5 vocabulary, but the self-praise tendency cannot be explained without it. Please check that the mistake (上手 about yourself) is framed as a tendency and not as an error of grammar.

reviews.note: The explanation, formation, examples, romanization, and usage distinctions are accurate.

title: Saying someone is bad at doing something
meaning: V (dictionary form) + のが下手です: someone is bad at V. A modest thing to say of yourself; blunt about others.
when: Use it to say that someone does an activity badly. It is most often said about yourself, as a modest admission: 私は歌うのが下手です. Said directly about the listener or another person, it can sound blunt, so people tend to soften it or avoid it. With a noun for the skill, no の is needed: 字が下手です.
why: 下手 is the opposite of 上手 and uses the same frame: the activity, made into a noun with の, is marked with が, and the person usually takes は. Because 下手 is a judgement of someone's skill, the social effect is the reverse of 上手: about yourself it sounds modest, about someone else it can sound like criticism. A close neighbour is 苦手, which says you are not good with something or find it hard. It is about how you feel towards the activity as much as about skill, so it can also cover things you simply do not like doing.

formation.form: V (dictionary form) + のが下手です
formation.note: Plain: のが下手だ.
With a noun for the skill, no の: 字が下手です.

formation.form: V (dictionary form) + のが苦手です
formation.note: A softer neighbour: not good with it, or finds it hard.

examples.japanese: 私は歌うのが下手です。
examples.reading: わたしはうたうのがへたです。
examples.romaji: watashi wa utau no ga heta desu.
examples.english: I'm bad at singing.

examples.japanese: 父は料理を作るのが下手です。
examples.reading: ちちはりょうりをつくるのがへたです。
examples.romaji: chichi wa ryōri o tsukuru no ga heta desu.
examples.english: My father is bad at cooking.

examples.japanese: 私は字が下手です。
examples.reading: わたしはじがへたです。
examples.romaji: watashi wa ji ga heta desu.
examples.english: My handwriting is bad.
examples.note: With a noun, no の is needed.

examples.japanese: 朝早く起きるのが苦手です。
examples.reading: あさはやくおきるのがにがてです。
examples.romaji: asa hayaku okiru no ga nigate desu.
examples.english: I'm not good at getting up early.
examples.note: 苦手: something you find hard, not only a lack of skill.

mistake.wrong: 私は泳ぐのを下手です。
mistake.problem: 下手 is an adjective, not a verb, so the activity is not its object. The thing you are bad at is marked with が.
mistake.right: 私は泳ぐのが下手です。

distinguish_from.note: 上手 is the opposite. 上手 tends to be said about others, 下手 about yourself.
Same frame, V + のが + adjective. 嫌い is about not liking an activity; 下手 is about not doing it well.

review.note: 苦手 is usually listed above N5; it is included only as a neighbour. The description of 苦手 (difficulty and dislike as well as skill) is kept short on purpose; please check it is not overstated.

reviews.note: The skill and social-use distinctions are sound, and the examples and correction are correct.

title: Not yet
meaning: まだ V-ていません: V has not happened yet, and the situation is still open.
when: Use it to say something expected has not happened so far: the homework is not finished yet, a friend has not arrived yet. It is the usual negative answer to a question with もう, “already”: もう食べましたか, “Have you eaten?”, いいえ、まだ食べていません. The short answer is まだです, or まだ in casual speech.
why: “Not yet” describes how things stand now, and it leaves room for the action to happen later. In this use, V-ていない describes an action as not having occurred or been completed up to the reference time. With まだ and a present reference time, it means “not yet”. The polite past negative V-ませんでした (plain: V-なかった) normally reports that an action did not occur in a past situation, rather than that it remains undone now, so it is not the usual form for answering “Have you eaten yet?” negatively. This is why the question and its answers do not match in form: yes is もう食べました (the action is done), but no is まだ食べていません (it has not happened up to now). To say something had not yet happened at a past point, the reference time moves to the past: その時はまだ来ていませんでした.

formation.form: まだ + V (て-form) + いません
formation.note: Polite.

formation.form: まだ + V (て-form) + いない
formation.note: Plain. Casual speech often drops the い: まだ食べてない.
Short answer to a もう question.

formation.form: (past point) まだ + V (て-form) + いませんでした
formation.note: Not yet, as of a point in the past.

examples.japanese: いいえ、まだ食べていません。
examples.reading: いいえ、まだたべていません。
examples.romaji: iie, mada tabete imasen.
examples.english: No, I haven’t eaten yet.
examples.note: An answer to もう昼ご飯を食べましたか.

examples.japanese: 宿題はまだ終わっていません。
examples.reading: しゅくだいはまだおわっていません。
examples.romaji: shukudai wa mada owatte imasen.
examples.english: My homework isn’t finished yet.

examples.japanese: 田中さんはまだ来ていません。
examples.reading: たなかさんはまだきていません。
examples.romaji: tanaka-san wa mada kite imasen.
examples.english: Mr Tanaka hasn’t come yet.

mistake.wrong: いいえ、まだ食べませんでした。
mistake.problem: English speakers reach for the past because of “I didn’t eat yet”. But “not yet” is about whether the action has happened up to now, so Japanese uses the negative of the ている form. ませんでした normally reports that something did not happen in a past situation, so it is not the usual answer here.
mistake.right: いいえ、まだ食べていません。

distinguish_from.note: まだ～ていません is the negative of the ている state: not having done something so far. With an affirmative ている, まだ means “still”: まだ寝ています, “He is still asleep”.
～たことがない says you have never had the experience at all. まだ～ていません says something expected has not happened yet. まだ can join ことがない to mean “have never yet”.

review.note: Revised after review: the why now uses the reviewer’s wording (ませんでした is the polite past negative, plain なかった; ていない described as not having occurred up to the reference time, since ていない can also negate an ongoing action or state). The mistake’s problem was aligned with it. The past-point form まだ～ていませんでした is only in formation and why, not in an example, to keep the entry at N5.

reviews.note: ませんでした is the polite past negative, not the plain past negative; the plain form is なかった. Also, the reasoning treats ていない too generally as meaning ‘not having done V’, although it can instead negate an ongoing action or state. Replace the relevant explanation with: “In this use, Vていない describes an action as not having occurred or been completed up to the reference time. With まだ and a present reference time, it means ‘not yet’. The polite past negative Vませんでした (plain: Vなかった) normally reports that an action did not occur in a past situation, rather than that it remains undone now, so it is not the usual form for answering ‘Have you eaten yet?’ negatively.”
Accurately explains the present-reference and past-reference uses of “not yet”; the forms, examples, and contrasts are sound.
The explanation correctly distinguishes an action not yet completed from a past nonoccurrence. The examples and forms are accurate.

title: Saying which of two things is more ...
meaning: A のほうが B より X: A is more X than B. より marks what A is compared against.
when: Use it to compare two things and say which has more of a quality: the train is faster than the bus. It is the usual answer to a question like AとBとどちらが…ですか. Either half can stand alone: AのほうがX when B is already clear, or AはBよりX when you are simply saying something about A.
why: Japanese adjectives have no comparative form: 速い can mean fast or faster depending on the sentence. The comparison is carried by other words. より means "than" and marks the standard you measure against. ほう means "side", so AのほうがX says "A's side is X": of the pair, A is the one. が marks A as the one picked out, which is why this shape fits an answer to "which one?". The halves can swap places (BよりAのほうがX) without changing the meaning. The adjective stays in its ordinary form. To compare two actions, ほう follows the verb directly, with no の.

formation.form: A のほうが B より + adjective
formation.note: Polite: add です after an い-adjective; a な-adjective takes です directly.

formation.form: B より A のほうが + adjective
formation.note: The same meaning with the halves swapped.
B is left out when it is clear, as in an answer to a question.

formation.form: A は B より + adjective
formation.note: A statement about A, measured against B, without picking one of a pair: 今日は昨日より寒いです.

formation.form: V1 (dictionary form) より V2 (dictionary form) ほうが + adjective
formation.note: Comparing two actions: ほう follows the verb directly, with no の.

examples.japanese: 電車のほうがバスより速いです。
examples.reading: でんしゃのほうがバスよりはやいです。
examples.romaji: densha no hō ga basu yori hayai desu.
examples.english: The train is faster than the bus.

examples.japanese: 犬と猫とどちらが好きですか。猫のほうが好きです。
examples.reading: いぬとねことどちらがすきですか。ねこのほうがすきです。
examples.romaji: inu to neko to dochira ga suki desu ka. neko no hō ga suki desu.
examples.english: Which do you like better, dogs or cats? I like cats better.
examples.note: The answer leaves out 犬より, because the question already named both.

examples.japanese: 今日は昨日より寒いです。
examples.reading: きょうはきのうよりさむいです。
examples.romaji: kyō wa kinō yori samui desu.
examples.english: Today is colder than yesterday.
examples.note: Here は, not のほうが: the sentence is simply about today, not picking one of a pair.

examples.japanese: バスで行くより歩くほうが早いです。
examples.reading: バスでいくよりあるくほうがはやいです。
examples.romaji: basu de iku yori aruku hō ga hayai desu.
examples.english: Walking is quicker than going by bus.

mistake.wrong: 電車よりバスのほうが速いです。
mistake.problem: Intended as "the train is faster than the bus". より marks the thing being compared against, the "than" side, not the winner, so this sentence says the bus is faster.
mistake.right: バスより電車のほうが速いです。

distinguish_from.note: のほうが contrasts two alternatives. の中で…いちばん identifies the highest-ranked member of a group, usually three or more; for two alternatives, のほうが is generally preferred.
The same ほう, "side", used for advice: 行ったほうがいい is "the side of going is good".

review.note: Revised after review: fixed the particle order in the example note (犬より), added the AはBより formation, and softened the OJG-0026 comparison ('usually three or more'). Still open: the verb comparison (歩くほうが早い) may be N4 in some lists, and 早い (quick in time) is used there rather than 速い; please confirm.

reviews.note: In the second example’s note, より犬 has the particle in the wrong position. Write: “The answer leaves out 犬より, because the question already named both.” Add the formation “A は B より + adjective,” which the explanation and third example use. In distinguish_from OJG-0026, “three or more” is not a grammatical requirement for いちばん. Write: “のほうが contrasts two alternatives. の中で…いちばん identifies the highest-ranked member of a group, usually three or more; for two alternatives, のほうが is generally preferred.”
The comparison structure, role of より, action comparisons, and correction are accurate.
The comparison structure, particle roles, examples, and correction are accurate.

title: Saying which one is the most ... in a group
meaning: Group の中で A がいちばん X: of everything in the group, A is the most X.
when: Use it to identify the highest-ranked member of a group, usually three or more: the fruit you like best, the tallest person in the class. It is also how you ask the question: …の中で何／どれ／だれがいちばん…ですか. For exactly two things, のほうが is generally preferred, though 一番 is also possible.
why: 中 means "inside", and で marks the range the choice is made within, so の中で sets out the group: "among these". いちばん, literally "number one", goes before the adjective and makes it "the most". The adjective itself does not change. が marks the one singled out, for the same reason as in のほうが: it answers "which one?". In the question, the question word fits what is being chosen: だれ for people, 何 or どれ for things, どこ for places. With a place or a period of time, で alone is common instead of の中で: 日本で一番高い山.

formation.form: group の中で A が一番 + adjective
formation.note: Polite: add です. 一番 is often written in kana, いちばん.

formation.form: group の中で 何／どれ／だれ／どこ が一番 + adjective + ですか
formation.note: The question. The question word matches what is being chosen.

formation.form: place / time で A が一番 + adjective
formation.note: With a place or a period, で alone is common.

examples.japanese: 果物の中でりんごが一番好きです。
examples.reading: くだもののなかでりんごがいちばんすきです。
examples.romaji: kudamono no naka de ringo ga ichiban suki desu.
examples.english: Of all fruit, I like apples best.

examples.japanese: クラスの中でだれが一番背が高いですか。
examples.reading: クラスのなかでだれがいちばんせがたかいですか。
examples.romaji: kurasu no naka de dare ga ichiban se ga takai desu ka.
examples.english: Who is the tallest in the class?

examples.japanese: 日本で一番高い山は富士山です。
examples.reading: にほんでいちばんたかいやまはふじさんです。
examples.romaji: nihon de ichiban takai yama wa fujisan desu.
examples.english: The highest mountain in Japan is Mount Fuji.
examples.note: With a place, で alone. Here 一番高い describes 山, and the answer comes after は.

mistake.wrong: 果物の中にりんごが一番好きです。
mistake.problem: の中に says where something is, as with ある or いる: 箱の中にりんごがあります. The range a choice is made within is marked with で.
mistake.right: 果物の中でりんごが一番好きです。

distinguish_from.note: のほうが…より contrasts two alternatives. の中で…一番 identifies the highest-ranked member of a group. For exactly two alternatives, のほうが is generally preferred, but 一番 is also possible.
で usually marks where an action happens. Here it marks the range a choice is made within.

review.note: Revised after review: three or more is now a tendency, not a requirement, in both when and the OJG-0025 note; 一番 with two alternatives is stated as possible.

reviews.note: The distinction treats three or more members as a requirement, but いちばん can also be used with a set of two. Change the opening of when to “Use it to identify the highest-ranked member of a group, usually three or more.” Replace the distinguish_from OJG-0025 note with: “のほうが…より contrasts two alternatives. の中で…一番 identifies the highest-ranked member of a group. For exactly two alternatives, のほうが is generally preferred, but 一番 is also possible.”
Correctly explains superlative comparisons and the range-marking use of で. The examples and readings are accurate.
The explanation of comparison within a group, including the qualification about two alternatives, is accurate. The examples are correct.

title: Saying what you intend to do
meaning: V (dictionary form) + つもりです: someone intends or plans to do V. V-ないつもりです: intends not to.
when: Use it to state a plan the speaker has already made: 来年日本へ行くつもりです. It is also used to ask about the listener's plans. The negative, V-ないつもり, says you intend not to do something.
why: つもり is a noun meaning an intention held in mind. A verb describes a noun by standing in front of it in its plain form, so the verb comes first and です follows: 行くつもりです, "it is my intention to go". Because つもり names what is in someone's mind, it is most natural about the speaker, or in a question to the listener. About someone else it is usually reported, since you are telling what they told you. つもり suggests a plan already decided, not a passing thought. Asking someone senior directly about their つもり can sound pointed, so people tend to phrase that question another way.

formation.note: Plain: つもりだ.
Intending not to do it.

formation.form: V (dictionary form) + つもりはありません
formation.note: I have no intention of doing it. This can serve as a firm refusal in context, but it does not in itself express refusal. Compare V-ないつもりです, which states an intention not to do it.

examples.japanese: 夏休みに日本へ行くつもりです。
examples.reading: なつやすみににほんへいくつもりです。
examples.romaji: natsuyasumi ni nihon e iku tsumori desu.
examples.english: I plan to go to Japan in the summer holidays.

examples.japanese: 今日はお酒を飲まないつもりです。
examples.reading: きょうはおさけをのまないつもりです。
examples.romaji: kyō wa osake o nomanai tsumori desu.
examples.english: I'm not planning to drink today.

examples.japanese: 週末は何をするつもりですか。
examples.reading: しゅうまつはなにをするつもりですか。
examples.romaji: shūmatsu wa nani o suru tsumori desu ka.
examples.english: What are you planning to do this weekend?
examples.note: Asking the listener about their plans.

mistake.wrong: 明日は雨が降るつもりです。
mistake.problem: English "going to" covers both plans and predictions, but つもり is only someone's intention, and rain has none. For a prediction, use でしょう.
mistake.right: 明日は雨が降るでしょう。

distinguish_from.note: ～たい says what you want to do. つもり says what you have decided to do; you can want something you do not intend.
でしょう is a guess about what will happen. つもり is a person's plan.
～ましょう proposes doing something together. つもり states a plan already made.

review.note: Revised after review: つもりはありません is no longer called a refusal. Still open: left out た + つもり ("I thought I had…", e.g. 閉めたつもり), usually taught at N4. Please check the two tendency claims: third-person つもり is usually reported, and asking a senior about their つもり can sound pointed.

reviews.note: The formation note labels Vつもりはありません a “firmer refusal,” but it states an absence of intention and need not be a refusal or a stronger decision not to act. Replace that note with: “I have no intention of doing it. This can serve as a firm refusal in context, but it does not inherently express refusal. Compare Vないつもりです, which explicitly states an intention not to do it.”
Accurately presents intentional plans, negative intentions, and the contrast with predictions and wishes.
The entry accurately explains intentional plans, their negative forms, and the contrast with predictions. The examples are natural and correct.

title: Saying something becomes or gets ...
meaning: い-adj (い→く) + なる; な-adj or noun + になる: something changes and becomes that way.
when: Use it for a change of state: it is getting cold, the room became clean, someone became a doctor. The past, なりました, is very common for a change that has happened, often where English would say "has got" or "is now".
why: なる means "become". To join a describing word to it, that word takes the form that describes a verb. An い-adjective swaps its final い for く, the same く you see in 寒くない: 寒い becomes 寒くなる, "become cold". な-adjectives and nouns take に, which marks the result of the change, much as に marks where you arrive: 静かになる, 医者になる. So the choice between く and に is decided by the kind of word, not by meaning. いい is irregular and uses its other stem, よ: よくなる. Some な-adjectives end in い, such as きれい, and still take に.

formation.note: 寒い → 寒くなる. いい becomes よくなる.
静か → 静かになる. No な before に.
医者 → 医者になる.

formation.form: Polite: なります; past: なりました
formation.note: なる is an ordinary う-verb.

examples.japanese: だんだん寒くなりました。
examples.reading: だんだんさむくなりました。
examples.romaji: dandan samuku narimashita.
examples.english: It has gradually got colder.

examples.japanese: 部屋がきれいになりました。
examples.reading: へやがきれいになりました。
examples.romaji: heya ga kirei ni narimashita.
examples.english: The room is clean now.
examples.note: きれい ends in い but is a な-adjective (きれいな部屋), so it takes に.

examples.japanese: 兄は医者になりました。
examples.reading: あにはいしゃになりました。
examples.romaji: ani wa isha ni narimashita.
examples.english: My older brother became a doctor.

examples.japanese: 天気がよくなりました。
examples.reading: てんきがよくなりました。
examples.romaji: tenki ga yoku narimashita.
examples.english: The weather has got better.
examples.note: いい becomes よく.

mistake.wrong: 寒いになりました。
mistake.problem: 寒い is an い-adjective, so it does not take に. Change the final い to く, then add なる.
mistake.right: 寒くなりました。

distinguish_from.note: する instead of なる: ～くする／～にする means someone makes something that way. なる says it becomes that way.
です states what something is now. なる states a change into it.

review.note: OJG-0084 (～く/～にする) is an N4 stub, used as a neighbour. The negative (～なくなる, e.g. 行かなくなる) is left out as more N4 than N5.

reviews.note: The adjective and noun formations, irregular よくなる, examples, and distinctions are accurate.

title: Saying what you want to do
meaning: V (ます-stem) + たい: I want to do V. It changes like an い-adjective: たくない, たかった.
when: Use it to say what the speaker wants to do, and to ask what the listener wants to do. For someone else's wish, Japanese usually uses たがっている or reports it. To want a thing rather than an action, use ほしい instead.
why: たい joins the verb stem, the part left when you take ます away: 食べます → 食べ, 飲みます → 飲み, します → し. The result is an い-adjective, so it changes like one: 食べたい, 食べたくない, 食べたかった, and 食べたいです for polite speech. As a word of feeling, it reports a wish from the inside. Japanese tends not to state another person's inner feelings as plain fact, because you cannot see inside them, so for someone else speakers usually say what they can observe (行きたがっています, "is showing that he wants to go") or report it (行きたいと言っていました). Asking the listener is fine, but asking someone senior what they want can sound too direct; offers are often made with ～ませんか or ～ましょうか instead. With a verb that takes を, the object can be marked with を or with が: 水を飲みたい, 水が飲みたい.

formation.note: 食べます → 食べたい; 行きます → 行きたい; します → したい; 来ます → 来たい (きたい).
Polite: add です; たい itself does not change.

formation.form: V (ます-stem) + たくない／たかった／たくなかった
formation.note: Negative, past, and negative past, as for any い-adjective.
With a verb that takes を, both を and が are used for the object.

formation.form: V (ます-stem) + たがっている
formation.note: For someone else's wish: they show that they want to.

title: Doing things like A and B
meaning: V1-たり V2-たりする: do things such as V1 and V2, as examples rather than a full list or a fixed order.
when: Use it to give a few sample activities: what you do on weekends, what you did on holiday. The listener understands there may be other things too, and that the order is not the point. With only one たり, it gives a single example and sounds less definite: 週末は映画を見たりします, “At weekends I watch films and so on”. A second common use pairs two opposite or alternating actions or states: 行ったり来たりする, “go back and forth”.
why: Each listed action is in the た-form with り added, and none of them carries its own tense. In the full paired pattern, each listed predicate takes たり, and the final する carries tense and politeness: 読んだり見たりしました. The final する gathers the actions into one activity, “doing things like these”. Because the actions are samples of one activity, the pattern does not say they happened in this order or that there were no others. For a sequence in order, Japanese uses the て-form or ～てから instead.

formation.form: V1 (た-form) + り、V2 (た-form) + り + する
formation.note: Polite: ～たりします. Past: ～たりしました. The た-form's sound changes carry over: 読んだり, 遊んだり.
Gives one example, or softens the statement; it does not necessarily imply additional activities.

formation.form: い-adj (かった) + り／noun, な-adj + だったり
formation.note: Also used with states, often alternating ones: 暑かったり寒かったり.
