title: Have done something before (experience)
meaning: V-たことがある: have the experience of doing V at some point; ～たことがない: have never done V.
when: Use it to talk about experiences in your life so far: places you have been, food you have eaten, things you have tried. It is how you ask “Have you ever…?” (～たことがありますか) and say “I have never…” (～たことがありません).
why: こと turns the clause before it into a thing: 行ったこと is “the fact of having gone”. がある then says that thing exists, in your life so far. So the sentence is about whether the experience exists, not about when it happened. That is why it usually sits badly with a specific recent time such as 昨日, where the plain past is used, and why it tends to sound odd with everyday actions nobody would count as an experience, unless the context makes them notable. The verb before こと is in the た-form; with the dictionary form, ～ることがある means something different, that something happens sometimes.

formation.note: Polite: ～たことがあります. Question: ～たことがありますか.
Never. Polite: ～たことがありません. In negatives, は often replaces が: 行ったことはありません.

title: And (giving some examples)
meaning: や joins nouns as examples from a longer list: "A and B, among others". Often followed by など.
when: Use it between nouns when the ones you name are examples, not the whole list: かばんの中に本やノートがあります, "there are books, notebooks and so on in the bag". It often ends with など, "and so on". Like と, it joins nouns only.
why: や tells the listener that the nouns named are a sample. Choosing between や and と is about how you present the list, not about how long the real list is: と says "these are the ones", や says "things like these". A speaker may use や without having anything particular in mind that was left out; the effect is to present the list as illustrative rather than exhaustive. など after the last item makes the "and so on" explicit. To list examples of actions rather than things, Japanese uses ～たり～たりする, not や.

formation.note: A non-exhaustive list.

formation.form: Noun A + や + Noun B + など
formation.note: など makes the "and so on" explicit.

title: Explaining, or asking for the story behind something
meaning: ～んです (のです): frames a statement as an explanation or background, or a question as asking for one.
when: It adds the sense that something is being explained, or that the speaker wants an explanation. Typical situations: giving the reason behind something the listener can see or has asked about (頭が痛いんです, “I have a headache”, when leaving early); asking about something you have noticed (どうしたんですか, “What's wrong?”); and setting up a request or a question with background (駅へ行きたいんですが…, “I want to go to the station, but…”). Without んです, the same sentence usually just reports a fact.
why: の turns a sentence into a thing, roughly “it is that…”. Wrapping a statement this way tends to link it to something both people are aware of: what just happened, what the listener can see, or what was asked. That is why it often sounds like an explanation, and why a question with んですか often sounds like asking about the story behind something you noticed, which can show interest. The same framing is why overuse can cause trouble: with nothing to explain, it can sound as if the speaker is insisting on a point or pressing for a reason, and some questions can come across as pushy or accusatory. Learners are usually safer using it when there is a clear situation to explain or ask about.

formation.note: 行くんです, 行ったんです, 高いんです. Written and formal speech use のです.
Affirmative nonpast だ becomes な: 学生なんです, 静かなんです. Other forms attach directly: 学生だったんです, 学生ではないんです, 静かではなかったんです.
Asking for an explanation or background.
Casual. In casual questions, ～の？ with rising intonation: どうしたの？

It often ends a sentence, but can also precede a connective, as in 駅へ行きたいんですが….”

title: Saying something is too much, or you did too much
meaning: V (ます-stem) / adjective stem + すぎる: too much. Doing V to excess, or being more X than is good.
when: Use it for going past the right amount: I ate too much, this bag is too expensive, the town is too quiet. It usually carries a complaint or explains a problem: 高すぎて買えません. In casual speech it is also used as strong praise, as in かわいすぎる, where nothing is really wrong.
why: すぎる on its own means "go past". Joined to a verb or an adjective, it says the action or the quality went past a proper point: 食べすぎる is "eat past the limit". Going past the right point is usually a problem, which is why the pattern normally sounds negative. The result is itself a る-verb, so it changes like one: すぎます, すぎました, すぎて, すぎない. Verbs join with the ます-stem; adjectives join with their stem: an い-adjective drops its final い, and a な-adjective drops な. いい is irregular: よすぎる. The adjective ない ("there is none") normally becomes なさすぎる, as in お金がなさすぎる, "I have far too little money". Adjectives ending in ない do not all behave alike: 少ない becomes 少なすぎる, while a compound such as 申し訳ない becomes 申し訳なさすぎる.

formation.note: 食べます → 食べすぎる; 飲みます → 飲みすぎる.

高い → 高すぎる. いい becomes よすぎる. The adjective ない normally becomes なさすぎる (お金がなさすぎる); adjectives ending in ない do not all behave alike: 少ない normally becomes 少なすぎる, whereas a compound such as 申し訳ない normally becomes 申し訳なさすぎる.
静か → 静かすぎる.

formation.form: …すぎます／すぎました／すぎて
formation.note: すぎる is a る-verb. すぎて often gives the reason for a problem.

title: Giving advice: you'd better, or you'd better not
meaning: V-たほうがいい: you'd better do V. V-ないほうがいい: you'd better not. Used to give advice.
when: Use it to advise someone to do something or not to do it: 早く寝たほうがいいですよ. You can also ask for advice about yourself: 私も行ったほうがいいですか. After a noun, のほうがいい says which one you prefer: コーヒーのほうがいいです, "I'd rather have coffee".
why: ほう means "side", as in comparisons with のほうが, and いい means "good". So 行ったほうがいい is literally "the side of going is good": out of doing it and not doing it, doing it is better. That is why it sounds like a recommendation, and it can be fairly firm. For advice to do something, the past た-form is the usual choice (行ったほうがいい). The dictionary form (行くほうがいい) is also used, often when weighing options in general. For ordinary advice not to do something, normally use V-ないほうがいい (行かないほうがいい). Because it presses an opinion on the listener, it is often softened with と思います, or said with よ as friendly advice; to someone senior it can sound presumptuous.

formation.note: The usual form of advice to do something: 休んだほうがいい.
Also used, often when comparing options in general.
For ordinary advice not to do something, normally use V-ないほうがいい.

formation.form: …ほうがいいです／ほうがいいと思います
formation.note: Polite forms. と思います softens the advice.
Saying which one is better or which you prefer.

mistake.problem: This copies the past form used in positive advice (飲んだほうがいい) onto the negative. Negative-past forms do occur, but for ordinary advice not to do something, the normal choice is V-ないほうがいい.
mistake.right: この水は飲まないほうがいいです。

distinguish_from.note: The same ほう, "side". のほうが…より compares two things; ほうがいい recommends one course of action.
～てください makes a request or gives an instruction. ～ほうがいい recommends an option as better.
～てはいけません forbids. ～ないほうがいい only advises against, and leaves the choice to the listener.

review.note: Revised after review: the ban on なかったほうがいい is gone; V-ないほうがいい is now 'the normal choice', and the mistake is framed as copying the positive past form. The てください comparison no longer says advice is for the listener's own good. Still open: た-form vs dictionary-form ほうがいい is stated only as a tendency (た for specific advice, dictionary form for general comparison); a reviewer may prefer to say less.

reviews.note: The categorical ban on negative-past forms is too strong: ～なかったほうがいい does occur, although ～ないほうがいい is the normal choice for prospective negative advice. Replace 'Always the ない-form, not a past form' and the corresponding explanation with 'For ordinary advice not to do something, normally use V-ないほうがいい.' Keep the corrected water sentence, but diagnose the mistake as mechanically copying the past form used in positive advice, rather than claiming that negative-past forms are universally impossible. Also replace the てください comparison with '～てください makes a request or gives an instruction; ～ほうがいい recommends an option as better.' Advice need not be for the listener's own good.
The advice constructions, qualifications about alternative forms, and examples are accurate.

title: Because (often softer than から)
meaning: X ので Y: Y because of X; often sounds softer or more matter-of-fact than から.
when: Use it to give a reason or cause, then the result: it is raining, so I will stay home. It is common when explaining yourself politely, in apologies and requests, and in speaking to someone you want to be polite to. In many sentences から would also be correct.
why: ので contains の, which presents what comes before it as a fact or circumstance. The reason then sounds like part of the situation, rather than the speaker's own argument, and that is why ので is often felt to be softer or more objective than から. This is a tendency, not a rule: both are used for ordinary reasons, and the choice often comes down to tone. Because of the の inside it, a noun or な-adjective before ので takes な, as it does before の elsewhere: 雨なので.

formation.note: 降るので, 降ったので, 高いので.
な replaces だ: 休みなので, 静かなので.
Very polite, heard in formal or service speech.

examples.japanese: 雨が降っているので、今日は家にいます。
examples.reading: あめがふっているので、きょうはいえにいます。
examples.romaji: ame ga futte iru node, kyō wa ie ni imasu.
examples.english: It’s raining, so I’ll stay home today.

examples.japanese: 明日はテストなので、早く寝ます。
examples.reading: あしたはテストなので、はやくねます。
examples.romaji: ashita wa tesuto na node, hayaku nemasu.
examples.english: I have a test tomorrow, so I’ll go to bed early.

examples.japanese: すみません、電車が遅れたので、遅くなりました。
examples.reading: すみません、でんしゃがおくれたので、おそくなりました。
examples.romaji: sumimasen, densha ga okureta node, osoku narimashita.
examples.english: I’m sorry, I’m late because the train was delayed.
examples.note: An apology: ので is a common choice for explaining yourself.

mistake.wrong: 明日は休みだので、映画を見に行きます。
mistake.problem: Before ので, a noun or な-adjective takes な, not だ. Learners who know だから often carry the だ across.
mistake.right: 明日は休みなので、映画を見に行きます。

distinguish_from.note: Both give a reason and are often interchangeable. から tends to put the speaker's own reasoning to the front; ので tends to present the reason as a circumstance, so it often sounds softer. Before a command or a strong statement of will, から is more common.
～んです also presents something as background, but ends the sentence; ので joins the reason to a result.

review.note: The distinguish_from note says から is “more common” before commands or strong will; I believe this holds as a tendency but have avoided saying ので cannot be used there. Casual contraction んで is left out.

reviews.note: The explanation, examples, readings, translations, and principal contrast with から are accurate; the level is plausible.

title: I have to... (casual)
meaning: V-なくちゃいけない: casual "have to V"; literally "if I don't V, it is no good".
when: Use it in casual speech to say that something has to be done, often by the speaker (もう帰らなくちゃいけない). It is often cut short to なくちゃ alone: 行かなくちゃ, "I have to go". In formal speech and formal writing, prefer fuller forms such as ～なくてはいけません and ～なければなりません.
why: Start from the ない-form, "not doing V". Its て-form is なくて, and なくては sets up the condition "if (you) don't do V". いけない means "it won't do". So the sentence says "not doing V is no good", and two negatives make an obligation: you must do V. なくちゃ contracts なくては: ては → ちゃ. The corresponding voiced contraction is では → じゃ, as in 飲んではいけない → 飲んじゃいけない. The logic matches てはいけません (OJG-0016), which says doing V is no good; here it is not doing V that is no good. なければなりません is built the same way with a different conditional (なければ, "if not") and a different ending (ならない, "it won't do"), and is the usual choice in formal speech and writing.

formation.form: V (ない-form, drop い) + くちゃいけない
formation.note: 行かない → 行かなくちゃいけない; 食べない → 食べなくちゃいけない.
Casual, with いけない left unsaid: 帰らなくちゃ.

formation.form: V-なくてはいけません / V-なければなりません
formation.note: Polite and formal relatives with the same meaning.
Another casual contraction, from なければ.

examples.japanese: 明日は早く起きなくちゃいけない。
examples.reading: あしたははやくおきなくちゃいけない。
examples.romaji: ashita wa hayaku okinakucha ikenai.
examples.english: I have to get up early tomorrow.

examples.japanese: もう九時だ。帰らなくちゃ。
examples.reading: もうくじだ。かえらなくちゃ。
examples.romaji: mō kuji da. kaeranakucha.
examples.english: It's already nine. I have to go home.

examples.japanese: 毎日、薬を飲まなければなりません。
examples.reading: まいにち、くすりをのまなければなりません。
examples.romaji: mainichi, kusuri o nomanakereba narimasen.
examples.english: I have to take medicine every day.
examples.note: The formal relative, for polite speech or writing.

mistake.wrong: 明日、会社に行かないちゃいけない。
mistake.problem: ない becomes なく before て or ちゃ, just as an い-adjective does (高い → 高くて). The contraction comes from 行かなくては, so it is 行かなくちゃ.
mistake.right: 明日、会社に行かなくちゃいけない。

distinguish_from.note: てはいけない says doing V is no good (must not); なくちゃいけない says not doing V is no good (must).
ほうがいい gives advice ("you had better"); なくちゃいけない states an obligation.

review.note: Revised after review: the contraction sentence now separates ては → ちゃ from では → じゃ, and the register claim in when is limited to formal speech and formal writing (なくちゃいけません does occur in conversational polite speech). The differences between なければならない and なくてはいけない (ならない often felt more general or formal, いけない more personal) are deliberately not stated as a rule; only "usual choice in formal speech and writing" is claimed for なければなりません. Please check that claim.

reviews.note: The contraction illustrated by 飲んじゃいけない is では → じゃ, not literally ては → ちゃ. Write: 'なくちゃ contracts なくては: ては → ちゃ. The corresponding voiced contraction is では → じゃ, as in 飲んではいけない → 飲んじゃいけない.' Also, fuller forms are not obligatory in all polite speech or writing: なくちゃいけません occurs in conversational polite speech, and contractions occur in informal writing. Replace that register claim with 'In formal speech and formal writing, prefer fuller forms such as ～なくてはいけません and ～なければなりません.'

title: Probably; or “…, right?”
meaning: ～でしょう: says something is probably so; with rising intonation, asks the listener to agree.
when: Use it for a guess or a prediction you are fairly but not fully sure of: weather forecasts use it constantly (明日は雨が降るでしょう). It is often paired with たぶん, “probably”. With rising intonation, でしょう？ asks the listener to confirm something you expect they will agree with: “…, right?”. でしょうか is a softer, polite question, “I wonder…?” or “Would it be…?”. The plain form is だろう.
why: In its conjectural use, でしょう presents something as probable rather than asserting it outright: です says “it is”, でしょう says “it would be”, which is why it fits guesses and forecasts. In its confirmation-seeking use, said with rising intonation, it presents something as expected to be shared or accepted by the listener; the speaker may be fully confident, and it can sometimes sound insistent. Normally attach でしょう directly to the plain form, omitting present affirmative だ after nouns and な-adjectives. ～ますでしょう(か) also occurs in especially polite speech, but plain form + でしょう is the standard learner pattern. In conversation, plain だろう can sound blunt, and casual speech often uses でしょ？ for “right?”.

formation.note: 降るでしょう, 降ったでしょう, 高いでしょう.
No だ: 雨でしょう, 静かでしょう.
Asking for agreement. Casual: ～でしょ？
The plain form, common in writing and in thinking to oneself.

examples.japanese: 明日は雨が降るでしょう。
examples.reading: あしたはあめがふるでしょう。
examples.romaji: ashita wa ame ga furu deshō.
examples.english: It will probably rain tomorrow.
examples.note: The typical weather-forecast sentence.

examples.japanese: 田中さんはたぶん来ないでしょう。
examples.reading: たなかさんはたぶんこないでしょう。
examples.romaji: tanaka-san wa tabun konai deshō.
examples.english: Mr Tanaka probably won’t come.

examples.japanese: この店のケーキ、おいしいでしょう？
examples.reading: このみせのケーキ、おいしいでしょう？
examples.romaji: kono mise no kēki, oishii deshō?
examples.english: The cakes at this shop are good, aren’t they?
examples.note: Rising intonation: the speaker expects agreement.

mistake.wrong: 明日は暑いですでしょう。
mistake.problem: In the standard learner construction, でしょう attaches directly to 暑い, without です. 暑いですでしょう layers polite endings and is not the standard form.
mistake.right: 明日は暑いでしょう。

distinguish_from.note: です states something as so. でしょう presents it as probable, or, rising, as something the listener should confirm.
～ましょう proposes an action, including invitations and offers; ～でしょう expresses conjecture or seeks confirmation. The two only look alike.

review.note: Revised after review: the why no longer says ます can never come before でしょう; it now gives plain form + でしょう as the standard pattern and notes ～ますでしょう(か) in especially polite speech. The mistake calls 暑いですでしょう redundant and non-standard rather than impossible, and the ましょう comparison no longer limits ましょう to doing something together. Still open: whether “it would be” is a fair gloss, and whether “だろう can sound blunt” is safe. The link between だろう and male speakers is left out on purpose.

reviews.note: The claim that でしょう never has ます before it is false in contemporary usage: forms such as 分かりますでしょうか occur in especially polite speech, though they can be criticized as redundant. Write: 'Normally attach でしょう directly to the plain form, omitting present affirmative だ after nouns and な-adjectives. ～ますでしょう(か) also occurs in especially polite speech, but plain form + でしょう is the standard learner pattern.' Keep 暑いでしょう as the correction, but explain that 暑いですでしょう is redundant and not the standard construction, rather than deriving a universal ban from politeness. In the ましょう comparison, write '～ましょう proposes an action, including invitations and offers; ～でしょう expresses conjecture or seeks confirmation,' since ましょう is not limited to doing something together.

The reasoning incorrectly extends lack of full commitment to confirmation-seeking でしょう. Speakers can use that construction for something they know confidently, including insistently reminding the listener. Replace the opening reasoning with: “In conjectural use, でしょう presents something as probable rather than asserting it outright. In confirmation-seeking use, it presents something as expected to be shared or accepted by the listener; the speaker may be fully confident, and the expression can sometimes sound insistent.” Also replace the mistake diagnosis's semantic ‘says the same thing twice’ explanation with: “In the standard learner construction, でしょう attaches directly to 暑い, without です. 暑いですでしょう layers polite endings and is not the standard form.”
The entry correctly distinguishes conjecture from confirmation-seeking and gives appropriate formation and register guidance. The examples and correction are sound.

title: Before doing something
meaning: V (dictionary form) + まえに / N + の + まえに: do the main action before V or N.
when: Use it to say that one thing is done before another: brush your teeth before bed, study a little before coming to Japan, wash your hands before a meal. With a length of time, 前 has a related meaning, “ago”: 三年前に, “three years ago”.
why: 前 means “front”, and in time it means “earlier”. The clause before まえに names a point in time, and the main action happens before it. At the time of the main action, that later event has not happened yet, so the verb before まえに is in the dictionary (non-past) form, even when the whole sentence is about the past: 来る前に勉強しました, “I studied before I came”. The tense of the sentence goes on the main verb at the end. A noun is joined with の, as nouns usually are before 前.

formation.note: The verb stays in the dictionary form even in a past sentence.
食事の前に, 授業の前に.
“Ago”: 三日前に, 二年前に. No の.

examples.japanese: 寝る前に歯をみがきます。
examples.reading: ねるまえにはをみがきます。
examples.romaji: neru mae ni ha o migakimasu.
examples.english: I brush my teeth before I go to bed.

examples.japanese: 日本へ来る前に、少し日本語を勉強しました。
examples.reading: にほんへくるまえに、すこしにほんごをべんきょうしました。
examples.romaji: nihon e kuru mae ni, sukoshi nihongo o benkyō shimashita.
examples.english: Before I came to Japan, I studied a little Japanese.
examples.note: 来る stays in the dictionary form; the past is on 勉強しました.

examples.japanese: 食事の前に手を洗いましょう。
examples.reading: しょくじのまえにてをあらいましょう。
examples.romaji: shokuji no mae ni te o araimashō.
examples.english: Let’s wash our hands before the meal.

mistake.wrong: 日本へ来た前に、日本語を勉強しました。
mistake.problem: English “before I came” is in the past, so learners put the verb in the た-form. Before まえに the verb stays in the dictionary form; the past goes on the main verb.
mistake.right: 日本へ来る前に、日本語を勉強しました。

distinguish_from.note: ～まえに: the main action comes first, before V. ～てから: V comes first, then the main action.

review.note: The spatial meaning of 前 (駅の前に, “in front of the station”) is not mentioned; it could confuse, but it is vocabulary rather than this grammar point. The scope asked for the pattern as ～まえに; the Japanese examples write 前 in kanji.

reviews.note: The formation, relative-time explanation, examples, readings, translations, and correction are accurate; the level is plausible.

title: After doing something, then…
meaning: V-てから Y: after V, Y; also, since V.
when: Use it to say one action comes first and another follows it, especially when the order matters: wash your hands, then eat; finish homework, then go out. A second common use counts time from an event: 日本に来てから一年, “a year since I came to Japan”. ～たあとで also means “after”, and the two often overlap; ～てから tends to stress that the first action is done first, while ～たあとで tends to focus on the time that follows.
why: から marks a starting point. After a verb’s て-form, it sets an earlier event or situation as the starting point for what follows: 洗ってから is “starting from having washed”. In a sequence of actions, the first is normally finished before the next begins. In the “since” use, the starting point can be the beginning of a situation that is still going on: 東京に住んでから、もう十年になります. The tense and politeness go on the final verb, not on the て-form. After a plain form such as 帰った, から means “because” instead, so the form before から decides the meaning.

formation.note: Tense and politeness go on the main clause: 食べてから出かけました.

formation.form: V (て-form) + から + length of time
formation.note: Time since: 来てから三年.

examples.japanese: 手を洗ってから、ご飯を食べます。
examples.reading: てをあらってから、ごはんをたべます。
examples.romaji: te o aratte kara, gohan o tabemasu.
examples.english: I wash my hands, then eat.

examples.japanese: 宿題をしてから、遊びに行きました。
examples.reading: しゅくだいをしてから、あそびにいきました。
examples.romaji: shukudai o shite kara, asobi ni ikimashita.
examples.english: I did my homework and then went out to play.

examples.japanese: 日本に来てから、一年になります。
examples.reading: にほんにきてから、いちねんになります。
examples.romaji: nihon ni kite kara, ichinen ni narimasu.
examples.english: It has been a year since I came to Japan.
examples.note: The second use: time counted from an event.

mistake.wrong: 家に帰ったから、テレビを見ました。
mistake.problem: Meant as “after I got home”. But から after a plain past verb means “because”, so this says “Because I got home, I watched TV”. For “after”, から follows the て-form.
mistake.right: 家に帰ってから、テレビを見ました。

distinguish_from.note: から after a plain form (帰ったから) gives a reason. から after the て-form (帰ってから) gives an order in time.
～てから: V first, then the main action. ～まえに: the main action first, before V.
～たり～たりする lists sample actions in no particular order; ～てから fixes the order.

review.note: The contrast with ～たあとで is kept short and stated as a tendency; あとで has no OJG id in the N5 list, so it is only in `when`. Please confirm the time-since use belongs at N5; ～になる in the third example is OJG-0028 (N5).

reviews.note: The explanation, formation, examples, readings, translations, and contrasts are accurate. The mistake correctly distinguishes causal 帰ったから from temporal 帰ってから, and N5 is a plausible level.

The meaning and reasoning overstate completion: ～てから does not always mean that V has finished. In its “since” use, it can establish the beginning of an ongoing situation: 東京に住んでから、もう十年になります means “It has already been ten years since I started living in Tokyo,” without implying that the residence ended. Replace the meaning with “V-てから Y: after V, Y; also, since V.” Replace the first two sentences of the reasoning with “から marks a starting point. After a verb’s て-form, it establishes an earlier event or situation as the starting point for what follows. In action sequences, the first action is normally completed before the next begins; in the ‘since’ use, the starting point can be the beginning of a situation that continues.” The examples and their translations are correct.
The explanation, formation, examples, and contrasts are accurate.

title: Giving reasons, and there may be more
meaning: Plain form + し: lines up reasons or points, often towards a conclusion; a single し can hint that there are others.
when: Use it to list reasons or features that add up to a conclusion: この店は安いし、おいしいし、よく来ます, "this shop is cheap, and it's good, so I come often". A single し gives one reason and often suggests it is not the only one. When the conclusion is obvious, it can be left unsaid: 今日は忙しいし… can be a gentle way of saying no.
why: し adds a point to a pile. Each clause before it is a complete statement, so it keeps its own tense and negation (高いし, 高くないし, 雨だったし). For an affirmative non-past noun or な-adjective, that means keeping だ (静かだし, 学生だし); in polite speech, です can take its place. Because the points are piled up towards one conclusion, they usually point the same way. A single し often suggests there are other reasons too, and so can sound softer than から, though that depends on the context. から presents the cause; し offers supporting points.

formation.note: 行くし, 行かないし, 行ったし; 高いし, 高くないし. In polite speech, polite forms also occur before し: 行きますし.
学生だし, 静かだし; polite 学生ですし; past 雨だったし; negative 静かじゃないし. Do not drop the だ of an affirmative non-past form.

examples.japanese: この部屋は広いし、駅から近いし、とてもいいです。
examples.reading: このへやはひろいし、えきからちかいし、とてもいいです。
examples.romaji: kono heya wa hiroi shi, eki kara chikai shi, totemo ii desu.
examples.english: This room is spacious, and it's close to the station; it's really good.

examples.japanese: 今日は雨だし、寒いし、うちにいます。
examples.reading: きょうはあめだし、さむいし、うちにいます。
examples.romaji: kyō wa ame da shi, samui shi, uchi ni imasu.
examples.english: It's raining today, and it's cold, so I'm staying home.

examples.japanese: もう遅いし、そろそろ帰ります。
examples.reading: もうおそいし、そろそろかえります。
examples.romaji: mō osoi shi, sorosoro kaerimasu.
examples.english: It's late, for one thing, so I'll be heading home.
examples.note: One し, which here suggests there may be other reasons too.

mistake.wrong: この町は静かし、きれいだし、大好きです。
mistake.problem: A な-adjective needs だ before し, because each item has to be a complete statement. 静か on its own is not one.
mistake.right: この町は静かだし、きれいだし、大好きです。

distinguish_from.note: から states the reason as the cause of what follows. し offers one or more reasons as supporting points and often leaves room for more, which can make it sound less absolute.

reviews.note: The copula explanation is too broad: nouns and な-adjectives can form independent casual statements without だ, although affirmative plain nonpast predicates require it before し. Formation also omits polite copulas and negative forms. Write: 'Before し, use the predicate's conjugated form: 学生だし／学生ですし, 静かだったし, 静かじゃないし, 静かでしたし.' Replace 'The だ cannot be left out' with 'Do not omit だ from an affirmative plain nonpast noun or な-adjective predicate before し.' Also replace the categorical claims about additional reasons and softness with: 'A single し often suggests other supporting considerations and can soften a reason, but neither implication nor softness is guaranteed.' Apply that qualification to the meaning, why, example note, and から comparison.

title: I hear that… (passing on what you heard)
meaning: Plain form + そうです: reports something the speaker heard or read, "I hear that…", "apparently".
when: Use it to pass on information that came from someone else, the news, a notice: 明日は雨が降るそうです, "I hear it's going to rain tomorrow". The source can be named first with によると: 天気予報によると.
why: そう here means "so, like that", and points back at a statement: "it is said so". Because it attaches to a complete statement, the reported part keeps its own tense and negation (降った, 降らない), and an affirmative non-past noun or な-adjective keeps its だ (雨だそうです). The そうです itself normally stays non-past: tense and negation go in the part before it. The form marks the content as information from an outside source.

formation.form: Verb / い-adjective (plain form, any tense) + そうです
formation.note: 降るそうです, 降ったそうです, 降らないそうです; 高いそうです. Casual: そうだ.

formation.form: Noun / な-adjective + だ + そうです
formation.note: 雨だそうです, 静かだそうです; past 雨だったそうです.

examples.japanese: 天気予報によると、明日は雨が降るそうです。
examples.reading: てんきよほうによると、あしたはあめがふるそうです。
examples.romaji: tenki yohō ni yoru to, ashita wa ame ga furu sō desu.
examples.english: According to the weather forecast, it's going to rain tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 田中さんは来月結婚するそうです。
examples.reading: たなかさんはらいげつけっこんするそうです。
examples.romaji: tanaka-san wa raigetsu kekkon suru sō desu.
examples.english: I hear Tanaka-san is getting married next month.

examples.japanese: あの店のラーメンはとてもおいしいそうです。
examples.reading: あのみせのラーメンはとてもおいしいそうです。
examples.romaji: ano mise no rāmen wa totemo oishii sō desu.
examples.english: I hear the ramen at that shop is really good.

mistake.wrong: ニュースによると、明日はとても寒そうです。
mistake.problem: This is grammatical, but it says the speaker infers from the news that tomorrow looks likely to be cold. To pass on what the news said, use the full plain form before そうです.
mistake.right: ニュースによると、明日はとても寒いそうです。

distinguish_from.note: The "looks like" そうです attaches to a stem (降りそう, 寒そう) and gives your own impression. The hearsay そうです attaches to a full plain form (降るそう, 寒いそう) and passes on what you heard.

review.note: Tanos lists そうです (486) and ～そうです (505) separately; this entry takes 486 as the hearsay use, since Hanabira's ～そうだ was mapped to 0061 as "looks like". Is that the right split?

reviews.note: The mistake sentence is valid: 寒そうです can express the speaker's inference from a news report, not just something directly seen. Replace the diagnosis with: 'This says that tomorrow looks likely to be cold, based on the news. To transmit the news report itself rather than draw your own inference, use 寒いそうです.' Label this a meaning mismatch, not an ungrammatical sentence. Also, 'そうです itself does not change' and 'has no past form' are too absolute; retrospective reporting can use そうだった／そうでした. Write: 'Hearsay normally uses nonpast そうだ／そうです. Put the reported proposition's tense and negation before そう; do not confuse its forms with appearance そう.' Finally, replace 'not your own knowledge' with 'information attributed to an external source'; the speaker may also know it independently.

title: Try doing something to see how it goes
meaning: V-てみる: do V to see what it is like or what happens; "try V-ing".
when: Use it when you do something as an experiment, or for the first time, to find out the result: 着てみる, "try it on"; 食べてみる, "try eating it". It is common in requests (聞いてみてください) and wishes (行ってみたい).
why: みる is "see, look". After the て-form it says "do V, and see": you try the action out to find out what happens or what it is like. In an affirmative past statement, the trial normally was carried out, though it need not have succeeded (問題を解いてみたが、解けなかった). V-ようとする is different: it focuses on setting out to do something. Because the point is to find something out, てみる suits new and unfamiliar things. As a helper verb, みる is normally written in kana.

formation.note: Polite: てみます. Wish: てみたい. Request: てみてください.

examples.japanese: この靴をはいてみてもいいですか。
examples.reading: このくつをはいてみてもいいですか。
examples.romaji: kono kutsu o haite mite mo ii desu ka.
examples.english: May I try these shoes on?

examples.japanese: 初めて納豆を食べてみました。
examples.reading: はじめてなっとうをたべてみました。
examples.romaji: hajimete nattō o tabete mimashita.
examples.english: I tried natto for the first time.

examples.japanese: わからないときは、先生に聞いてみてください。
examples.reading: わからないときは、せんせいにきいてみてください。
examples.romaji: wakaranai toki wa, sensei ni kiite mite kudasai.
examples.english: When you don't understand, try asking the teacher.

mistake.wrong: 早く起きてみましたが、起きられませんでした。
mistake.problem: 起きてみました presents getting up as something actually tried out, which clashes with saying you could not get up. For an attempt that failed, 起きようとしました says what is meant.
mistake.right: 早く起きようとしましたが、起きられませんでした。

reviews.note: The claim that てみる 'is not an attempt that can fail' is false. For example, 問題を解いてみたが、解けなかった naturally describes trying the problem without succeeding. Write: 'てみる presents an action as a trial to discover its result. In an affirmative past statement, it normally indicates that the trial was undertaken, but it does not guarantee successful completion. ようとする focuses instead on attempting or intending to initiate the action.' Revise the mistake diagnosis to: '起きてみました normally presents getting up as something actually tried out, which clashes here with saying you could not get up. 起きようとしました clearly expresses the intended unsuccessful attempt.'

title: If it's that…, if that's the case
meaning: X なら: "if it's X", "if (as you say) X"; takes up something given and says what applies to it.
when: Use it to respond to something just said or to the situation, with advice, a suggestion or an opinion about it: 京都に行くなら、秋がいいですよ, "if you're going to Kyoto, autumn is good". After a noun, it picks that thing out as the topic of what you are about to say: 駅なら、あそこです, "the station? it's over there".
why: なら takes something as given, usually from the listener or the context, and then says what applies if that is so. It only sets up a premise, so the advice can be something to do before A: in 京都に行くなら、ガイドブックを買ったほうがいい, you buy the guidebook before you go. With two successive events, たら normally puts B after A has happened, which is why なら is the natural choice for advice about someone's plan.

formation.note: 駅なら, 静かなら; past 学生だったなら; negative 静かではないなら. のなら also occurs (学生なのなら).
行くなら, 行かないなら, 行ったなら; 寒いなら. のなら and, in speech, んなら also occur.

examples.japanese: 京都に行くなら、秋がいいですよ。
examples.reading: きょうとにいくなら、あきがいいですよ。
examples.romaji: kyōto ni iku nara, aki ga ii desu yo.
examples.english: If you're going to Kyoto, autumn is a good time.

examples.japanese: 「駅はどこですか。」「駅なら、あそこです。」
examples.reading: 「えきはどこですか。」「えきなら、あそこです。」
examples.romaji: "eki wa doko desu ka." "eki nara, asoko desu."
examples.english: "Where is the station?" "The station? It's over there."

examples.japanese: 寒いなら、窓を閉めましょうか。
examples.reading: さむいなら、まどをしめましょうか。
examples.romaji: samui nara, mado o shimemashō ka.
examples.english: If you're cold, shall I close the window?

mistake.wrong: 駅に着くなら、電話してください。
mistake.problem: The call should come after arriving. なら does not set an order, so this reads as "if you are going to arrive, call me", possibly beforehand. For "when you have arrived, then call", use たら.
mistake.right: 駅に着いたら、電話してください。

distinguish_from.note: With two successive events, たら normally puts B after A has happened. なら takes A as given and can give advice for before A.

reviews.note: The temporal contrast overstates たら and と: they do not universally require an earlier event followed by a later event. In particular, conditional states and hypothetical past situations need not have that sequence. Replace the why claim and distinguish_from note with: 'With successive events, たら normally places B after A occurs, whereas なら can introduce a premise for advice to be acted on before A. This is not a universal temporal-order rule for every use of たら or と.' Expand noun/な-adjective formation to include conjugated predicates: '学生なら／静かなら; 学生だったなら／静かだったなら; 学生ではないなら／静かではないなら. Before のなら, use 学生なのなら／静かなのなら.'

title: How many times in a period
meaning: Period + に + count: "so many times per period", as in 一週間に三回, "three times a week".
when: Use it to say how often something happens within a length of time: 一日に三回, "three times a day"; 一か月に一度, "once a month". The period comes first, then に, then the number of times.
why: に marks the frame an action is placed in. Here the frame is a length of time, and the count says how many times the action fits into it. The count works like an adverb and needs no particle of its own: 一週間に三回、プールで泳ぎます. With 週, 月 and 年, the 一 is often dropped: 週に二回, 月に一回, 年に一度.

formation.form: Period (一日, 一週間, 一か月, 一年; or 週, 月, 年) + に + number + 回／度
formation.note: 回 is the everyday counter for times; 度 is a little more formal.

examples.japanese: 一週間に三回、プールで泳ぎます。
examples.reading: いっしゅうかんにさんかい、プールでおよぎます。
examples.romaji: isshūkan ni sankai, pūru de oyogimasu.
examples.english: I swim at the pool three times a week.

examples.japanese: この薬は一日に二回飲んでください。
examples.reading: このくすりはいちにちににかいのんでください。
examples.romaji: kono kusuri wa ichinichi ni nikai nonde kudasai.
examples.english: Please take this medicine twice a day.

examples.japanese: 母には月に一度電話します。
examples.reading: ははにはつきにいちどでんわします。
examples.romaji: haha ni wa tsuki ni ichido denwa shimasu.
examples.english: I call my mother once a month.

mistake.wrong: 三回一週間にジムに行きます。
mistake.problem: This follows the English order, "three times a week". For an ordinary statement of how often, the period comes first and frames the count; 三回一週間に sounds awkward here.
mistake.right: 一週間に三回ジムに行きます。

review.note: Is 一週間で三回 worth mentioning as a neighbour (a total within one week, rather than a regular rate)? Left out as uncertain.

reviews.note: The count does not have to sit 'just before the verb'; your own examples put プールで or プールに between it and the verb. Replace that explanation with: 'The count functions adverbially and normally needs no additional particle. It need not be immediately adjacent to the verb: 一週間に三回、プールで泳ぎます.' The mistake diagnosis also treats the normal order as an absolute Japanese word-order rule. Write: 'For a neutral frequency expression, put the period before the count: 一週間に三回. 三回一週間に is awkward here without special emphasis or a pause, although Japanese allows reordered quantities in suitable contexts.'

title: Wanting a thing
meaning: N がほしい: "I want N". ほしい is an い-adjective for wanting a thing; in a plain statement, normally the speaker's want.
when: Use it to say what you want to have: 新しいかばんがほしいです. In a question, ask what the listener wants: 何がほしいですか. For what someone else wants, see ～たがる.
why: ほしい is an い-adjective describing a feeling: the thing is "wanted". Like other feeling words such as 好き or 痛い, it reports an inner state. In an ordinary statement about a present want, the one who wants is the speaker, and in a question, usually the listener. For someone else, Japanese normally reports what shows (ほしがっている) or what they said (ほしいと言っている), though ほしい can describe another person in suitable contexts, such as a story told from their point of view. The wanted thing is marked with が, not を, because ほしい is an adjective, not a verb: the thing is what the feeling is about, just as in 犬が好き. ほしい is for things; to want to do something, use the verb with たい.

formation.note: Polite: ほしいです. Negative: ほしくない; past: ほしかった. は replaces が for contrast: お金はほしくないです.

examples.japanese: 新しいパソコンがほしいです。
examples.reading: あたらしいパソコンがほしいです。
examples.romaji: atarashii pasokon ga hoshii desu.
examples.english: I want a new computer.

examples.japanese: 誕生日に何がほしいですか。
examples.reading: たんじょうびになにがほしいですか。
examples.romaji: tanjōbi ni nani ga hoshii desu ka.
examples.english: What do you want for your birthday?

examples.japanese: 子どものころ、犬がとてもほしかったです。
examples.reading: こどものころ、いぬがとてもほしかったです。
examples.romaji: kodomo no koro, inu ga totemo hoshikatta desu.
examples.english: When I was a child, I really wanted a dog.

mistake.wrong: 水をほしいです。
mistake.problem: ほしい is an adjective, not a verb, so the thing wanted is not its object. It takes が.
mistake.right: 水がほしいです。

distinguish_from.note: たい is for wanting to do something (水を飲みたい). ほしい is for wanting a thing (水がほしい).
てほしい is for wanting someone else to do something (手伝ってほしい). ほしい on its own wants a thing.
ほしい states a want directly, normally your own. ほしがる reports someone else's want as it shows.

reviews.note: The person restriction is overstated. A plain statement with ほしい need not describe the speaker: third-person uses occur when the desire is established in context or the speaker adopts that person's perspective. Replace the relevant explanation with: 'In an ordinary direct statement about a current personal desire, ほしい normally describes the speaker; questions commonly ask about the listener. For another person's desire, use ほしがっている for outward indications, or ほしいと言っている／ほしいそうだ for a report. Direct third-person ほしい is possible with suitable context or perspective.' Qualify the ほしがる comparison accordingly.

title: Someone else wants to (as it shows)
meaning: V-たがる: a third person shows signs of wanting to do V; "X wants to V", judged from how they act.
when: Use it to say what someone other than you wants to do, going by what they say or do: 弟は外で遊びたがっています. It is usually in the ている form for a current want, or the plain form for a habit. ほしがる does the same for wanting a thing.
why: たい and ほしい describe feelings from the inside, so Japanese usually avoids stating another person's want as plain fact. がる turns an inner feeling into outward behaviour: "show signs of wanting". So 行きたがる reports what can be seen from outside. It makes an ordinary godan verb, and since it now describes an action, the object takes を: 水を飲みたがる, ゲームをほしがる. For the same reason it is normally not used of yourself in an ordinary statement.

formation.note: 行きたがる, 行きたがっている, 行きたがらない. Polite: 行きたがっています.
The same change made from ほしい.

examples.japanese: 弟は毎日外で遊びたがります。
examples.reading: おとうとはまいにちそとであそびたがります。
examples.romaji: otōto wa mainichi soto de asobitagarimasu.
examples.english: My little brother wants to play outside every day.

examples.japanese: 息子が新しいゲームをほしがっています。
examples.reading: むすこがあたらしいゲームをほしがっています。
examples.romaji: musuko ga atarashii gēmu o hoshigatte imasu.
examples.english: My son wants a new video game.

examples.japanese: 子どもは野菜を食べたがりません。
examples.reading: こどもはやさいをたべたがりません。
examples.romaji: kodomo wa yasai o tabetagarimasen.
examples.english: The children don't want to eat vegetables.

mistake.wrong: 友だちは日本へ行きたいです。
mistake.problem: Without context, this states your friend's inner feeling directly, as if you felt it. To describe what shows, use 行きたがっています; to report their words, 行きたいと言っています. Direct たい about someone else is possible in some contexts, such as a story told from their point of view.
mistake.right: 友だちは日本へ行きたがっています。

distinguish_from.note: たい states a want directly, normally the speaker's in an ordinary statement. たがる presents it through outward signs, and normally describes someone else.

review.note: Should the entry warn that たがる can sound presumptuous or childish when said of someone of higher status? Left out as unsure how strong that is.

reviews.note: 友だちは日本へ行きたいです is not categorically wrong. Third-person たい is possible when the desire is already established or the speaker presents that person's perspective. Replace the mistake diagnosis with: 'Without context, this directly attributes an inner desire to your friend. To explicitly describe outward signs, use 行きたがっています; to report their words, use 行きたいと言っています. Direct third-person たい can nevertheless be appropriate in context.' Likewise, write in distinguish_from: 'たい directly presents a desire, normally the speaker's in an unqualified personal statement; たがる presents it through outward indications and normally describes someone else.'

title: Maybe, might
meaning: Plain form + かもしれない: "may", "might"; presents something as possible without claiming that it is true.
when: Use it for a possibility you cannot rule out: 午後から雨が降るかもしれません, "it might rain this afternoon". It works for the past and present too: かぎを忘れたかもしれない. Polite: かもしれません. Casual speech often shortens it to かも.
why: The pieces say it: か is "whether", も is "even", しれない is "cannot be known". "Whether it is so cannot even be known": the speaker admits a possibility without committing to it. The chance can be low or fairly high; かもしれない only says it is possible, where でしょう leans towards yes. Before かもしれない, an affirmative non-past noun or な-adjective drops だ (雨かもしれない), as in a plain question (学生か); other forms keep their endings (雨だったかもしれない, 雨ではないかもしれない).

formation.form: Verb / い-adjective (plain form) + かもしれない
formation.note: 降るかもしれない, 降ったかもしれない, 降らないかもしれない; 高いかもしれない.

formation.form: Noun / な-adjective + かもしれない
formation.note: Drop only affirmative non-past だ: 雨かもしれない, 静かかもしれない; but 雨だったかもしれない, 静かではないかもしれない.

examples.japanese: 午後から雨が降るかもしれません。
examples.reading: ごごからあめがふるかもしれません。
examples.romaji: gogo kara ame ga furu ka mo shiremasen.
examples.english: It might rain from the afternoon.

examples.japanese: かぎを家に忘れたかもしれない。
examples.reading: かぎをいえにわすれたかもしれない。
examples.romaji: kagi o ie ni wasureta ka mo shirenai.
examples.english: I might have left my keys at home.

examples.japanese: あの人は先生かもしれません。
examples.reading: あのひとはせんせいかもしれません。
examples.romaji: ano hito wa sensei ka mo shiremasen.
examples.english: That person might be a teacher.

mistake.wrong: あの人は学生だかもしれません。
mistake.problem: Before かもしれない, the affirmative non-past だ of a noun or な-adjective is dropped.
mistake.right: あの人は学生かもしれません。

distinguish_from.note: でしょう says "probably": the speaker leans towards yes. かもしれない says "maybe": only that it is possible.

reviews.note: The meaning's 'far from sure' imposes too strong a certainty restriction. Replace it with: 'presents something as possible without asserting that it is true'; かもしれない can also hedge something the speaker considers fairly likely. Formation is incomplete for the described past and negative uses with nouns and な-adjectives. Write: 'Use the plain predicate, omitting only affirmative nonpast だ: 雨かもしれない, 雨だったかもしれない, 雨ではないかもしれない, 静かではなかったかもしれない.' Qualify the mistake explanation accordingly. Under the required separate-particle romanization, replace 'kamo shiremasen' with 'ka mo shiremasen' in examples 1 and 3, and 'kamo shirenai' with 'ka mo shirenai' in example 2.

title: Suggesting, "why don't you…?"
meaning: V-たらどうですか: "how about V-ing?"; a suggestion about what the listener could do.
when: Use it to suggest a course of action to someone, often about a problem they have: 疲れているなら、少し休んだらどうですか. More politely, たらいかがですか; casually, たらどう？
why: たら sets up a condition, "if you did V", and どうですか asks "how would that be?". So the sentence asks the listener to picture doing V and judge it, and leaves the decision with them. It gives advice or proposes an option; to invite someone to do something with you, ませんか is the usual choice. Because it tells the listener what they could do, some care is needed in using it to people above you.

formation.form: V (た-form) + ら + どうですか
formation.note: 休んだらどうですか. Politer: たらいかがですか. Casual: たらどう？

examples.japanese: 疲れているなら、少し休んだらどうですか。
examples.reading: つかれているなら、すこしやすんだらどうですか。
examples.romaji: tsukarete iru nara, sukoshi yasundara dō desu ka.
examples.english: If you're tired, why don't you rest a little?

examples.japanese: わからないなら、先生に聞いたらどうですか。
examples.reading: わからないなら、せんせいにきいたらどうですか。
examples.romaji: wakaranai nara, sensei ni kiitara dō desu ka.
examples.english: If you don't understand, why not ask the teacher?

examples.japanese: そんなに好きなら、買ったらどう？
examples.reading: そんなにすきなら、かったらどう？
examples.romaji: sonna ni suki nara, kattara dō?
examples.english: If you like it that much, why not buy it?

mistake.wrong: いっしょに映画を見たらどうですか。
mistake.problem: Meant as an invitation to watch a film with you. たらどうですか sounds like advice, for example that two other people watch one together. To invite, use ませんか.
mistake.right: いっしょに映画を見ませんか。

distinguish_from.note: ほうがいい says one choice is better and often sounds firmer. たらどうですか offers an idea; depending on the tone, it can also sound impatient.
ませんか invites the listener to do something with you. たらどうですか gives advice.

review.note: How presumptuous is たらどうですか (and たらいかがですか) towards a superior? The entry only says some care is needed.

reviews.note: The restriction to 'the listener alone' is too strong. Suggested actions can involve other people, and いっしょに does not necessarily mean 'with me'. Replace that explanation and the ませんか comparison with: 'たらどうですか normally gives advice or proposes an option; ませんか is the usual choice for directly inviting someone to join you.' The mistake sentence is grammatical advice, for example suggesting that two people watch a film together. Rewrite its diagnosis as: 'If you mean to invite the listener to watch a film with you, 見ませんか expresses that intention more clearly.' Also qualify the ほうがいい comparison: 'ほうがいい often sounds firmer, but tone and context matter; たらどう can also sound impatient or critical.'

title: As many as (more than expected)
meaning: Number + も: stresses that an amount is large, "as many as", "a whole…"; 一 + counter + も + negative is "not even one".
when: Use it after a number and counter when the amount strikes you as a lot: 一時間も待ちました, "I waited a whole hour". With 一 and a negative verb it means "not a single one": 一人もいません.
why: も means "too, even". After a quantity it says "even this much": the speaker measures the amount against what was expected and finds it more. It stresses the amount as large, and can carry surprise, admiration or complaint; 一時間待ちました only states the time. With a negative, "not even one" becomes "none at all": 一つもない. A number with its counter normally sits just before the verb without a particle, and も simply follows it there.

formation.note: 三時間も, 五つも, 二杯も.

formation.form: 一 + counter + も + negative verb
formation.note: 一人もいない, 一回も行ったことがない.

examples.japanese: 駅で一時間も待ちました。
examples.reading: えきでいちじかんもまちました。
examples.romaji: eki de ichijikan mo machimashita.
examples.english: I waited a whole hour at the station.

examples.japanese: 兄はケーキを五つも食べました。
examples.reading: あにはケーキをいつつもたべました。
examples.romaji: ani wa kēki o itsutsu mo tabemashita.
examples.english: My older brother ate as many as five pieces of cake.

examples.japanese: 教室には学生が一人もいません。
examples.reading: きょうしつにはがくせいがひとりもいません。
examples.romaji: kyōshitsu ni wa gakusei ga hitori mo imasen.
examples.english: There isn't a single student in the classroom.

mistake.wrong: 今朝、りんごを一つも食べました。
mistake.problem: Meant as a neutral "I ate one apple this morning". For that, leave out も. A number + も stresses the amount as large, and 一 + counter + も with a negative means "not even one".
mistake.right: 今朝、りんごを一つ食べました。

distinguish_from.note: After a noun, も means "too, also" (私も). After a number and counter, it means "as many as".

reviews.note: The mistake diagnosis falsely says that 一 + counter + も requires a negative. Affirmative 一時間も, already used in this entry, disproves this; even 一つも can emphasize one whole item when that counts as a lot. Replace the diagnosis with: 'For the neutral statement “I ate one apple,” omit も. Affirmative quantity + も presents that amount as unusually large; 一 + counter + も with a negative means “not even one.”' Label the original as unsuitable for that neutral intended meaning, not ungrammatical. Also replace 'So it carries surprise or complaint' with 'It emphasizes the amount as large and can express surprise, admiration, or complaint.'

title: Only, nothing but
meaning: X しか + negative: "only X", "nothing but X"; often suggests that X is little, or less than wanted.
when: Use it to say something is limited to X, often with a feeling that it is not enough: 五百円しかありません, "I only have 500 yen". It follows nouns and numbers, and can follow other particles: 日曜日にしか, 田中さんとしか.
why: しか marks X as the one exception to a negative: "apart from X, there is none". So the verb must be negative, even though English says it positively ("I only have…"). With amounts, this framing often suggests shortage: 五百円しかない can sound like "just 500 yen, not enough", where 五百円だけある is neutral. With habits it may simply mean "nothing else": 朝はコーヒーしか飲みません. しか normally replaces が and を; other particles usually stay in front of it (にしか, からしか).

formation.note: しかない, しかありません, しか食べない. が and を are normally replaced by しか.
にしか, でしか, としか, からしか.

examples.japanese: 財布に五百円しかありません。
examples.reading: さいふにごひゃくえんしかありません。
examples.romaji: saifu ni gohyakuen shika arimasen.
examples.english: I only have 500 yen in my wallet.

examples.japanese: 朝はコーヒーしか飲みません。
examples.reading: あさはコーヒーしかのみません。
examples.romaji: asa wa kōhī shika nomimasen.
examples.english: In the morning, I drink nothing but coffee.

examples.japanese: この店は日曜日にしか開いていません。
examples.reading: このみせはにちようびにしかあいていません。
examples.romaji: kono mise wa nichiyōbi ni shika aite imasen.
examples.english: This shop is only open on Sundays.

mistake.wrong: 五百円しかあります。
mistake.problem: しか needs a negative verb, even though English says "only have".
mistake.right: 五百円しかありません。

distinguish_from.note: だけ expresses a limit with a positive or negative verb (五百円だけある). しか needs a negative, excludes everything else, and with amounts often suggests it is not enough.

reviews.note: しか emphasizes exclusion or limitation, but does not necessarily express shortage or dissatisfaction; the coffee example can simply describe a habit. Replace the title with 'Only; nothing except', the meaning with 'X しか + negative: only X; nothing except X', and the categorical shortage claims with: 'It often suggests that an amount is small or insufficient, but this depends on context.' Replace the だけ comparison with: 'だけ expresses restriction and can occur with affirmative or negative predicates. しか normally requires a negative predicate and explicitly excludes alternatives; with quantities it often suggests insufficiency.' The particle rule also needs qualification: write 'が and を are normally replaced by しか. Other particles can precede it; に and へ can sometimes be omitted.'

title: Do something in advance, or leave it as it is
meaning: V-ておく: do V now, ready for later; or do V and leave the result as it is.
when: Use it for preparation (旅行の前にホテルを予約しておく), for getting something done ahead of time, and for leaving a state as it is on purpose (窓を開けておいてください, "please leave the window open"). Casual speech shortens ておく to とく, and でおく to どく: 買っとく, 読んどく.
why: おく means "put, place". After the て-form it says "do V and put it in place": the action is done now with a later need in mind. That is why it covers both preparing and leaving something as it is for a reason. The sentence is about what the person does, so the object keeps を, unlike てある, which describes the state a thing is left in and usually marks the thing with が.

formation.note: Polite: ておきます. Request: ておいてください. Casual: とく／どく (買っとく, 読んどく).

examples.japanese: 旅行の前に、ホテルを予約しておきました。
examples.reading: りょこうのまえに、ホテルをよやくしておきました。
examples.romaji: ryokō no mae ni, hoteru o yoyaku shite okimashita.
examples.english: I booked a hotel before the trip.

examples.japanese: 友だちが来るから、ビールを買っておきます。
examples.reading: ともだちがくるから、ビールをかっておきます。
examples.romaji: tomodachi ga kuru kara, bīru o katte okimasu.
examples.english: Friends are coming over, so I'll buy some beer.

examples.japanese: 暑いので、窓を開けておいてください。
examples.reading: あついので、まどをあけておいてください。
examples.romaji: atsui node, mado o akete oite kudasai.
examples.english: It's hot, so please leave the window open.

mistake.wrong: 窓が開けておきます。
mistake.problem: ておく says what someone does, so the thing acted on is the object and takes を. が with a transitive verb here is borrowed from てある, which describes the resulting state.
mistake.right: 窓を開けておきます。

distinguish_from.note: ておく says what someone does now for later (窓を開けておく). てある describes the state that has been prepared (窓が開けてある).

title: Let's…, I'll… (the volitional form)
meaning: The volitional form (食べよう, 行こう): "let's V" in casual speech, or the speaker's own will, "I'll V".
when: Use it in casual speech to suggest doing something together (映画を見よう, "let's watch a film") or to state, to yourself or others, what you have decided to do (もう寝よう, "I'll go to bed now"). With か it offers or consults: 持とうか, "shall I carry it?". It is the plain counterpart of ましょう, and the base of ～ようと思う.
why: The volitional form expresses the speaker's will. Whether it comes out as "let's" or "I'll" depends on who is included: about something you and the listener can do together, it invites; about yourself, it declares an intention. Ichidan verbs add よう to the stem (食べよう, 見よう). Godan verbs move their last sound to the お-row and add う (行く → 行こう, 飲む → 飲もう, 待つ → 待とう, 買う → 買おう), which is why lists name the form by both endings, ～よう and ～おう. Because it states a will, everyday speech does not use it for things nobody controls, such as the weather.

formation.note: 食べる → 食べよう, 起きる → 起きよう, 見る → 見よう.

formation.form: Godan verb (last sound to the お-row) + う
formation.note: 行く → 行こう, 飲む → 飲もう, 話す → 話そう, 待つ → 待とう, 帰る → 帰ろう, 買う → 買おう.

formation.form: する → しよう; 来る → 来よう (こよう)

formation.note: Offers or consults: 持とうか, "shall I carry it?"; どうしようか, "what shall we do?". Polite: ましょうか.

examples.japanese: 疲れたね。ちょっと休もう。
examples.reading: つかれたね。ちょっとやすもう。
examples.romaji: tsukareta ne. chotto yasumō.
examples.english: We're tired, aren't we. Let's take a short break.

examples.japanese: 明日から毎日走ろう。
examples.reading: あしたからまいにちはしろう。
examples.romaji: ashita kara mainichi hashirō.
examples.english: From tomorrow, I'll run every day.
examples.note: Said to yourself, it states an intention.

examples.japanese: 重そうだね。持とうか。
examples.reading: おもそうだね。もとうか。
examples.romaji: omosō da ne. motō ka.
examples.english: That looks heavy. Shall I carry it?

examples.japanese: 週末、いっしょに映画を見よう。
examples.reading: しゅうまつ、いっしょにえいがをみよう。
examples.romaji: shūmatsu, issho ni eiga o miyō.
examples.english: Let's watch a film together this weekend.

mistake.wrong: 早く行きよう。
mistake.problem: 行く is a godan verb, so よう is not added to its stem. Its last sound moves to the お-row and takes う.
mistake.right: 早く行こう。

distinguish_from.note: ましょう is the polite form of the same will and invitation. The volitional form is the plain one, for friends and family and for talking to yourself.
ようと思う reports an intention you hold ("I'm thinking of…"). The volitional form on its own states the decision, or invites.

review.note: Tanos lists ～よう (497) and ～おう (498) separately. They are one form, the volitional, split by verb class, so this entry covers both; OJG-0054 is left as a stub for the owner to retire as a duplicate.

title: Doing something for someone
meaning: V-てあげる: do V for someone else's benefit; the action is presented as a favour done for another person.
when: Use it when you, or anyone, do something for another person: 妹に本を読んであげました, "I read a book to my little sister"; 兄は友だちに料理を作ってあげました. The person who benefits keeps whatever particle the verb needs (友だちを駅まで送ってあげた, 友だちの宿題を見てあげた), or takes に where the verb has no place for them.
why: あげる is "give", towards someone other than the speaker. After the て-form it gives the action itself as a favour. The doer is often the speaker, but can be anyone doing something for someone else; what it never describes is a favour coming to you. Because it presents the action as a kindness, saying it to the person you are helping can sound condescending. For an offer, especially to a superior, ましょうか is safer (持ちましょうか); with friends and family, てあげようか is also heard. For a favour that comes to you, use てくれる or てもらう.

formation.note: Polite: てあげます. Humble: てさしあげる (OJG-0326), to show respect to the one who benefits; said to their face, it can still sound like pointing out a favour.

examples.japanese: 妹に本を読んであげました。
examples.reading: いもうとにほんをよんであげました。
examples.romaji: imōto ni hon o yonde agemashita.
examples.english: I read a book to my little sister.

examples.japanese: 友だちを車で駅まで送ってあげました。
examples.reading: ともだちをくるまでえきまでおくってあげました。
examples.romaji: tomodachi o kuruma de eki made okutte agemashita.
examples.english: I gave my friend a lift to the station.

examples.japanese: 兄は友だちに料理を作ってあげました。
examples.reading: あにはともだちにりょうりをつくってあげました。
examples.romaji: ani wa tomodachi ni ryōri o tsukutte agemashita.
examples.english: My older brother cooked for his friend.

mistake.wrong: 先生、荷物を持ってあげます。
mistake.problem: てあげる frames your help as a favour you are granting. Said to the person you are helping, and especially to a superior, it sounds condescending. For a tactful offer, use ましょうか.
mistake.right: 先生、荷物を持ちましょうか。

distinguish_from.note: てくれる is a favour coming to you or your side. てあげる is a favour done for someone else.
あげる gives a thing. てあげる gives an action.

reviews.note: てあげる is not restricted to actions by the speaker or the speaker's side; it also describes favors between third parties. Replace the meaning and directional explanation with: 'Someone does V for someone else's benefit. The doer can be the speaker or a third party; the action is presented as a favor to the beneficiary.' Update the てくれる comparison accordingly. 'Offers are made with ましょうか instead' is too absolute: てあげようか is possible with friends or family. Write: 'For a tactful offer, especially to a superior, ましょうか is usually safer.' Finally, 'towards someone above the receiver' reverses the relevant relationship. Replace it with: 'Humble: てさしあげる, used to show respect to the beneficiary, often someone of higher status than the doer; directly offering it can still sound patronizing.'

title: Someone does something for me
meaning: V-てくれる: someone does V for the speaker or the speaker's side; the doer is the subject, and the favour comes in.
when: Use it when someone does something that benefits you or someone on your side, and you want to show it was a kindness: 友だちが駅まで迎えに来てくれました. The doer is the subject (が or は); since the favour comes to you, 私に is usually left out. It also makes casual requests: 手伝ってくれる？
why: くれる is "give (to me)": it points inward, towards the speaker's side. After the て-form it hands an action to you as a gift. 母が弁当を作りました only states a fact; 母が弁当を作ってくれました shows it was done for you and that you appreciate it, and leaving it out where someone did you a favour can sound cold. Because the direction is fixed, the one who benefits is you, or someone you speak of as on your side.

formation.note: Polite: てくれます. Honorific: てくださる (OJG-0326). Requests: てくれる？, てくれませんか (OJG-0327).

examples.japanese: 友だちが駅まで迎えに来てくれました。
examples.reading: ともだちがえきまでむかえにきてくれました。
examples.romaji: tomodachi ga eki made mukae ni kite kuremashita.
examples.english: My friend came to meet me at the station.

examples.japanese: 母がお弁当を作ってくれました。
examples.reading: ははがおべんとうをつくってくれました。
examples.romaji: haha ga obentō o tsukutte kuremashita.
examples.english: My mother made me a packed lunch.

examples.japanese: 田中さんが道を教えてくれました。
examples.reading: たなかさんがみちをおしえてくれました。
examples.romaji: tanaka-san ga michi o oshiete kuremashita.
examples.english: Tanaka-san showed me the way.

mistake.wrong: 私は友だちに宿題を手伝ってくれました。
mistake.problem: To say your friend helped you, the friend is the doer and takes が, not に. 私は can stay as the topic (私は、友だちが宿題を手伝ってくれました), or keep 私は as the receiver and use てもらう (友だちに手伝ってもらいました).
mistake.right: 友だちが宿題を手伝ってくれました。

distinguish_from.note: Same event, other viewpoint. てくれる makes the doer the subject; てもらう makes the receiver the subject and marks the doer with に.
てあげる is a favour done for someone else, by you or by anyone. てくれる is one coming to you or your side.

reviews.note: The mistake's claim that 私は necessarily makes the speaker the doer is incorrect: は marks a topic, not necessarily the grammatical subject. Replace the diagnosis with: 'To mean that your friend helped you, mark the friend as the doer with が, not に. 私は can remain as a broader topic: 私は友だちが宿題を手伝ってくれました. Alternatively, use 私は友だちに宿題を手伝ってもらいました.' Also replace 'always you or your side, never an outsider' with: 'The benefit is viewed as coming toward the speaker or someone the speaker identifies with; context can extend this viewpoint beyond a fixed personal group.' The てあげる comparison should say that it presents a favor to someone else and can also describe favors between third parties, not only favors originating on the speaker's side.

title: Having someone do something for you
meaning: V-てもらう: have someone do V for you; the receiver is the subject, and the doer is usually marked with に.
when: Use it to tell a favour from the receiver's side: 友だちに宿題を手伝ってもらいました, "I had my friend help me with my homework". It also covers getting something done by someone (時計を直してもらう, "get a watch repaired") and forms polite requests (てもらえませんか).
why: もらう is "receive". After the て-form it receives an action: you receive someone's doing V. So the subject is the one who benefits, and the one who acts is the source, marked with に just as in 友だちにもらった. Compared with てくれる, the event is the same but told from the receiver's side, and it can suggest you asked for it or arranged it. For a kindness nobody asked for, てくれる is often more natural.

formation.form: (receiver は) doer に … V (て-form) + もらう
formation.note: Polite: てもらいます. Humble: ていただく (OJG-0326). Request: てもらえませんか (OJG-0327). With verbs like 教える, から also marks the doer (先生から教えてもらった).

examples.japanese: 友だちに宿題を手伝ってもらいました。
examples.reading: ともだちにしゅくだいをてつだってもらいました。
examples.romaji: tomodachi ni shukudai o tetsudatte moraimashita.
examples.english: I had my friend help me with my homework.

examples.japanese: 店の人に写真を撮ってもらいました。
examples.reading: みせのひとにしゃしんをとってもらいました。
examples.romaji: mise no hito ni shashin o totte moraimashita.
examples.english: I had someone from the shop take a photo for me.

examples.japanese: 壊れた時計を直してもらいました。
examples.reading: こわれたとけいをなおしてもらいました。
examples.romaji: kowareta tokei o naoshite moraimashita.
examples.english: I had my broken watch repaired.

mistake.wrong: 友だちが私に本を貸してもらいました。
mistake.problem: Meant as "I had my friend lend me a book", but the roles are reversed. With てもらう the receiver is the subject and the one who acts takes に; as written, the friend is the receiver.
mistake.right: 私は友だちに本を貸してもらいました。

distinguish_from.note: てくれる tells the same favour with the doer as subject. てもらう tells it with the receiver as subject.
もらう receives a thing. てもらう receives an action.

reviews.note: The mistake sentence does not establish that the friend did the lending. With its actual marking, the friend is the receiver and 私に identifies the lender; that reading is possible in an appropriate context. Replace the diagnosis with: 'If you mean “I had my friend lend me a book,” the participant roles are reversed here: make yourself the receiver-subject and mark the friend with に.' Keep the proposed correction. The formation also omits a valid source marker: add 'The doer is usually marked with に; から is also possible when the person is construed as an information or service source, as in 先生から日本語を教えてもらいました. It is not interchangeable with に for every action.' Qualify the meaning's categorical に statement accordingly.

title: Could you possibly…? (a very polite request)
meaning: V-ていただけませんか: "could you please V?"; a very polite request, asked as whether you may receive the favour.
when: Use it for polite requests to strangers, customers, teachers, or anyone above you, especially for a real favour: もう少しゆっくり話していただけませんか. Other members of the same family are てもらえませんか and てくれませんか, which are less deferential, and てくださいませんか, which is also very polite.
why: いただく is the humble verb for "receive", and いただける is its potential form, "can receive". ませんか asks in the negative. Put together: "can't I receive your doing V?". The request is softened twice: it asks about your receiving instead of telling the listener to act, and the negative question leaves room for no. Since the speaker is the one receiving, the listener, who does the action, is usually not named.

formation.form: V (て-form) + いただけませんか
formation.note: いただけますか is a little less soft. いただけないでしょうか is softer still.

examples.japanese: もう少しゆっくり話していただけませんか。
examples.reading: もうすこしゆっくりはなしていただけませんか。
examples.romaji: mō sukoshi yukkuri hanashite itadakemasen ka.
examples.english: Could you speak a little more slowly, please?

examples.japanese: すみません、この字の読み方を教えていただけませんか。
examples.reading: すみません、このじのよみかたをおしえていただけませんか。
examples.romaji: sumimasen, kono ji no yomikata o oshiete itadakemasen ka.
examples.english: Excuse me, could you tell me how to read this character?

examples.japanese: 明日までに書類を送っていただけませんか。
examples.reading: あしたまでにしょるいをおくっていただけませんか。
examples.romaji: ashita made ni shorui o okutte itadakemasen ka.
examples.english: Could you send the documents by tomorrow?

mistake.wrong: 先生、この本を貸していただきませんか。
mistake.problem: The request needs the potential form いただける, "can I receive". いただきませんか asks "won't (we) receive?", which is not a request to the listener.
mistake.right: 先生、この本を貸していただけませんか。

distinguish_from.note: てくれませんか and てもらえませんか make the same request less deferentially. てくださいませんか is also very polite; it respectfully asks about the listener's giving, where ていただけませんか humbly asks about your receiving.

review.note: Overlaps OJG-0327 (the other request forms) and OJG-0326 (ていただく); a candidate to merge into one entry for the request family.

reviews.note: The politeness ranking is overstated: ～てくださいませんか is also a highly polite, honorific request, not categorically a less formal version of ～ていただけませんか. In 'when' and 'distinguish_from', replace the ranking with: 'てもらえませんか and てくれませんか are generally less deferential. てくださいませんか is another highly polite option: it respectfully asks about the listener’s giving the favour, whereas ていただけませんか humbly asks about the speaker’s receiving it. Their relative softness depends on context.' Delete 'the most polite of the everyday forms.'

title: I hope…, it would be good if…
meaning: Plain form + といいです(ね): "I hope…", "it would be nice if…"; a wish for something you cannot bring about yourself.
when: Use it to hope for an outcome that is not in your hands: 明日晴れるといいですね, "I hope it's sunny tomorrow". With ね, it shares the hope with the listener, often as a kind wish for them: 早くよくなるといいですね. For your own hopes, といいんですが or, casually, といいなあ is common.
why: This と is the conditional "if A, then B", so といい says "if A happens, it's good". Saying an outcome would be good is how Japanese states a hope without claiming control over it. When the hope is about the future, the part before と is in the non-past (晴れる), because the outcome still lies ahead. A trailing が or けど (といいんですが) adds "but I can't be sure", which suits your own hopes.

formation.form: Verb / い-adjective (plain form) + といいです(ね)
formation.note: 晴れるといい, 安いといい; negative 雨が降らないといい.

formation.form: Noun / な-adjective + だ + といい
formation.note: 晴れだといい, 元気だといい.

formation.form: … といいんですが／といいなあ
formation.note: For your own hopes, or to add that you are unsure.

examples.japanese: 明日、晴れるといいですね。
examples.reading: あした、はれるといいですね。
examples.romaji: ashita, hareru to ii desu ne.
examples.english: I hope it's sunny tomorrow.

examples.japanese: お母さんの病気が早くよくなるといいですね。
examples.reading: おかあさんのびょうきがはやくよくなるといいですね。
examples.romaji: okāsan no byōki ga hayaku yoku naru to ii desu ne.
examples.english: I hope your mother gets better soon.

examples.japanese: 試験に合格できるといいんですが。
examples.reading: しけんにごうかくできるといいんですが。
examples.romaji: shiken ni gōkaku dekiru to ii n desu ga.
examples.english: I hope I can pass the exam.

mistake.wrong: 明日、晴れたといいですね。
mistake.problem: The hope is about tomorrow, so the part before と stays non-past. The た-form belongs with たら (晴れたらいいですね), a different pattern with a similar meaning.
mistake.right: 明日、晴れるといいですね。

distinguish_from.note: といい, たらいい and ばいい can all express a hope or give advice, depending on the context. This entry covers the hope. For advice and questions about what to do, see OJG-0348.

review.note: A た-form before といい can hope about something already decided (間に合ったといいんですが, "I hope he made it"); the entry leaves this out for N4. Is that the right call?

reviews.note: The distinguish_from note draws an unreliable division between wish-oriented といい and mainly advice-oriented たらいい／ばいい. All three can express hopes or advice; といいです is also ordinary advice, as in 毎日少しずつ練習するといいです. Replace the note with: 'といい, たらいい and ばいい can all express hopes or advice, depending on context. This entry covers the hope use of といい. For advice and questions about what to do, see OJG-0348.'

title: Sorry for doing…
meaning: V-てすみません: "sorry for V-ing"; apologises for a specific thing you did or failed to do.
when: Use it to name what you are apologising for: 遅れてすみません, "sorry I'm late". For something you did not do, use the negative て-form なくて: 返事をしなくてすみません. For something over and done, すみませんでした; more formally, て申し訳ありません.
why: The て-form here gives a cause: "I did V, and so, I'm sorry". The part before すみません names what the apology is for. When the cause is something you did not do, the usual form is the negative て-form なくて (返事をしなくて).

formation.note: Past, for something finished: てすみませんでした.

formation.form: V (negative) → なくて + すみません
formation.note: 来なくて, 連絡しなくて.

formation.form: V (て-form) + 申し訳ありません
formation.note: More formal, for customers and superiors.

examples.japanese: 遅れてすみません。
examples.reading: おくれてすみません。
examples.romaji: okurete sumimasen.
examples.english: Sorry I'm late.

examples.japanese: 昨日は電話に出なくてすみませんでした。
examples.reading: きのうはでんわにでなくてすみませんでした。
examples.romaji: kinō wa denwa ni denakute sumimasen deshita.
examples.english: Sorry I didn't answer the phone yesterday.

examples.japanese: 夜遅くに電話してすみません。
examples.reading: よるおそくにでんわしてすみません。
examples.romaji: yoru osoku ni denwa shite sumimasen.
examples.english: Sorry for calling so late at night.

mistake.wrong: 遅れたすみません。
mistake.problem: The part before すみません names the reason, and that link is made with the て-form. A た-form cannot join directly to すみません.
mistake.right: 遅れてすみません。

reviews.note: The exclusion of ないで is incorrect. Apologies such as 返事をしないですみません and 連絡しないですみません are used naturally; なくて is not obligatory here. Replace the relevant explanation with: 'なくて explicitly presents the non-action as the reason for the apology. ないで can also occur in apologies for not doing something, although なくて is the standard form taught here.' Replace the mistake with wrong: '返事をしなくすみません。'; problem: 'The negative form needs the connective なくて, not なく alone, before すみません.'; right: '返事をしなくてすみません。'

title: Looks like, looks about to
meaning: Stem + そうです: "looks (adjective)", from appearance; after a verb stem, "looks likely to V" or "looks about to V".
when: Use it for your impression of something in front of you: このケーキはおいしそうです, "this cake looks delicious". After a verb stem, it says something looks likely, often that it is about to happen: 雨が降りそうです, "it looks like it's going to rain". Before a noun it becomes そうな (おいしそうなケーキ), and before a verb, そうに (楽しそうに遊ぶ).
why: This そう gives your own judgement from what you can see or sense, before you know for sure: the cake looks good, but you have not tasted it yet. That is why adjectives that simply name what you see, such as 赤い or きれい, are usually said directly instead. It joins to a stem, not to a full form: い-adjectives drop い (高い → 高そう), な-adjectives use the stem (元気そう), and verbs use the ます-stem (降りそう). The full form before そう (高いそう) is a different point, the hearsay そう. Two irregulars: いい → よさそう, ない → なさそう.

formation.note: 高そう, おいしそう. いい → よさそう; ない → なさそう (おいしくなさそう).
元気そう, ひまそう.
降りそう, 落ちそう.

formation.form: そうだ／そうです; そうな + noun; そうに + verb

examples.japanese: このケーキはおいしそうですね。
examples.reading: このケーキはおいしそうですね。
examples.romaji: kono kēki wa oishisō desu ne.
examples.english: This cake looks delicious.

examples.japanese: 空が暗いです。雨が降りそうです。
examples.reading: そらがくらいです。あめがふりそうです。
examples.romaji: sora ga kurai desu. ame ga furisō desu.
examples.english: The sky is dark. It looks like it's going to rain.

examples.japanese: 子どもたちが楽しそうに遊んでいます。
examples.reading: こどもたちがたのしそうにあそんでいます。
examples.romaji: kodomotachi ga tanoshisō ni asonde imasu.
examples.english: The children are playing, looking like they're having fun.

examples.japanese: 棚の上のコップが落ちそうです。
examples.reading: たなのうえのコップがおちそうです。
examples.romaji: tana no ue no koppu ga ochisō desu.
examples.english: The glass on the shelf looks like it's about to fall.

mistake.wrong: このかばんは高いそうです。
mistake.problem: Meant as "looks expensive", but with the full 高い this is the hearsay そう, "I hear it's expensive". For how it looks, drop the い.
mistake.right: このかばんは高そうです。

distinguish_from.note: The hearsay そう follows a full plain form (高いそう, 降るそう) and reports what you heard. This そう follows a stem (高そう, 降りそう) and gives your impression.
ようだ presents a conclusion drawn from evidence. Stem + そう gives an impression or prediction from what you can see or sense. They can overlap.

review.note: Is the restriction on visual adjectives (赤そう, きれいそう usually avoided for what is plainly in view) stated at the right strength?

reviews.note: The verb use is repeatedly restricted to something being 'about to' happen. Verb-stem そう also predicts likelihood without imminence, as in 来年は売り上げが伸びそうです. Replace the verb portion of the meaning with: 'after a verb stem, looks likely to V or looks about to V.' In 'when' and the ようだ comparison, write: 'With verbs, it expresses an expectation based on available indications, often—but not necessarily—that something is about to happen.'

title: Making or letting someone do something (the causative)
meaning: Causative V-させる／V-せる: make someone do V, or let them; the one who causes it is the subject.
when: Use it when one person makes or allows another to act: 母は弟に野菜を食べさせました, "my mother made my brother eat vegetables"; 子どもを公園で遊ばせました, "I let the children play in the park". Whether it means "make" or "let" comes from the context. Asking permission with させてください is its own point (OJG-0346).
why: The causative adds a causer on top of an action: the causer becomes the subject, and the one who actually acts is moved to another particle. With a verb that already has a を-object, the one who acts takes に (弟に野菜を食べさせる), since a clause does not normally carry two を. With a verb that has no object, the one who acts can often take を or に: を presents them more as directly acted on, に more as acting of their own will. This often lines up with "make" and "let", but not always: 子どもを遊ばせる can mean "let the children play". With things a person does not control, such as 泣く, を is normal (子どもを泣かせる). The causative verb is itself an ichidan verb (食べさせます, 食べさせた).

formation.note: 行く → 行かせる, 読む → 読ませる, 遊ぶ → 遊ばせる, 買う → 買わせる.
食べる → 食べさせる, 見る → 見させる.

formation.form: する → させる; 来る → 来させる (こさせる)

examples.japanese: 母は弟に野菜を食べさせました。
examples.reading: はははおとうとにやさいをたべさせました。
examples.romaji: haha wa otōto ni yasai o tabesasemashita.
examples.english: My mother made my little brother eat vegetables.

examples.japanese: 先生は学生に作文を書かせました。
examples.reading: せんせいはがくせいにさくぶんをかかせました。
examples.romaji: sensei wa gakusei ni sakubun o kakasemashita.
examples.english: The teacher had the students write an essay.

examples.japanese: 子どもを公園で遊ばせました。
examples.reading: こどもをこうえんであそばせました。
examples.romaji: kodomo o kōen de asobasemashita.
examples.english: I let the children play in the park.

mistake.wrong: 母は弟を野菜を食べさせました。
mistake.problem: 食べる already has a を-object (野菜), and a clause normally carries only one を, so the one made to eat takes に.
mistake.right: 母は弟に野菜を食べさせました。

distinguish_from.note: させられる is the causative made passive, told from the side of the one made to act. させる is told from the causer's side.
させてください uses the causative to ask to be allowed to do something yourself.

reviews.note: The statement that a causee with an objectless verb can take either を or に is too broad.
