reviews.note: The omission rule is too broad: being clear from context is not sufficient for every N2 to be omitted. In particular, position nouns do not freely disappear: 駅の前で会いましょう cannot become 駅ので会いましょう with the same meaning. Replace the omission statements and formation note with: 'When a recoverable noun refers to a thing, N1の can often stand for the whole noun phrase, especially for possession: この本は私のです. This substitution is not available for every noun or relation; retain position nouns in expressions such as 駅の前で.'

title: Joining two clauses with "but"
meaning: Clause が、clause / clause けど、clause: A, but B. Also a soft lead-in before a question, request or invitation.
when: Use it to set two facts against each other in one sentence: このかばんは高いですが、とても便利です. It also opens with background, with little or no contrast, before what you really want to say: 来週パーティーをしますが、来ませんか. が is neutral and common in polite speech and writing; けど is conversational; けれど and けれども are a little more formal than けど. Ending a sentence with が or けど leaves the rest unsaid; it often softens a request or a reservation, and with some intonations it can sound like a complaint.
why: が and けど join the first clause to the second and signal that the second may go against what the first suggests. The main point comes last, so in 高いですが、便利です the speaker's weight is on 便利: it is expensive, yet worth it. Because the connector only links and leaves room, Japanese also uses it just to set the scene before a question, request or invitation; the first clause gives the background, the second is the point. The clause before が or けど keeps its own ending. In polite speech, both halves are usually polite (高いですが); in casual speech, plain forms go before けど (高いけど). After a noun or な-adjective, だ or です is needed, as it would be at the end of a sentence: 学生だけど, 静かですが. This が follows a whole clause, which is how it differs from the が that marks a subject after a noun.

formation.note: Neutral; common in polite speech and writing: 高いですが、…
Conversational: 高いけど、… けれど and けれども are slightly more formal.

formation.form: Noun / な-adjective + だ or です + が / けど
formation.note: 学生だけど, 静かですが. 学生けど is wrong.
Ends the sentence and leaves the rest unsaid: ちょっと寒いんですけど…

examples.japanese: このかばんは高いですが、とても便利です。
examples.reading: このかばんはたかいですが、とてもべんりです。
examples.romaji: kono kaban wa takai desu ga, totemo benri desu.
examples.english: This bag is expensive, but it's very handy.

examples.japanese: 日本語は難しいけど、おもしろい。
examples.reading: にほんごはむずかしいけど、おもしろい。
examples.romaji: nihongo wa muzukashii kedo, omoshiroi.
examples.english: Japanese is hard, but it's interesting.
examples.note: Casual speech, with plain forms and けど.

examples.japanese: 来週パーティーをしますが、来ませんか。
examples.reading: らいしゅうパーティーをしますが、きませんか。
examples.romaji: raishū pātī o shimasu ga, kimasen ka.
examples.english: We're having a party next week. Would you like to come?
examples.note: No contrast; が just sets the scene before the invitation.

mistake.wrong: 私は学生けど、毎日働いている。
mistake.problem: After a noun, けど needs だ first, as the clause would have at the end of a sentence (学生だ). Without it the noun is left hanging.
mistake.right: 私は学生だけど、毎日働いている。

distinguish_from.note: でも and しかし start a new sentence: 高いです。でも、便利です. けれども can start a new sentence or join clauses like けど. This entry is the clause-joining が and けど.
The subject が follows a noun: 雨が降っています. This が follows a whole clause.

review.note: Questions: is けれど / けれども fairly described as "a little more formal than けど"? Is the sentence-final softening use (…んですけど) within N5, or should it be left to a later point? Revised after the first gpt-6-astra review to meet its objection (see reviews).

reviews.note: The distinction from OJG-0291 misleadingly assigns けれども to sentence-initial use, although it also joins clauses, as this entry itself acknowledges. Replace that note with: 'でも and しかし introduce a new sentence. けれども can either introduce a new sentence or join clauses, like けど. Here we explain clause-joining が and けど.' Also qualify the sentence-final claim: write 'Ending with が or けど leaves a continuation implicit and often softens a request or reservation; depending on context and intonation, it can also express an objection or complaint.'

title: "But" at the start of a sentence
meaning: A。でも、B。: A. But B. でも is everyday speech, しかし formal or written, けれども in between.
when: Use one of these to begin a sentence that goes against the one before: 昨日は雨でした。でも、楽しかったです. でも is the usual word in conversation. しかし sounds formal and is common in writing, speeches and the news. けれども, and the shorter けれど, is a little more formal than でも. In a conversation でも also starts a reply that raises an objection: 「あした、テニスをしましょう。」「でも、あしたは雨ですよ。」
why: Each of these words carries the "but" on its own, so it can stand at the head of a new sentence and point back to the last one. Splitting the contrast into two sentences lets the first finish on its own and gives the turn more weight than joining the halves with が or けど. The choice of word sets the tone: でも is soft and spoken; しかし is firm and belongs to writing and formal talk, so it sounds stiff in a chat with friends. In the use described here, these words begin a new sentence. でも and しかし cannot hang on the end of a clause, so 高いでもおいしい is not Japanese. けれども and けれど can also join clauses (高いけれども、おいしい), like けど. The でも here is a separate word; でも after a question word (何でも) is a different use.

formation.note: Everyday speech and informal writing.
Formal; writing, speeches, the news.
Between the two; けれど is a shorter form.

examples.japanese: 昨日は雨でした。でも、楽しかったです。
examples.reading: きのうはあめでした。でも、たのしかったです。
examples.romaji: kinō wa ame deshita. demo, tanoshikatta desu.
examples.english: It rained yesterday. But it was fun.

examples.japanese: この店は安いです。しかし、あまりおいしくありません。
examples.reading: このみせはやすいです。しかし、あまりおいしくありません。
examples.romaji: kono mise wa yasui desu. shikashi, amari oishiku arimasen.
examples.english: This restaurant is cheap. However, the food isn't very good.

examples.japanese: 「あした、テニスをしましょう。」「でも、あしたは雨ですよ。」
examples.reading: 「あした、テニスをしましょう。」「でも、あしたはあめですよ。」
examples.romaji: "ashita, tenisu o shimashō." "demo, ashita wa ame desu yo."
examples.english: "Let's play tennis tomorrow." "But it's going to rain tomorrow."

mistake.wrong: このかばんは高いでもいいです。
mistake.problem: でも cannot hang on the end of a clause like English "but". Either split the sentence and start the second with でも, or join the halves with けど or が.
mistake.right: このかばんは高いです。でも、いいです。

distinguish_from.note: が and けど join clauses. Sentence-initial でも, しかし and けれども open a contrasting statement; けれども also has a clause-joining use.
でも after a question word means "any": 何でも, いつでも. That is a different use.

review.note: Questions: is けれども at the start of a sentence common enough to present at N5 alongside でも and しかし? Is the right version of the mistake (…高いです。でも、いいです。) natural, or would a native prefer 高いけど、いいです? Revised after the first gpt-6-astra review to meet its objection (see reviews).

reviews.note: The statement that these words do not attach to a clause is false for けれども and けれど: 高いけれども、おいしい is correct. Replace it with: 'In the use explained here, these expressions introduce a new sentence. でも and しかし cannot be attached directly to 高い as clause-ending connectors; けれども and けれど can also join clauses, like けど.' Replace the distinction from OJG-0290 with: 'が and けど join clauses. Sentence-initial でも, しかし, and けれども introduce a contrasting statement; けれども also has a clause-joining use.'

title: "Well then": moving on from what was just said
meaning: では／じゃ／それでは at the start: well then, in that case. It takes what was just said and moves to the next step.
when: Use it to move on, based on what was just said or agreed: 「コーヒーはありません。」「じゃ、紅茶をください。」 It also opens or closes a stretch of talk: では、始めましょう; じゃ、またあした. じゃ (often じゃあ) is casual; では is neutral to polite; それでは and それじゃ are fuller forms, それでは sounding the most formal.
why: それでは is roughly "that being so": それ points back to what was just said, and the sentence that follows builds on it. では is the same without それ, and じゃ is its spoken contraction, just as じゃありません is of ではありません. Because the word treats the situation just described as settled ground, it naturally opens a choice, a decision or a goodbye, right after someone else has spoken or after one step is over. Which form you choose sets the tone: じゃ, また is for friends and family; to a teacher or a customer, では and a polite phrase fit.

formation.note: Fullest and most formal; meetings, announcements, lessons.
Neutral to polite.
Casual; じゃあ, with a long vowel, is common in speech.

examples.japanese: 「コーヒーはありません。」「じゃ、紅茶をください。」
examples.reading: 「コーヒーはありません。」「じゃ、こうちゃをください。」
examples.romaji: "kōhī wa arimasen." "ja, kōcha o kudasai."
examples.english: "We don't have any coffee." "Then I'll have tea, please."

examples.japanese: では、授業を始めましょう。
examples.reading: では、じゅぎょうをはじめましょう。
examples.romaji: dewa, jugyō o hajimemashō.
examples.english: Well then, let's start the lesson.

examples.japanese: じゃ、またあした。
examples.reading: じゃ、またあした。
examples.romaji: ja, mata ashita.
examples.english: OK, see you tomorrow.

mistake.wrong: 先生、じゃ、またね。
mistake.problem: じゃ and またね are casual, for friends and family. Taking leave of a teacher, では with a polite phrase fits.
mistake.right: 先生、では、失礼します。

distinguish_from.note: でも turns against what came before: "but". では moves on from it: "then, in that case". Both open a sentence, and じゃ and でも are easy to mix up.
そして and それから add the next thing; では draws the next step from what was said.

review.note: Questions: is "では is じゃ's full form, and それでは is roughly 'that being so'" a fair explanation without going into the copula で + は? Romaji: the sentence-initial conjunction is written dewa (one word); is that the right call, or should it be de wa like the copula? Is 先生、では、失礼します natural as the polite leave-taking?

title: "And", "and then" at the start of a sentence
meaning: そして: and, adding the next point or event. それから: and then, after that; also "and also" when adding to a list.
when: Use そして to add another point or the next event: この部屋は広いです。そして、明るいです. Use それから for what happens next in time: 朝ご飯を食べました。それから、学校に行きました. それから also adds one more item, as when ordering: コーヒーを一つください。それから、ケーキも一つ.
why: それから is それ, "that", with から, "from": from that point on, which is why it orders events in time. そして simply carries on from the last sentence and adds to it, so it fits both a further fact and a next event. Both usually link statements, most often at the start of a new sentence. After a pause they can also add one more item to a list of nouns (コーヒー、それからケーキ), but for a simple list of nouns と is the ordinary word: 犬と猫. Inside one sentence, a string of actions is usually joined with the て-form instead (起きて、食べて、出かけます); そして and それから are clearer when each step is its own sentence.

formation.note: Adds a further point or the next event.
The next event in time, or one more item in a list.

examples.japanese: この部屋は広いです。そして、明るいです。
examples.reading: このへやはひろいです。そして、あかるいです。
examples.romaji: kono heya wa hiroi desu. soshite, akarui desu.
examples.english: This room is spacious. And it's bright.

examples.japanese: 朝ご飯を食べました。それから、学校に行きました。
examples.reading: あさごはんをたべました。それから、がっこうにいきました。
examples.romaji: asagohan o tabemashita. sorekara, gakkō ni ikimashita.
examples.english: I ate breakfast. Then I went to school.

examples.japanese: コーヒーを一つください。それから、ケーキも一つください。
examples.reading: コーヒーをひとつください。それから、ケーキもひとつください。
examples.romaji: kōhī o hitotsu kudasai. sorekara, kēki mo hitotsu kudasai.
examples.english: One coffee, please. And one cake as well.

mistake.wrong: 私は犬そして猫が好きです。
mistake.problem: For a simple list of two nouns, と is the ordinary connector. そして usually links statements; between two bare nouns with no pause it sounds like translated English.
mistake.right: 私は犬と猫が好きです。

distinguish_from.note: と is the ordinary way to list nouns: 犬と猫. そして and それから usually link statements.
～てから joins two predicates inside one sentence: 食べてから行きました. それから is a separate connector, usually starting the next sentence.
The て-form joins predicates inside one sentence; そして and それから are separate connectors, usually starting a new sentence but also possible after a pause within one.

review.note: Question: そして can join nouns in formal writing (AそしてB); is the mistake's problem worded carefully enough ("sounds like translated English" in everyday Japanese)? Revised after the first gpt-6-astra review to meet its objection (see reviews).

reviews.note: The categorical claim that そして and それから cannot link nouns is false. Both can introduce another item in a noun list, for example 犬、そして猫 or コーヒー、それからケーキ. Replace the relevant explanation, mistake diagnosis, and distinction from と with: 'と is the ordinary connector for a simple noun list: 犬と猫. そして and それから usually connect statements, but can also introduce another noun-list item after a pause. 私は犬と猫が好きです is the neutral way to express the intended sentence.' The other distinction notes also overstate the sentence boundary. Write: 'The て-form and ～てから connect predicates within a sentence; そして and それから are independent connectors, often starting a new sentence but also possible after a pause within one.'

title: "So", "that's why", at the start of a sentence
meaning: A。だから、B。: A. So B. だから opens a sentence giving the result of the last one. ですから is the polite form.
when: Use it to begin a sentence that follows from the one before: あしたはテストがあります。だから、今日は早く寝ます. In polite speech ですから is the matching form. In conversation だから can also sound insistent, like "that's what I'm saying", so take care using it in reply to someone above you.
why: だから is だ, the plain "is", with から, "because": "it is so, and because of that". It works like the から that ends a reason clause, but the reason is the whole previous sentence, so だから opens the next one with the result. That fixes the order: the reason first, then だから, then what follows from it; it never introduces the reason itself, as English "because" can. Because it is built on plain だ, it is plain or casual; ですから keeps a polite conversation polite.

formation.note: Plain or casual.
Polite.

examples.japanese: あしたはテストがあります。だから、今日は早く寝ます。
examples.reading: あしたはテストがあります。だから、きょうははやくねます。
examples.romaji: ashita wa tesuto ga arimasu. dakara, kyō wa hayaku nemasu.
examples.english: There's a test tomorrow. So I'm going to bed early tonight.

examples.japanese: 昨日は雨だった。だから、家にいた。
examples.reading: きのうはあめだった。だから、いえにいた。
examples.romaji: kinō wa ame datta. dakara, ie ni ita.
examples.english: It rained yesterday. So I stayed home.

examples.japanese: この道は危ないです。ですから、気をつけてください。
examples.reading: このみちはあぶないです。ですから、きをつけてください。
examples.romaji: kono michi wa abunai desu. desu kara, ki o tsukete kudasai.
examples.english: This road is dangerous. So please be careful.

mistake.wrong: だから、雨が降りました。家にいました。
mistake.problem: Intended as "Because it rained, I stayed home." だから introduces the result, not the reason. The reason comes first, then だから and what follows from it.
mistake.right: 雨が降りました。だから、家にいました。

distinguish_from.note: から goes at the end of the reason clause inside one sentence: 雨だから、家にいました. だから begins a new sentence after the reason.

listed.item: 文A。だから 文B (Bun A. Dakara Bun B)

review.note: Questions: romaji for sentence-initial ですから is written desu kara here; is that preferable to desukara? Is the note that だから can sound insistent in replies accurate and useful at N5?

title: And so, that's why
meaning: それで: "and so", "that's why"; starts a sentence that gives the result of what was just said. Also "and then?".
when: Use it at the start of a sentence to give what followed from the previous one: 昨日は熱がありました。それで、学校を休みました, "I had a fever yesterday. So I stayed home from school". In conversation, それで？ asks the other person to go on: "and then?".
why: それ points back at the previous sentence, and で presents it as the cause: "with that, …". So the second sentence is what came about because of the first. Because it reports a result, it is used for things that happened or hold, and not to lead into your own request, suggestion or order; だから is used for those.

examples.japanese: 昨日は熱がありました。それで、学校を休みました。
examples.reading: きのうはねつがありました。それで、がっこうをやすみました。
examples.romaji: kinō wa netsu ga arimashita. sorede, gakkō o yasumimashita.
examples.english: I had a fever yesterday. So I stayed home from school.

examples.japanese: 電車が遅れました。それで、会議に間に合いませんでした。
examples.reading: でんしゃがおくれました。それで、かいぎにまにあいませんでした。
examples.romaji: densha ga okuremashita. sorede, kaigi ni maniaimasen deshita.
examples.english: The train was late. That's why I didn't make it to the meeting on time.

examples.japanese: 「駅で田中さんに会ったんです。」「それで？」
examples.reading: 「えきでたなかさんにあったんです。」「それで？」
examples.romaji: "eki de tanaka-san ni atta n desu." "sorede?"
examples.english: "I ran into Tanaka-san at the station." "And then?"

mistake.wrong: 明日はテストがあります。それで、今日は早く寝てください。
mistake.problem: それで introduces a result that came about. It does not lead into a request; use だから.
mistake.right: 明日はテストがあります。だから、今日は早く寝てください。

distinguish_from.note: だから can introduce the speaker's conclusion, decision, request or suggestion, as well as a result. それで normally reports what followed from the situation.

listed.item: 文A。それで 文B (Bun A. Sorede Bun B)

reviews.note: The second translation loses the timing distinction: 会議に間に合いませんでした means failure to arrive in time, not necessarily failure to attend. Replace it with: 'The train was late. That's why I didn't make it to the meeting on time.' The comparison's 'だから can lead into anything' is too unrestricted. Replace it with: 'だから can introduce a speaker's conclusion, decision, request, suggestion, or command, as well as a result. Resultative それで normally reports what followed from the preceding situation.'

title: Besides, what's more
meaning: それに／そのうえ: "besides", "on top of that"; adds another point, usually supporting the same line as the first.
when: Use it at the start of a sentence to add a further point pushing in the same direction: この店は安いです。それに、料理もおいしいです. それに is common in conversation; そのうえ is a little more formal and suggests "and even more than that". Both often add one more reason.
why: それ points back at what was said, and に adds to it: "to that, (add) this". そのうえ is literally "on top of that". Both add another point, usually one that supports the same conclusion; how the points relate depends on the speaker's argument. To add a point that goes against the first, use でも or しかし.

examples.japanese: この店は安いです。それに、料理もおいしいです。
examples.reading: このみせはやすいです。それに、りょうりもおいしいです。
examples.romaji: kono mise wa yasui desu. soreni, ryōri mo oishii desu.
examples.english: This restaurant is cheap. Besides, the food is good too.

examples.japanese: 今日は雨です。それに、とても寒いです。
examples.reading: きょうはあめです。それに、とてもさむいです。
examples.romaji: kyō wa ame desu. soreni, totemo samui desu.
examples.english: It's raining today. And on top of that, it's very cold.

examples.japanese: 道に迷いました。そのうえ、スマホの電池も切れてしまいました。
examples.reading: みちにまよいました。そのうえ、スマホのでんちもきれてしまいました。
examples.romaji: michi ni mayoimashita. sono ue, sumaho no denchi mo kirete shimaimashita.
examples.english: I got lost. On top of that, my phone battery ran out.

mistake.wrong: このアパートは駅から近いです。それに、家賃が高いです。
mistake.problem: Meant as a contrast between the handy location and the high rent. For a contrast, use でも. それに adds a point that supports the same line, which is not what is meant here.
mistake.right: このアパートは駅から近いです。でも、家賃が高いです。

distinguish_from.note: そして broadly joins facts or events; それから often introduces the next event or item. それに specifically adds another point.
し links points or reasons inside one sentence. それに starts a new sentence to add one.

listed.item: 文A。それに 文B (Bun A. Soreni Bun B)

reviews.note: The same-direction explanation is too categorical: the points need not both be objectively good or both bad; their relationship depends on the speaker's argument. Replace 'good on good, or bad on bad' with 'usually adding another supporting point; whether the points support the same conclusion depends on context'. In the mistake, write: 'If the intended meaning contrasts convenient location with expensive rent, use でも. The original can work when both facts support the speaker’s argument.' The distinction notes also overstate things. Replace them with: 'そして broadly connects facts or events and can also add reasons; それから often introduces the next event or item. それに specifically adds another point.' And: 'し links cumulative points or reasons and can also end an utterance with the continuation implied. それに is a connector introducing an additional point.'

title: Asking which of two
meaning: AとBとどちらがXですか: which is more X, A or B? どっち is the casual form. The answer usually uses のほうが.
when: Use it to ask someone to choose between two: 電車とバスとどちらが速いですか. The answer normally picks one with のほうが: 電車のほうが速いです. Among friends, どっち replaces どちら. The second と is often left out: 電車とバスどちらが速いですか.
why: どちら asks "which way, which side", so it is the usual question word when two alternatives are set against each other. どれ picks one from a set, especially of three or more, and の中で何が…いちばん compares a larger group. The two options are listed with と, and the choice is the unknown, so どちら takes が, as a question word asking who or what does. The answer picks one side with のほうが, since ほう also means "side". As in any comparison, the adjective does not change form: 速い means "faster" here because of the question.

formation.form: A と B と どちらが + adjective + ですか / verb (ます-form) + か
formation.note: Polite: どちらが速いですか, どちらがよく売れますか.

formation.form: A と B と どっちが + adjective / verb (plain)
formation.note: Casual: 夏と冬とどっちが好き？

formation.form: A と B どちらが …
formation.note: The second と is often dropped.

formation.form: Answer: A のほうが + adjective or verb predicate
formation.note: When both are equal: どちらも好きです.

examples.japanese: 「電車とバスとどちらが速いですか。」「電車のほうが速いです。」
examples.reading: 「でんしゃとバスとどちらがはやいですか。」「でんしゃのほうがはやいです。」
examples.romaji: "densha to basu to dochira ga hayai desu ka." "densha no hō ga hayai desu."
examples.english: "Which is faster, the train or the bus?" "The train is."

examples.japanese: 夏と冬とどっちが好き？
examples.reading: なつとふゆとどっちがすき？
examples.romaji: natsu to fuyu to dotchi ga suki?
examples.english: Which do you like better, summer or winter?

examples.japanese: 紅茶とコーヒーとどちらがいいですか。
examples.reading: こうちゃとコーヒーとどちらがいいですか。
examples.romaji: kōcha to kōhī to dochira ga ii desu ka.
examples.english: Which would you like, tea or coffee?

mistake.wrong: 電車とバスとどれが速いですか。
mistake.problem: When two alternatives are named and compared, どちら (or どっち in casual speech) is the natural word. どれ usually picks one from a larger set.
mistake.right: 電車とバスとどちらが速いですか。

distinguish_from.note: The answer to this question: のほうが picks one side, and より names the other if needed.
For three or more, ask with の中で: 果物の中で何がいちばん好きですか.

listed.item: Aと Bと どちら～ (A to B to dochira~)
AとBと どっち〜 (A to B to docchi〜)

review.note: Question: is どれ between two options really an error, or just less usual? The mistake currently says to use どちら. Revised after the first gpt-6-astra review to meet its objection (see reviews).

reviews.note: The polite formation incorrectly allows a verb directly before ですか. Replace it with: 'AとBとどちらが + い-adjective / な-adjective stem + ですか; or AとBとどちらが + verb in ～ますか, e.g. どちらが長持ちしますか.' Allow a verb predicate in the answer formation as well: 'Aのほうが + adjective or verb predicate.' The strict two-versus-three rule also needs qualification: どれ is not grammatically restricted to three or more options. Replace the explanation and mistake diagnosis with: 'どちら／どっち is the usual choice when explicitly contrasting two alternatives. どれ commonly selects one from a set, especially three or more. In this two-option comparison, 電車とバスとどちらが速いですか is the natural model to learn.'

title: "As for A, B is ...": a topic and a subject together
meaning: AはBがX: about A, B is X. は sets the topic; が marks what X is said of. Used for features, likes, skills and feelings.
when: Use it to describe someone or something by one of its features: この部屋は窓が大きいです (This room has big windows; literally, as for this room, the windows are big). The same shape says what someone likes, is good at or understands (妹は歌が上手です), and how a part of the body feels: 私は頭が痛いです.
why: は and が do different jobs, so one sentence can have both. は names what the whole sentence is about. が marks the subject of the adjective or verb at the end. In この部屋は窓が大きいです, what is big is the windows, while the sentence as a whole is about the room. English usually folds the two layers into one ("the room has big windows", "my sister sings well"). For a plain report of how your body feels, Japanese commonly makes the person the topic and the body part the subject, and often leaves the person out: 頭が痛いです. (私の頭が痛いです is also possible, when you need to say whose head it is.) With 好き, 上手, わかる and similar words, the thing liked or understood takes が and the person takes は: 私は犬が好きです.

formation.form: A は B が + adjective
formation.note: A feature of A: この部屋は窓が大きい.

formation.form: Person は thing が + 好き / 上手 / わかる / 痛い
formation.note: Likes, skills, understanding, how the body feels.

examples.japanese: この部屋は窓が大きいです。
examples.reading: このへやはまどがおおきいです。
examples.romaji: kono heya wa mado ga ōkii desu.
examples.english: This room has big windows.

examples.japanese: 妹は歌が上手です。
examples.reading: いもうとはうたがじょうずです。
examples.romaji: imōto wa uta ga jōzu desu.
examples.english: My younger sister is good at singing.

examples.japanese: 私は頭が痛いです。
examples.reading: わたしはあたまがいたいです。
examples.romaji: watashi wa atama ga itai desu.
examples.english: I have a headache.
examples.note: In conversation 私は is usually left out: 頭が痛いです.

mistake.wrong: 私は頭を痛いです。
mistake.problem: 痛い is an adjective describing the part that hurts, so that part is its subject and takes が, not を.
mistake.right: 私は頭が痛いです。

distinguish_from.note: は on its own sets up the topic; this pattern adds a が subject inside the comment.
が on its own marks the subject; here it marks the subject of the comment about the topic.

listed.item: A は B が〜 (A wa B ga〜)

review.note: Questions: is 私の頭が痛いです fairly called unnatural (rather than wrong)? Would a native prefer the right version without 私は, and if so, should the mistake's right version be 頭が痛いです? Revised after the first gpt-6-astra review to meet its objection (see reviews).

reviews.note: 私の頭が痛いです is grammatical and can naturally describe the speaker's own bodily sensation; it is not categorically excluded in favor of 私は頭が痛いです. Replace the relevant reasoning with: 'For a neutral report of a bodily sensation, Japanese commonly uses the person as the topic and the body part with が, often omitting the person when understood. 私の頭が痛いです is also possible when explicitly identifying whose head hurts.' Replace the mistake with wrong: 私は頭を痛いです; problem: '痛い describes the painful body part, which takes が here, not を'; right: 私は頭が痛いです.

title: A is not as … as B
meaning: A は B ほど + negative: "A is not as (adjective) as B", or does not do something as much; B is the standard.
when: Use it to compare by saying one thing falls short of another: 今年の夏は去年ほど暑くない, "this summer isn't as hot as last year's". It is a natural way to say something is less so, and it can sound gentler than a direct comparison with より.
why: ほど means "extent, degree". B ほど is "to B's degree", and the negative says A does not reach it. In this "not as … as" pattern, the end of the sentence must be negative. B is the standard; the context may suggest that B has the quality strongly, but it need not.

formation.form: A は B ほど + negative
formation.note: い-adjective 暑くない; な-adjective にぎやかではない／じゃない; verb 読まない. Polite くないです／くありません, ではありません, ません.

examples.japanese: 今年の夏は去年ほど暑くないです。
examples.reading: ことしのなつはきょねんほどあつくないです。
examples.romaji: kotoshi no natsu wa kyonen hodo atsuku nai desu.
examples.english: This summer isn't as hot as last year's.

examples.japanese: 私の町は東京ほどにぎやかではありません。
examples.reading: わたしのまちはとうきょうほどにぎやかではありません。
examples.romaji: watashi no machi wa tōkyō hodo nigiyaka de wa arimasen.
examples.english: My town isn't as lively as Tokyo.

examples.japanese: 弟は私ほど本を読みません。
examples.reading: おとうとはわたしほどほんをよみません。
examples.romaji: otōto wa watashi hodo hon o yomimasen.
examples.english: My little brother doesn't read as much as I do.

mistake.wrong: 東京は大阪ほど大きいです。
mistake.problem: Meant as "Tokyo is bigger than Osaka". ほど does not express "more than"; use より.
mistake.right: 東京は大阪より大きいです。

distinguish_from.note: より and のほうが say which one has more of the quality. ほど～ない says one falls short of the other.

listed.item: A は B ほど～ありません (A wa B hodo ～ arimasen)
A は B ほど～ない (A wa B hodo ~ nai)

reviews.note: B need not possess the quality to a clearly high degree: 去年ほど暑くない compares temperatures without necessarily asserting that last year was hot. Replace that claim with: 'B supplies the comparison standard; context may suggest that B has the quality strongly, but this is not required.' The negative requirement must be limited to this pattern, not all comparisons using ほど; affirmative uses exist, such as 去年ほどの暑さだ. Write: 'This “not as … as” pattern requires a negative ending.' Replace the mistake diagnosis with: 'To mean “Tokyo is bigger than Osaka”, use より; ほど does not express “more than”.' Also change 'it sounds gentler' to 'it can sound gentler', and broaden the meaning to include the verb use shown: 'A does not have the quality, or do the activity, to the same degree as B.'
The explanation, formation, examples, romanization, and comparison with より are accurate.

title: Using an adjective to say how something is done
meaning: い-adjective く / な-adjective に + verb: do something in that way. 早く起きる, きれいに書く.
when: Use it to say how an action is done: 早く起きます (get up early), 名前をきれいに書いてください (please write your name neatly), 静かに話しましょう (let's talk quietly).
why: An adjective in its basic form describes a noun (早い電車, 静かな部屋) or ends a sentence. To describe a verb it needs its adverb form, made by changing the ending: い becomes く, and a な-adjective takes に instead of な. The adjective then goes before the verb. The same forms appear before なる, "become", because that is a verb too: 大きくなる. いい is the one irregular い-adjective: its adverb form is よく, from the older form よい, and よく also means "often". Watch for な-adjectives that happen to end in い, such as きれい and 嫌い: they take に, so きれいに.

formation.note: 早い → 早く起きる. いい → よく.
静か → 静かに話す. きれい → きれいに書く.

examples.japanese: あしたは早く起きます。
examples.reading: あしたははやくおきます。
examples.romaji: ashita wa hayaku okimasu.
examples.english: I'll get up early tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 名前をきれいに書いてください。
examples.reading: なまえをきれいにかいてください。
examples.romaji: namae o kirei ni kaite kudasai.
examples.english: Please write your name neatly.

examples.japanese: 図書館では静かに話しましょう。
examples.reading: としょかんではしずかにはなしましょう。
examples.romaji: toshokan de wa shizuka ni hanashimashō.
examples.english: Let's talk quietly in the library.

examples.japanese: 昨日はよく寝ました。
examples.reading: きのうはよくねました。
examples.romaji: kinō wa yoku nemashita.
examples.english: I slept well yesterday.
examples.note: よく is the adverb form of いい.

mistake.wrong: 名前をきれく書いてください。
mistake.problem: きれい ends in い but is a な-adjective, so its adverb form is きれいに, not きれく.
mistake.right: 名前をきれいに書いてください。

distinguish_from.note: The same forms before なる: 大きくなる, 静かになる. There the adjective says what something becomes, not how an action is done.
The same forms before する: 部屋をきれいにする, make the room clean.

listed.item: い-Adjective く + Verb (i-Adjective + ku + Verb)

review.note: Question: 昨日はよく寝ました is glossed "last night"; is that the natural reading, or should the English be "I slept well yesterday"? Revised after the first gpt-6-astra review to meet its objection (see reviews).

reviews.note: 有名（ゆうめい）does not end in い in the relevant sense: its final い is part of めい, not an apparent adjective ending. Replace 'such as きれい and 有名' with 'such as きれい and 嫌い'. Also, 昨日はよく寝ました says 'I slept well yesterday,' not specifically 'last night'. Use that translation, or change the Japanese to 昨夜はよく寝ました, the reading to ゆうべはよくねました。, and the romaji to yūbe wa yoku nemashita.

title: Saying an い-adjective is not so, politely
meaning: い-adjective, drop い, + くないです or くありません: is not X. いい becomes よくないです.
when: Use it to say something is not cold, not expensive, not interesting: 今日は寒くないです. くありません means the same and sounds a little more formal; くないです is common in everyday polite speech. Past: くなかったです, くありませんでした.
why: An い-adjective behaves like a verb: it carries its own tense and its own negative, and in plain speech it ends a sentence with nothing after it (高い, 高くない). です after an い-adjective only adds politeness; it is not a verb to be made negative. So the negative is built on the adjective itself, 高い → 高くない, and です is added on top: 高くないです. So the ordinary negative is 高くないです. じゃない is the negative of だ, used after nouns and な-adjectives; 高いじゃないです does not give the plain "is not expensive", and with some intonations is heard instead as confirmation or surprise ("it's expensive, isn't it!"). くありません is the same く form with ありません, the polite negative of ある. The only irregular one is いい, whose forms are built on よい: よくないです. な-adjectives that end in い, like きれい and 嫌い, are not い-adjectives: きれいじゃないです.

formation.form: い-adjective (drop い) + くないです
formation.note: 高い → 高くないです. Plain: 高くない.

formation.form: い-adjective (drop い) + くありません
formation.note: A little more formal.

formation.form: い-adjective (drop い) + くなかったです / くありませんでした
formation.note: Past.

formation.form: いい → よくないです
formation.note: Irregular.

examples.japanese: 今日は寒くないです。
examples.reading: きょうはさむくないです。
examples.romaji: kyō wa samukunai desu.
examples.english: It isn't cold today.

examples.japanese: このカレーは辛くありません。
examples.reading: このカレーはからくありません。
examples.romaji: kono karē wa karaku arimasen.
examples.english: This curry isn't spicy.

examples.japanese: 昨日の映画はよくなかったです。
examples.reading: きのうのえいがはよくなかったです。
examples.romaji: kinō no eiga wa yokunakatta desu.
examples.english: Yesterday's film wasn't good.

mistake.wrong: この本はおもしろいじゃないです。
mistake.problem: Intended as "This book isn't interesting". おもしろい is an い-adjective, so it makes its own negative: おもしろくない. おもしろいじゃないです does not give that ordinary negative meaning.
mistake.right: この本はおもしろくないです。

distinguish_from.note: Nouns and な-adjectives use the negative of the copula: ではない or じゃない, made polite as じゃありません or じゃないです (学生じゃありません, 静かじゃないです). い-adjectives change their own ending.
あまり + くない softens it: not very.

review.note: Questions: is くないです vs くありません described fairly (the entry says くありません is a little more formal)? Romaji joins the adjective and ない (samukunai), following ikitakunai desu elsewhere in the file. Revised after the first gpt-6-astra review to meet its objection (see reviews).

reviews.note: 高いじゃないです and おもしろいじゃないです are not inherently ungrammatical: with suitable context and intonation, they can express confirmation or an exclamation, such as 'It's expensive, isn't it!' Replace the categorical rejection in why with: '高いじゃないです does not express the ordinary negative “is not expensive”; it can instead express confirmation or surprise. For the ordinary negative, use 高くないです.' In the mistake, specify that the intended meaning is 'This book isn't interesting' and explain that おもしろいじゃないです does not give that ordinary negative meaning. Also replace 'Nouns and な-adjectives make the negative through です' with 'Nouns and な-adjectives use negative copular forms such as ではない／じゃない, made polite as ではありません／じゃありません or ではないです／じゃないです.'

title: Joining adjectives: ... and ...
meaning: い-adjective くて / な-adjective or noun で: X and Y. It links a description to what follows, and can give a light reason.
when: Use it to give two qualities of one thing: この部屋は広くて明るいです; 図書館は静かできれいです. With a noun, it joins two statements: 兄は医者で、姉は先生です. The same form can give a loose cause for what follows: この本は難しくて、よくわかりません.
why: Japanese does not join adjectives with と, which joins nouns only. Instead the first adjective takes its て-form, the form that links it to what comes next, the way verbs do (起きて、食べる). For an い-adjective, い becomes くて; for a な-adjective or a noun, で, the て-form of だ. Only the last word carries the tense and politeness: 広くて明るかったです is "was spacious and bright". Because the て-form only says "and, and so", context decides whether it is a list or a cause. Two qualities joined this way usually point the same way, both good or both bad; to set a good point against a bad one, use が or けど. いい becomes よくて.

formation.note: 広い → 広くて. いい → よくて.
静か → 静かで.
医者で, 学生で.

examples.japanese: この部屋は広くて明るいです。
examples.reading: このへやはひろくてあかるいです。
examples.romaji: kono heya wa hirokute akarui desu.
examples.english: This room is spacious and bright.

examples.japanese: 図書館は静かできれいです。
examples.reading: としょかんはしずかできれいです。
examples.romaji: toshokan wa shizuka de kirei desu.
examples.english: The library is quiet and clean.

examples.japanese: 兄は医者で、姉は先生です。
examples.reading: あにはいしゃで、あねはせんせいです。
examples.romaji: ani wa isha de, ane wa sensei desu.
examples.english: My older brother is a doctor, and my older sister is a teacher.

examples.japanese: この本は難しくて、よくわかりません。
examples.reading: このほんはむずかしくて、よくわかりません。
examples.romaji: kono hon wa muzukashikute, yoku wakarimasen.
examples.english: This book is difficult, so I don't really understand it.
examples.note: Here the first half reads as the cause.

mistake.wrong: 図書館は静かくて、きれいです。
mistake.problem: 静か is a な-adjective; its joining form is で, not くて.
mistake.right: 図書館は静かで、きれいです。

distinguish_from.note: と joins nouns only: 犬と猫. Adjectives are joined with くて or で.
The same て-form, on verbs: 起きて、食べます.
To set a good point against a bad one, use が or けど: 高いけど、おいしいです.

review.note: Question: is "two qualities joined this way usually point the same way" stated carefully enough? 安くておいしい is typical; mixed pairs sound odd, but not always wrong.

title: A or B
meaning: AかB: A or B, one of them. The phrase acts as one noun, so a particle after it covers both.
when: Use it to offer alternatives: 朝はパンかご飯を食べます (I have bread or rice in the morning). It is common in suggestions and requests: 土曜日か日曜日に会いませんか; ペンか鉛筆で書いてください.
why: か is the question particle: it marks something as not settled. Between nouns it keeps the choice open: A, or B, one of them, without saying which. The whole phrase AかB then works as a single noun, so any particle comes after it: パンかご飯を, 土曜日か日曜日に. Compare と, which takes both: パンとご飯を食べます means you eat both. A か can also follow the last option (AかBか), which stresses that it is one or the other; in everyday sentences the final か is usually left out.

formation.note: The particle follows the whole phrase: パンかご飯を.

formation.form: N1 か N2 か (+ particle)
formation.note: Stresses the choice; the final か is often dropped.

examples.japanese: 朝はパンかご飯を食べます。
examples.reading: あさはパンかごはんをたべます。
examples.romaji: asa wa pan ka gohan o tabemasu.
examples.english: In the morning I have bread or rice.

examples.japanese: 土曜日か日曜日に会いませんか。
examples.reading: どようびかにちようびにあいませんか。
examples.romaji: doyōbi ka nichiyōbi ni aimasen ka.
examples.english: Shall we meet on Saturday or Sunday?

examples.japanese: ペンか鉛筆で書いてください。
examples.reading: ペンかえんぴつでかいてください。
examples.romaji: pen ka enpitsu de kaite kudasai.
examples.english: Please write in pen or pencil.

mistake.wrong: 土曜日と日曜日に会いませんか。
mistake.problem: Intended as "Saturday or Sunday". と takes both, so this asks to meet on both days. For one or the other, use か.
mistake.right: 土曜日か日曜日に会いませんか。

distinguish_from.note: と joins nouns and takes all of them: パンとご飯 is both.
や gives examples from a longer list: パンや果物, bread, fruit and so on. か offers a choice.
The same か after a question word: 何か, something.

listed.item: Noun か Noun か～ (Noun ka Noun ka～)

review.note: Question: is AかBか (with the second か) described correctly as stressing the choice? Is the mistake a real learner error (と for "or")?

title: Saying someone can do something
meaning: Nができる / V (dictionary form) + ことができる: can do, is able to. What can be done takes が.
when: Use Nができる with a skill, sport or language: 日本語ができます, テニスができます. Use ～ことができる with a verb to say someone can do an action: 漢字を読むことができます. It also says something is possible or allowed somewhere: この部屋でご飯を食べることができます.
why: できる means "can be done, is possible". In this ability pattern, できる takes the skill or activity with が: テニスができる. Learn this as the particle pattern of できる, as with わかる and 好き; it is not a rule for every word that describes a state. A verb cannot directly take this が, which marks a noun, so it is first turned into a noun with こと, "the act of": 読むこと. Then ができる follows. The verb keeps its own object with を inside that phrase: 漢字を読むことができます. Japanese also has a shorter potential form of the verb (読める), which is very common in speech and usually taught at N4; ことができる sounds more formal, and it is built the same way for every verb.

formation.note: 日本語ができます. For skills, sports, languages.

formation.form: V (dictionary form) + こと + が + できる
formation.note: 泳ぐことができます. する-verbs: 運転することができます.

formation.form: ～ことができません / ～ことができました
formation.note: Negative and past.

examples.japanese: 兄は中国語ができます。
examples.reading: あにはちゅうごくごができます。
examples.romaji: ani wa chūgokugo ga dekimasu.
examples.english: My older brother can speak Chinese.

examples.japanese: 私は泳ぐことができません。
examples.reading: わたしはおよぐことができません。
examples.romaji: watashi wa oyogu koto ga dekimasen.
examples.english: I can't swim.

examples.japanese: この部屋でご飯を食べることができます。
examples.reading: このへやでごはんをたべることができます。
examples.romaji: kono heya de gohan o taberu koto ga dekimasu.
examples.english: You can eat in this room.

mistake.wrong: 私は泳ぐができます。
mistake.problem: In this pattern, what can be done must be a noun before が. A verb cannot take that が directly; turn it into a noun with こと first.
mistake.right: 私は泳ぐことができます。

distinguish_from.note: The こと that makes a verb into a noun, used here before が.
The potential form (泳げる) says the same more briefly, and is more common in speech.

listed.item: Noun が できます (Noun ga dekimasu)
Verb る こと が できます (ru koto ga dekimasu)
Verb る こと ができる (ru koto ga dekiru)
Verb ることができる (〜ru koto ga dekiru)

review.note: Question: 兄は中国語ができます is glossed "can speak Chinese"; できる with a language covers more than speaking. Is that gloss acceptable? Revised after the first gpt-6-astra review to meet its objection (see reviews).

reviews.note: The reasoning incorrectly makes stativity the reason for choosing が rather than を. Stative predicates do not universally take が; for example, 知っている takes an object with を. Replace that explanation with: 'In this ability construction, できる takes the activity or skill with が: テニスができる. Learn this as the particle pattern of できる, rather than as a rule for all predicates describing states.' Also qualify 'A verb cannot stand before が' in both why and the mistake: 'A verb cannot directly take the noun-marking が in this construction; nominalize it with こと first.' Verbs can directly precede the conjunction が, as in 泳ぐが、速くはない.

title: From ... to ..., until ...
meaning: AからBまで: from A to B, in time or place. まで alone: until, as far as. まで marks an end point or limit.
when: Use it for the start and end of a span of time or a distance: 銀行は九時から三時までです; 家から駅まで歩きます. まで can be used on its own: 駅まで歩きます (walk as far as the station), 夜十一時まで勉強しました (studied until eleven at night).
why: から marks the starting point and まで the end point; together they frame everything in between. With a time, まで usually means something goes on, or keeps happening, up to that time: 三時まで待つ, 三時まで寝る. With a place, it marks how far something goes: 駅まで歩く. For a deadline, the time by which something must happen or be done, Japanese uses までに instead (N4): 三時までに来てください. Either half can be left out when it is clear.

formation.form: A から B まで
formation.note: Time or place.
Until, as far as: 三時まで, 駅まで.
Until something happens: 雨がやむまで待ちます.

examples.japanese: 銀行は九時から三時までです。
examples.reading: ぎんこうはくじからさんじまでです。
examples.romaji: ginkō wa kuji kara sanji made desu.
examples.english: The bank is open from nine to three.

examples.japanese: 家から駅まで歩いて十五分です。
examples.reading: いえからえきまであるいてじゅうごふんです。
examples.romaji: ie kara eki made aruite jūgofun desu.
examples.english: It's fifteen minutes on foot from my house to the station.

examples.romaji: kinō wa yoru jūichiji made benkyō shimashita.
examples.english: Yesterday I studied until eleven at night.

mistake.wrong: あしたの十時まで宿題を出してください。
mistake.problem: For a deadline to hand in the homework, use までに. まで would suggest the handing in goes on, or keeps happening, up to ten o'clock.
mistake.right: あしたの十時までに宿題を出してください。

distinguish_from.note: までに marks a deadline: an event happens, or a task is done, no later than that time.
から after a clause gives a reason; after a noun it means "from", as here.

listed.item: Noun から Noun まで (Noun kara Noun made)

review.note: Question: is the までに contrast (N4) appropriate to include in an N5 entry? It is the most common mistake with まで. Revised after the first gpt-6-astra review to meet its objection (see reviews).

reviews.note: The claim that the action always runs across the whole span is too broad, especially for spatial endpoints: 東京まで荷物を送る does not mean the sending action continues throughout the journey. Replace the meaning's final sentence and the corresponding reasoning with: 'から marks a starting point and まで an endpoint or limit. With a time endpoint, まで commonly indicates continuation or repetition up to that time; with a place, it marks how far something goes.' Also, までに does not require something to happen exactly once. Replace the deadline explanation with: 'までに marks a deadline by which an event must occur or a task must be completed.' In the mistake, write: 'For the intended submission deadline, use までに; まで instead suggests continuation or repetition up to that time.' Replace the OJG-0306 note with: 'までに marks a deadline: an event occurs or a task is completed no later than that time.'

title: By (a deadline)
meaning: Time + までに: "by (then)"; marks a deadline by which something happens or is completed.
when: Use it for a deadline: 金曜日までにレポートを出してください, "please hand in the report by Friday". The action is done at some point up to that time. It can also follow a verb: 暗くなるまでに帰ります, "I'll be home before it gets dark".
why: まで marks the end of a stretch of time; に marks a point where something happens. Together they give a deadline: by X, the thing happens or is completed. It does not say how many times. まで without に says an activity or state goes on all the way to X (五時まで働く).

formation.note: 金曜日までに, 三時までに.
暗くなるまでに, 母が帰るまでに.

examples.japanese: 金曜日までにレポートを出してください。
examples.reading: きんようびまでにレポートをだしてください。
examples.romaji: kin'yōbi made ni repōto o dashite kudasai.
examples.english: Please hand in the report by Friday.

examples.japanese: 暗くなるまでに帰ります。
examples.reading: くらくなるまでにかえります。
examples.romaji: kuraku naru made ni kaerimasu.
examples.english: I'll be home before it gets dark.

examples.japanese: 三時までに駅に来てください。
examples.reading: さんじまでにえきにきてください。
examples.romaji: sanji made ni eki ni kite kudasai.
examples.english: Please come to the station by three.

mistake.wrong: 五時までに働きます。
mistake.problem: Meant as "I work until five". That is まで, for an activity that lasts up to a time. までに sets a deadline for something to happen or be completed.
mistake.right: 五時まで働きます。

distinguish_from.note: まで marks how long an activity or state goes on ("until"). までに marks a deadline for something to happen or be completed ("by").

reviews.note: までに does not require an action to happen only once. It can set a deadline for repeated actions or a bounded amount of activity: 五時までに三回電話してください and 五時までに二時間働いてください. Replace the repeated 'one-time action' claims in the meaning, when, why, mistake and distinction with: 'までに marks a deadline by which an event must occur or an action or specified amount of activity must be completed. It does not specify how many times the action happens.' Explain the contrast as: 'まで marks the endpoint through which an activity or state continues; までに marks a deadline for occurrence or completion.' In the mistake, write: 'For the intended meaning “work continuously until five”, use まで. 働く is not inherently incompatible with までに, but working must be presented as something to accomplish by that deadline.'
The deadline meaning and distinction from まで are correctly explained; all examples and readings match.

pattern: 数量 + くらい／ぐらい
title: About, roughly (with amounts)
meaning: Amount + くらい／ぐらい: about, roughly that much. 二十分ぐらい, 三十人くらい.
when: Use it after an amount to show it is approximate: 駅までバスで二十分ぐらいかかります; 教室に学生が三十人くらいいます. どのくらい or どれくらい asks "about how much, how long". For a point in time, like three o'clock, ごろ is the usual word.
why: くらい and ぐらい mark an extent: "to about this degree". After a number, that makes it approximate. The two forms mean the same thing, and both are correct; after a number, ぐらい is very common in speech. An amount includes a length of time: 二時間ぐらい, "about two hours". A point in time takes ごろ: 三時ごろ, "around three". In everyday speech くらい is also heard after a clock time (三時ぐらいに), but ごろ never goes after a length of time.

formation.form: Number + counter + くらい／ぐらい

title: Around (a point in time)
meaning: Time + ごろ: at about that time. 七時ごろ, 四月ごろ. Only for points in time, not for lengths of time.
when: Use it after a clock time, a date or a month to show the time is approximate: 毎朝七時ごろ起きます; 去年の四月ごろ日本に来ました. いつごろ asks "about when?"
why: ごろ means "around the time of". It attaches to a point in time, so it answers いつ (when?), never どのくらい (how long?). A length of time takes くらい or ぐらい instead: 三時ごろ is a moment, 三時間ぐらい a duration. Because ごろ already makes a time phrase, the に that normally follows a clock time is optional after it: 三時ごろ来ます and 三時ごろに来ます are both used.

formation.note: 七時ごろ, 七時ごろに. に is optional.

title: Only, just
meaning: N + だけ: only N, just N, nothing more. だけ follows the thing it limits.
when: Use it to limit something to what is named: 朝はコーヒーだけ飲みました (I only had coffee this morning), りんごを一つだけください (just one apple, please). It also follows a verb: 見ているだけです, "I'm just looking", in a shop.
why: だけ marks a limit: this much and no further. It goes right after the word it limits, so moving it changes what is limited: 私だけ行きます is "only I go". が and を after だけ are often left out, though they can stay (コーヒーだけ飲みました, コーヒーだけを飲みました); other particles stay, and usually come before だけ: 田中さんにだけ話しました. だけ restricts whatever it follows and can go with a positive or a negative verb, but the meaning differs: コーヒーだけ飲みました is "I drank only coffee"; コーヒーだけ飲みませんでした is "coffee was the one thing I didn't drink". The pattern しか～ない (N4) says "only" through what is missing, with a negative verb, and often suggests "not enough".

一つだけ, 五分だけ.

title: Choosing: I'll have ..., let's go with ...
meaning: Nにする／Nにします: decide on N, choose N. Common when ordering and making plans: コーヒーにします.
when: Use it when you choose among options: in a café, 私はコーヒーにします (I'll have coffee); making plans, パーティーは土曜日にしましょう. 何にしますか asks "what will you have?" or "what will you choose?". The past, にしました, reports a choice already made.
why: に marks where something ends up, and する here means "make". So Nにする is "make it N": of the possible choices, the outcome is N. That is why it is the natural phrase for ordering and deciding, where ください is only a request for something. Compare Nになる, "become N": になる presents the result without itself saying who chose it; にする presents someone as choosing it.

formation.form: Noun + に + する／します
formation.note: Choosing or deciding.
What will you have? What will you choose?
Reports a choice already made.

title: After ...
meaning: V (た-form) + あとで / N + のあとで: after doing V, after N. The first event is over before the second.
when: Use it to put one event after another: 晩ご飯を食べたあとで、散歩します; 授業のあとで、図書館に行きました. あとで on its own means "later": あとで電話します.
why: あと (後) means "after, behind", the time that comes later. The verb before it takes the た-form because, by the time of the main event, the first one is already finished, even when both are still in the future: 食べたあとで散歩します. A noun joins with の, as other time and position nouns do: 授業のあと. で marks the point at which the main event happens; あと with a comma and no で is also common. Compared with ～てから, あとで simply puts the two events in order; てから stresses that the second follows once the first is done, often straight after it.

title: Joining actions with the て-form
meaning: V-て, …: joins a verb to what follows: "and", "and then", how something is done, or why.
when: Use the て-form to join several actions into one sentence in the order they happen: 朝起きて、顔を洗って、朝ご飯を食べます. It also says how something is done (歩いて学校に行きます, "walk to school"), and loosely why: 風邪をひいて、学校を休みました.
why: The て-form is the connecting form of a verb: it says "and" and leaves the sentence open. It has no tense or politeness marking of its own; the last verb supplies those for the sentence, and context and time words say when each action happens: 起きて、食べました is read as all in the past. In a sequence, the clauses normally follow the order of events, which is why て naturally reads "and then". When the first action is the way the second is done, it reads "by, on": 歩いて行く, バスに乗って行く. When the first is something that happened to the subject, it often reads as the cause: 風邪をひいて休みました. How the て-form is made depends on the verb group.

formation.note: For a sequence, the actions normally come in the order they happen; the last verb carries the sentence's tense.
How you go: 歩いて行く, バスに乗って来る.

formation.form: Group 2 (る-verbs): drop る, add て
formation.note: 食べる → 食べて, 見る → 見て.

formation.form: Group 1 (う-verbs): う, つ, る → って; む, ぶ, ぬ → んで; く → いて; ぐ → いで; す → して
formation.note: 会う → 会って, 読む → 読んで, 書く → 書いて. The exception: 行く → 行って.

formation.form: Irregular: する → して, 来る → 来て

title: Turning a verb into a noun with こと
meaning: V (plain form) + こと: an action or a fact, as a noun. With the dictionary form, often "doing V": 趣味は写真を撮ることです.
when: Use it when an action has to fill a noun's place: 私の趣味は写真を撮ることです (My hobby is taking photos); 毎日日本語を話すことは大切です. It is also the piece used in ことができる (can do).
why: To use a verb phrase as the subject, object or topic in sentences like these, it has to be turned into a noun first; a plain verb also cannot stand before です when saying what something is (趣味は…です). こと is a noun meaning "matter, thing" in the abstract, and a verb phrase in front of it describes it, the way a clause describes any noun. So the whole phrase becomes a noun: 写真を撮ること, "the matter of taking photos". The verb keeps its own particles inside the phrase. こと suits naming an action as an idea: a hobby, a rule, a skill. Often の can replace it (読むのが好き, 読むことが好き), but not always: after は…です saying what something is, use こと (趣味は読むことです); for seeing or hearing an event as it happens, use の. こと can go with 聞く when you hear a fact: 田中さんが結婚したことを聞きました.

formation.note: The dictionary form for an activity: 読むこと, 泳ぐこと. Past and negative forms also occur: 結婚したこと, 行かないこと. The verb keeps its own object: 本を読むこと.
Saying what something is: 趣味は…ことです.

title: Turning a verb into a noun with の
meaning: V (plain form) + の: "doing V", as a noun. Common before が好き, は楽しい, を忘れる, and with seeing and hearing.
when: Use it to put an action where a noun is needed, especially in everyday speech: 走るのは楽しいです; 宿題を持ってくるのを忘れました. It is the usual choice for something seen or heard happening: 子どもたちが遊んでいるのを見ました.
why: の after a verb phrase does the job it does in 私のです: it stands in for a noun, and the words before it describe it. So 走るの is "running", a noun that can take は, が or を. Compared with こと, の tends to present the action as a concrete event, which is why verbs of seeing and hearing take の: you see children playing, an event in front of you. こと suits an action named as an idea, as in 趣味は読むことです; 読むのです would instead be read as the explaining の (see ～んです). The verb before の is in the plain form, and can be past or ている: 遊んでいるのを見ました.

formation.form: V (plain form) + の + は／が／を
formation.note: 走るのは, 泳ぐのが, 持ってくるのを.

formation.form: V (ている) + の + を + 見る／聞く

mistake.right: 走るのは楽しいです。

distinguish_from.note: こと also turns a verb into a noun, and is the one to use before です when saying what something is: 趣味は走ることです.
のが好きです is this の in its most common frame.
の or ん at the end of a sentence (走るんです) explains. That is a different use.
Between two nouns, の links them: 私の本.

listed.item: Verb る の～ (Verb + ru + no~)

review.note: Question: 宿題を持ってくるのを忘れました uses ～てくる as a single verb "bring"; is that fine at N5? Revised after the first gpt-6-astra review to meet its objection (see reviews).

reviews.note: The mistake diagnosis 'は needs a noun before it' is an overgeneralization: は can also follow other particles and verbal forms, as in 読んではいけません. Replace it with 'Here, the action of running is the topic, so the verb phrase must be nominalized before は. Add の: 走るのは楽しいです.' The wrong and corrected examples themselves are appropriate.

title: Not very, not much
meaning: あまり + negative: not very, not much, not often. あまり高くない, あまり食べません.
when: Use it to soften a negative: この店はあまり高くないです (not very expensive); 私は肉をあまり食べません (I don't eat much meat). It is gentler than a flat negative, and is often a polite way of saying no.
why: With a negative, あまり says the amount or degree does not reach far: "not to any great extent". For this meaning, "not very, not much, not often", あまり is paired with a negative ending later in the sentence. With a positive ending it never means a neutral "very"; あまり(に) with a positive belongs to a different use, "too, excessively". Because it avoids a flat no, Japanese speakers use it where English might just say no: 「辛いものは好きですか。」「あまり好きじゃないです。」 あんまり is a common spoken form.

formation.note: あまり食べません.
あまり高くないです.

formation.form: あまり + な-adjective + じゃない／ではない
formation.note: あまり好きじゃないです. Not with just any noun: the word has to allow "how much".

そんなに～ない is "not that much", measured against something expected or just said.

あまり～ないです (amari ~ nai desu)

review.note: Question: あまり(に) with a positive ("too, so much") is left out as beyond N5; is that the right call? Revised after the first and second gpt-6-astra reviews to meet their objections; the text as it stands has not been reviewed again, because this batch stopped at two review rounds.

reviews.note: The statements that あまり 'needs a negative ending' need to be explicitly limited to the meaning taught here. Affirmative あまり／あまりに is possible with an excessive-degree meaning, as in あまりに高いです. In why, write 'For the meaning “not very/much/often,” あまり is paired with a negative predicate. Affirmative あまり（に） can instead mean “excessively” or “too,” rather than neutral “very.”' In the mistake explanation, write 'For neutral “very interesting,” use とてもおもしろいです. あまりおもしろくないです means “not very interesting”; affirmative あまり（に） belongs to a different, excessive-degree use.'

The formation treats nouns as freely interchangeable with な-adjectives, but あまり requires a predicate that supports an amount or degree interpretation. Replace the third formation with 'あまり + な-adjective + ではない／じゃない'. If retaining nouns, add: 'Also possible with noun predicates that allow a degree interpretation, such as あまり好みじゃない (not really to my taste); this is not a general pattern for all nouns.'
The negative pattern and its contrast with affirmative あまり(に) are explained accurately. The examples and correction are sound.

title: Not at all
meaning: ぜんぜん + negative: not at all, not in the least. ぜんぜんわかりません.
when: Use it for a complete negative: この問題はぜんぜんわかりません (I don't understand this problem at all); 私はお酒をぜんぜん飲みません. It is the strong end of a scale that あまり～ない sits lower on.
why: ぜんぜん (全然) means "wholly". With a negative, it says the negative holds completely: not even a little. あまり～ない is "not much"; ぜんぜん～ない is "not at all". For this "not at all" pattern, use a negative ending. ぜんぜん is also used with some positive words, especially ぜんぜん大丈夫です ("totally fine") in reply to a worry; this is common in conversation, polite conversation included, but is generally avoided in formal prose. Positive expressions of complete difference, such as 全然違う, also occur in writing.

formation.note: ぜんぜんわかりません.
ぜんぜん寒くないです.

mistake.problem: Intended as "really interesting". ぜんぜん is not a general word for "very"; its positive uses depend on context, usually answering a worry or an expectation. For a neutral "really, very", use とても.

review.note: Question: is the caveat about positive ぜんぜん (ぜんぜん大丈夫) scoped correctly: common in casual speech, avoided in polite speech? reviews.note: The instruction to keep affirmative ぜんぜん out of polite speech is too strong: 全然大丈夫です is common in polite conversation. Replace the last two sentences of why with: 'For this “not at all” pattern, use a negative predicate. Affirmative uses such as 全然大丈夫です (“totally fine”) are also common, including in polite conversation, though they are generally conversational rather than formal.' In the mistake diagnosis, replace 'In standard use ぜんぜん goes with a negative' with 'ぜんぜん is not a general substitute for とても; affirmative uses depend on context, often contradicting an expectation or concern.' The proposed correction with とても is appropriate for the intended neutral meaning.

The statement that affirmative ぜんぜん 'is not used in formal writing' is too absolute. Affirmative 全然 occurs in writing, particularly with expressions of difference such as 全然異なる. Replace the final sentence of why with: 'ぜんぜん also occurs with affirmative expressions. Conversational uses such as ぜんぜん大丈夫です (totally fine), often answering a worry, are common even in polite conversation but are generally avoided in formal prose. Affirmative expressions of complete difference, such as 全然異なる, also occur in writing.'
The explanation correctly distinguishes the complete negative from context-dependent affirmative uses. The examples, readings, romaji, and correction are accurate.

title: Not that (much), not so
meaning: そんなに + negative: "not that (adjective)", "not so much"; tones down a degree the listener might expect.
when: Use it to say something is less than might be thought: この料理はそんなに辛くないですよ, "this dish isn't that spicy". It is common in modest or reassuring answers: 「日本語が上手ですね。」「いいえ、そんなに上手じゃないです。」. Without a negative, そんなに means "that much", usually with surprise: そんなに食べたの？
why: そんな points at something near the listener or already mentioned: "that kind, to that degree". So そんなに～ない says "not to the degree you have in mind", measured against what the listener said or might expect. That is why it sits naturally in answers and reassurances. あまり～ない is a general "not very"; そんなに ties the degree to what was said or expected.

formation.note: い-adjective 辛くない; な-adjective 上手じゃない; verb 食べない.

pattern: ～はどうですか／～はいかがですか
title: How about ...? How is ...?
meaning: Nはどうですか: how is N? or how about N? Nはいかがですか is the politer form, for offers to guests and customers.
when: Use it to ask how something is or was: 日本の生活はどうですか (How is life in Japan?), 昨日のパーティーはどうでしたか. Use it also to suggest something: 「いつ会いましょうか。」「あしたはどうですか。」 いかがですか is the polite version, used when offering something to a guest or customer: お茶はいかがですか.
why: どう is the question word for "how, in what way", so Nはどうですか asks for your view of N or how N is going. When N is something offered or proposed, a day or a drink, asking how it is becomes a suggestion: what do you think of this one? いかが means the same, but belongs to polite speech, so it suits offering a guest a drink or a shop suggesting an item. For something already over, use the past: どうでしたか.

title: Someone, something, somewhere, sometime
meaning: Question word + か: some ... . 何か (something), だれか (someone), どこか (somewhere), いつか (sometime).
when: Use it when you mean one that is not named: 何か飲みませんか (Would you like something to drink?), だれか来ましたよ (Someone's here), いつか日本に住みたいです (Someday I'd like to live in Japan). In a question, 何か and だれか cover "anything" and "anyone" too: 何か質問はありますか.
why: か marks something as open, not settled, as it does at the end of a question. On a question word it keeps the word's open slot but stops the question: 何 asks "what?", 何か says "some thing, I'm not saying which". が and を after these words are usually left out: 何か食べましたか. Other particles are kept, after か: どこかへ行きましたか, だれかと話しました. These words mean an unnamed person, thing, place or time, and can appear in positive and negative sentences and in questions: 何か足りません, "something is missing". They do not themselves mean "nothing" or "nobody"; for those, Japanese uses the question word with も and a negative: 何も食べません.

formation.form: 何か / だれか / どこか / いつか
formation.note: Something, someone, somewhere, sometime. 何か is read なにか.

formation.form: Question word + か (が / を dropped)

どこかへ, どこかに, だれかと.

title: Any ..., whatever, whenever
meaning: Question word + でも: any at all, no matter which. 何でも (anything), いつでも (any time), だれでも (anyone).
when: Use it to say the choice does not matter because every option is fine: 私は何でも食べます (I'll eat anything); いつでも電話してください; 「どれがいいですか。」「どれでもいいです。」 The basic use is with a positive statement.
why: でも here means "even": 何でも is "even what(ever)". If the statement holds even for the least likely choice, it holds for every choice, which gives "any, no matter which". That leaves the choice to the listener: どれでもいいです, "any one is fine". が and を are dropped: 何でも食べます. These words can appear with a negative too, but they never mean "none": 何でも食べません does not mean "I eat nothing". For that, the question word takes も: 何も食べません.

formation.form: 何でも / だれでも / いつでも / どこでも / どれでも
formation.note: Anything, anyone, any time, anywhere, any one of several. 何でも is read なんでも.

title: Nobody, nothing, nowhere
meaning: Question word + も + negative: no one, nothing, nowhere. だれもいません, 何も食べません, どこにも行きません.
when: Use it for a complete no: 教室にはだれもいません (There's no one in the classroom); 冷蔵庫に何もありません; 日曜日はどこにも行きませんでした. The verb or adjective at the end must be negative.
why: も means "also, even". On a question word it covers every possible answer, and with a negative it says the negative is true of each one: not this person, not that one, nobody. That is why the verb must be negative. が and を are dropped (だれもいません, 何も食べません), but other particles are kept, before も: どこにも, どこへも, だれにも, だれとも. For the "nobody, nothing" meaning taught here, the ending must be negative. だれも also has positive uses meaning "everyone", usually as だれもが, but that is a later point; みんな is the simple way to say "everyone".

formation.note: Nobody.
Nothing. 何も is read なにも.

formation.form: どこにも／どこへも + negative
formation.note: Nowhere. The particle stays, before も. In speech どこも is also heard.

title: Giving (to someone else)
meaning: AはBにNをあげる: A gives N to B. Used for giving by the speaker, or between others; not for giving to the speaker.
when: Use it when you, or someone else, give something to another person: 私は友だちにプレゼントをあげました; 田中さんは山田さんに花をあげました. It is not used when the receiver is you; for that, use くれる. You can use it for your own gift to your family: 私は妹に本をあげました.
why: Japanese chooses its verb of giving by the direction the thing moves, seen from the speaker. あげる is for giving by the speaker to someone else, or between other people when the gift is not seen as coming toward the speaker. Giving to the speaker takes くれる, and so, normally, does giving to someone close to the speaker when the speaker sides with that person (友だちが妹にお菓子をくれました). So 友だちが私に本をあげました is wrong: the book is coming to me. The receiver is marked with に and the thing with を. Toward someone above you, such as a teacher, あげる can sound like doing them a favour; the respectful verb is さしあげる (N4). For animals and plants, あげる is widely used (犬に水をあげる), and やる is also heard.

formation.form: Giver は Receiver に Thing を あげる
formation.note: Polite: あげます. The receiver is not the speaker; it can be the speaker's family, when the speaker is the giver.

mistake.problem: The chocolate comes to the speaker, so the verb is くれる. あげる is not used for giving to the speaker.
mistake.right: 友だちが私にチョコレートをくれました。

distinguish_from.note: くれる is giving that comes to the speaker, or to someone the speaker sides with: 友だちが本をくれました.
もらう tells the event from the receiver's side: 山田さんは田中さんに花をもらいました.
～てあげる is doing something for someone, with the same direction as あげる.

listed.item: Noun を あげる (Noun wo ageru)

review.note: Question: is the remark that あげる to someone above you can sound like doing them a favour accurate and N5-appropriate? Revised after the first gpt-6-astra review to meet its objection (see reviews).

reviews.note: The absolute exclusion of recipients on the speaker's side is incorrect. 私は妹に本をあげました is natural, and family membership alone does not require くれる. Replace the meaning and directional explanation with: 'あげる describes giving by the speaker to someone else, or giving between other people without presenting it as coming toward the speaker's viewpoint. For giving to the speaker, normally use くれる. For giving to someone close to the speaker, くれる is used when the speaker adopts that recipient's viewpoint; あげる can also be possible.' Replace the formation note with: 'Polite: あげます. In ordinary speaker-centered narration, the recipient is not the speaker; the recipient may be a family member.' In the mistake diagnosis, replace 'あげる only moves away from the speaker’s side' with 'あげる is not normally used for giving to the speaker in this sentence'.

title: Someone gives (to me or my side)
meaning: AがNをくれる: A gives N to me, or to someone on my side. The thing moves toward the speaker.
when: Use it when someone gives something to you or to someone close to you, such as your family: 友だちが本をくれました; 田中さんが妹にお菓子をくれました. 私に is usually left out, because くれる already says it came to you.
why: くれる is the inward verb of giving: the thing moves toward the speaker's side. Because the verb itself says where it went, 私に is normally left out: 友だちが本をくれました already means "gave me". The speaker's side is the speaker and the people the speaker counts as their own, such as family, as against the giver. Giving the other way, from you to someone, takes あげる. For someone above you giving to you, the respectful verb is くださる (N4).

formation.form: Giver が／は (Receiver に) Thing を くれる
formation.note: Polite: くれます. The receiver is the speaker or someone on the speaker's side; 私に is usually left out.

mistake.right: 私は友だちに花をあげました。

～てくれる is someone doing something for you, with the same direction as くれる.

listed.item: ～が 私に くれます (〜ga watashi ni kuremasu)
Noun を くれる (Noun wo kureru)

review.note: Question: is "the speaker's side" explained well enough for N5 without going into in-group and out-group in detail?

title: Receiving: getting something from someone
meaning: AはBに／からNをもらう: A receives N from B. The receiver is the subject, and the event is told from their side.
when: Use it to tell a gift from the receiver's point of view: 私は友だちに本をもらいました; 母から手紙をもらいました. The receiver can be you, someone close to you, or someone else. When the gift comes to you, the same event can also be told with くれる.
why: もらう makes the receiver the subject, so the sentence is about the person who got something. The giver is marked with に or から. から marks the source explicitly, and is generally the safest choice when the giver is a group such as a school or a company: 学校から手紙をもらいました. に is also possible when the group is treated as the one giving. The same event can be told with different subjects: 友だちが本をくれました makes the giver the subject and presents the gift as coming toward me; 私は友だちに本をもらいました makes me, the receiver, the subject. When the speaker is the one giving, あげる is the usual way to tell it; that is a matter of viewpoint, not a strict ban, and 私から何をもらいたいですか is natural. For receiving from someone above you, the humble verb is いただく (N4).

formation.form: Receiver は Giver に Thing を もらう
formation.note: Polite: もらいます.

formation.form: Receiver は Giver から Thing を もらう
formation.note: から marks the source explicitly, and is generally preferred with a school, a company or another group, though に is also possible.

examples.japanese: 私は友だちに本をもらいました。
examples.reading: わたしはともだちにほんをもらいました。
